check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the better that person is”. “Better” is still heard as the comparative of “good”, the word the argument has just used twice.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek words for “human being” and “a person” do not single out a man, but the draft had “he”, “him” and “himself” throughout chapter 15.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now uses “a human being”, “a person” and “they” throughout, as in the passages settled earlier.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek has a strengthened “if” (“if indeed”), which the draft gave as a bare “if”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “if these things really were goods”.

passages.greek: Ἀρκεῖται πᾶσα φύσις ἑαυτῇ εὐοδούσῃ, φύσις δὲ λογικὴ εὐοδεῖ ἐν μὲν φαντασίαις μήτε ψευδεῖ μήτε ἀδήλῳ συγκατατιθεμένη, τὰς ὁρμὰς δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ κοινωνικὰ ἔργα μόνα ἀπευθύνουσα, τὰς ὀρέξεις δὲ καὶ τὰς ἐκκλίσεις τῶν ἐφ’ ἡμῖν μόνων πεποιημένη, τὸ δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως ἀπονεμόμενον πᾶν ἀσπαζομένη· μέρος γὰρ αὐτῆς ἐστιν ὡς ἡ τοῦ φύλλου φύσις τῆς τοῦ φυτοῦ φύσεως· πλὴν ὅτι ἐκεῖ μὲν ἡ τοῦ φύλλου φύσις μέρος ἐστὶ φύσεως καὶ ἀναισθήτου καὶ ἀλόγου καὶ ἐμποδίζεσθαι δυναμένης, ἡ δὲ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσις μέρος ἐστὶν ἀνεμποδίστου φύσεως καὶ νοερᾶς καὶ δικαίας, εἴγε ἴσους καὶ κατ’ ἀξίαν τοὺς μερισμοὺς χρόνων, οὐσίας, αἰτίου, ἐνεργείας, συμβάσεως ἑκάστοις ποιεῖται. σκόπει δέ, μὴ εἰ τὸ ἓν πρὸς τὸ ἓν ἴσον εὑρήσεις ἐπὶ παντός, ἀλλὰ εἰ συλλήβδην τὰ πάντα τοῦδε πρὸς ἀθρόα τὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου.
passages.english: Every nature is content with itself when its road goes well. And a rational nature’s road goes well when, among its impressions, it assents to nothing false and nothing unclear; when it directs its impulses only to social acts; when it has confined its desires and aversions to the things that are up to us alone; and when it welcomes everything allotted by the common nature. For it is a part of that nature, as the nature of the leaf is a part of the nature of the plant; except that there the nature of the leaf is part of a nature that is without sensation, without reason, and able to be hindered, while the nature of the human being is part of a nature that is unhindered, has mind and is just, seeing that it makes the apportionments of time, substance, cause, activity and circumstance equal for each thing and according to what each deserves. But look, not at whether you will find one thing equal to one thing in every case, but at whether all that belongs to this one, taken together, is equal to the whole of what belongs to the other.

notes.note: The verb literally means “to have a good road” and commonly just “to prosper”. The road is kept, since road language runs through the neighbouring passages.
notes.other_reading: Every nature is content with itself when it prospers

notes.note: “Assent” is the Stoic term for accepting an impression as true. The second adjective means “not evident”, what has not been made clear.
notes.other_reading: assenting neither to what is false nor to what is not evident

notes.note: The adjective means “belonging to fellowship or community”. “Social” is the word used for it throughout this translation; it does not mean sociable. The noun is literally “works”.
notes.other_reading: works that serve the community

notes.greek: τὰς ὀρέξεις δὲ καὶ τὰς ἐκκλίσεις
notes.note: Two Stoic terms, literally “reachings-for and turnings-away”. The Greek says the rational nature “has made them of the things up to us only”; “confined … to” is the English for that.
notes.other_reading: when it has made its desires and avoidances to be only of the things in our power

notes.note: The nature common to all things, that is, the nature of the whole. “The common nature” is kept wherever this phrase occurs.
notes.other_reading: by universal nature

notes.note: An adjective from the Greek noun for mind: “having mind”. “Mind” is kept for this root throughout the translation.
notes.other_reading: a nature that is unhindered, intelligent and just

notes.note: Either “seeing that” (giving the ground for calling it just) or “if, that is” (a condition, which the closing “But look” would then help to test). The English takes it as the ground.
notes.other_reading: if, that is, it makes the apportionments equal for each thing

notes.note: A bare list. The first word is a plural, “times”, that is, spans of time. “Substance” is the stuff a thing is made of and “cause” the forming principle in it, a pair Marcus uses often; the last word means what befalls a thing.
notes.other_reading: of spans of time, matter, form, activity and what happens

notes.greek: συλλήβδην τὰ πάντα τοῦδε πρὸς ἀθρόα τὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου
notes.note: The Greek is compressed and has no adjective here; “is equal” is carried over from the clause before.
notes.other_reading: but whether, taken all together, the whole of this one against the total of the other

check.note: The Greek is “has made”: it has made its desires and aversions be of the things up to us alone. “Kept … for” suggests saving something up, where the Greek is about confining.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “when it has confined its desires and aversions to the things that are up to us alone”. “Alone” keeps the Greek “only”.

check.note: The Greek has two coordinate qualities joined by “and”: the apportionments are equal and according to worth. The English dropped “and” and made the second a trailing qualifier.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “it makes the apportionments of time, substance, cause, activity and circumstance equal for each thing and according to what each deserves”. Both qualities are joined by “and”, and both are what the common nature makes the apportionments be, as the Greek word order has it.

check.note: The word can give a ground (“seeing that”) or a real condition (“if, that is”); the English takes it as settled fact, though the following “But look” would also suit the condition.
check.decided: Declined: “Seeing that” stays. With a plain statement of fact after it this word commonly gives a ground that is taken as granted, and the sentence has just called that nature just without qualification. The note sets out the conditional reading and what speaks for it.

check.note: “Social works” is not natural English and may suggest social work or charity.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “social acts”, which removes the echo of “social work”. “Social” stays because it is the one word used for this Greek adjective across the translation, and the note says what it means.

check.note: The literal plural “of times” reads oddly in an English list of abstract nouns.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “of time”. The note records that the Greek is a plural, spans of time.

check.greek: τὸ δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως ἀπονεμόμενον πᾶν ἀσπαζομένη
check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “everything allotted to it”, but the Greek has no “to it”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “everything allotted by the common nature”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “intelligent” for an adjective built on the Greek noun for mind, where the passages settled earlier keep “mind” for this root.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a nature that is unhindered, has mind and is just”, and a note gives “intelligent” as the other wording.

passages.greek: Μὴ περιβλέπου ἀλλότρια ἡγεμονικά, ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖ βλέπε κατ’ εὐθὺ ἐπὶ τί σε ἡ φύσις ὁδηγεῖ, ἥ τε τοῦ ὅλου διὰ τῶν συμβαινόντων σοι καὶ ἡ σὴ διὰ τῶν πρακτέων ὑπὸ σοῦ· πρακτέον δὲ ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ κατασκευῇ· κατεσκεύασται δὲ τὰ μὲν λοιπὰ τῶν λογικῶν ἕνεκεν, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐπὶ παντὸς ἄλλου τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν, τὰ δὲ λογικὰ ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν. τὸ μὲν οὖν προηγούμενον ἐν τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κατασκευῇ τὸ κοινωνικόν ἐστι, δεύτερον δὲ τὸ ἀνένδοτον πρὸς τὰς σωματικὰς πείσεις· λογικῆς γὰρ καὶ νοερᾶς κινήσεως ἴδιον περιορίζειν ἑαυτὴν καὶ μήποτε ἡττᾶσθαι μήτε αἰσθητικῆς μήτε ὁρμητικῆς κινήσεως· ζῳώδεις γὰρ ἑκάτεραι, ἡ δὲ νοερὰ ἐθέλει πρωτιστεύειν καὶ μὴ κατακρατεῖσθαι ὑπ’ ἐκείνων. δικαίως γε· πέφυκε γὰρ χρηστικὴ πᾶσιν ἐκείνοις. τρίτον ἐν τῇ λογικῇ κατασκευῇ τὸ ἀπρόπτωτον καὶ ἀνεξαπάτητον. τούτων οὖν ἐχόμενον τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν εὐθεῖαν περαινέτω καὶ ἔχει τὰ ἑαυτοῦ.
passages.english: Do not look around at other people’s ruling parts, but look straight ahead to where nature is leading you, both the nature of the whole, through the things that happen to you, and your own nature, through the things you have to do. What each being has to do is what follows from its make-up. Now everything else has been made for the sake of the rational beings, just as in every other case the inferior things are for the sake of the superior, and the rational beings have been made for the sake of one another. So what comes first in the human make-up is being social. Second is not giving way to what the body undergoes; for it is proper to movement that is rational and of mind to draw a boundary around itself and never to be beaten by the movement of the senses or the movement of impulse. For both of those are of the animal kind, while the movement of mind wants to hold first place and not to be overpowered by them. And rightly so, for it is by nature fitted to make use of all of those. Third in the rational make-up is not being hasty and not being deceived. So let the ruling part hold to these and carry its straight road through, and it has what is its own.

notes.note: The Stoic term for the commanding part of the soul, rendered “the ruling part”. The plural is unusual in English.
notes.other_reading: Do not look around at what rules in other people

notes.note: Literally “guides along a road”, which prepares the “straight road” at the end of the passage.
notes.other_reading: to where nature is guiding you on your road

notes.note: The noun means how a thing is constructed, and the verb from the same root follows at once. “Make-up” and “made” are used so the link shows.
notes.other_reading: what is in line with its constitution

notes.note: Literally “what goes in front”: first in rank among the features of the human make-up, with “second” and “third” following. “What comes first” is used for this word here and in 5.20 and 4.1.
notes.other_reading: So the principal thing in the constitution of a human being

notes.note: A neuter adjective used as a noun: “the social”, the fact of being made for fellowship. The English turns it as “being social”.
notes.other_reading: is fellowship with others

notes.note: The noun means being acted on, as opposed to acting: here whatever the body is made to feel. “Undergo” is used for this word here and in 9.16.
notes.other_reading: not yielding to the feelings of the body

notes.note: The second adjective is built on the Greek noun for mind. “Of mind” is the wording kept for it throughout the translation.
notes.other_reading: for it is proper to rational and intelligent movement

notes.note: Literally “to mark a boundary round itself”. It can be heard as keeping itself apart or as keeping within its own limits.
notes.other_reading: to keep itself within its own limits

notes.note: The first is a Stoic term, literally “not falling forward”, meaning not assenting before one should. “Hasty” is used for this root here and in 11.10.
notes.other_reading: freedom from rash assent and from being deceived

notes.greek: εὐθεῖαν περαινέτω καὶ ἔχει τὰ ἑαυτοῦ
notes.note: “Straight” is a feminine adjective with “road” understood, and the verb means to carry a thing through to completion. The last verb is a plain present, “it has”, not a future or a command.
notes.other_reading: let it finish a straight course, and it is in possession of what belongs to it

check.greek: ἐκεῖ βλέπε κατ’ εὐθὺ ἐπὶ τί
check.note: The Greek is directional: “look straight there, to where nature is guiding you”. “At this: what” turns a direction into a topic.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “look straight ahead to where nature is leading you”, which keeps the direction and fits the road image of the verb.

check.note: Found while settling: the same Greek word was “the leading thing” here and “leading aim” in 5.20 and 4.1, where “aim” was questioned.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “what comes first in the human make-up”, which counts on naturally to “Second” and “Third”, and the same words are used in 5.20 and 4.1.

check.greek: λογικῆς γὰρ καὶ νοερᾶς κινήσεως ἴδιον
check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “intelligent” for the adjective built on the Greek noun for mind, and “it belongs to” for the word rendered “proper to” in 8.26.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “it is proper to movement that is rational and of mind” and, further on, “the movement of mind”, so that “mind” is kept for this root as in the passages settled earlier.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “go straight on to the end of its road”, which can be heard as going on until death; the Greek verb means to carry a thing through.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “carry its straight road through”, in line with “is carried through” for the same verb in the passages settled earlier.

passages.greek: Τὸ μὲν πνευμάτιόν σου καὶ τὸ πυρῶδες πᾶν, ὅσον ἐγκέκραται, καίτοι φύσει ἀνωφερῆ ὄντα, ὅμως πειθόμενα τῇ τῶν ὅλων διατάξει παρακρατεῖται ἐνταῦθα ἐπὶ τοῦ συγκρίματος. καὶ τὸ γεῶδες δὲ τὸ ἐν σοὶ πᾶν καὶ τὸ ὑγρόν, καίτοι κατωφερῆ ὄντα, ὅμως ἐγήγερται καὶ ἕστηκε τὴν οὐχ ἑαυτῶν φυσικὴν στάσιν. οὕτως ἄρα καὶ τὰ στοιχεῖα ὑπακούει τοῖς ὅλοις, ἐπειδάν που καταταχθῇ σὺν βίᾳ, μένοντα μέχρις ἂν ἐκεῖθεν πάλιν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον τῆς διαλύσεως σημήνῃ. οὐ δεινὸν οὖν μόνον τὸ νοερόν σου μέρος ἀπειθὲς εἶναι καὶ ἀγανακτεῖν τῇ ἑαυτοῦ χώρᾳ; καίτοι οὐδέν γε βίαιον τούτῳ ἐπιτάσσεται, ἀλλὰ μόνα ὅσα κατὰ φύσιν ἐστὶν αὐτῷ· οὐ μέντοι ἀνέχεται, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐναντίαν φέρεται. ἡ γὰρ ἐπὶ τὰ ἀδικήματα καὶ τὰ ἀκολαστήματα καὶ τὰς ὀργὰς καὶ τὰς λύπας καὶ τοὺς φόβους κίνησις οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ ἀφισταμένου τῆς φύσεως. καὶ ὅταν δέ τινι τῶν συμβαινόντων δυσχεραίνῃ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, καταλείπει καὶ τότε τὴν ἑαυτοῦ χώραν· πρὸς ὁσιότητα γὰρ καὶ θεοσέβειαν κατεσκεύασται οὐχ ἧττον ἢ πρὸς δικαιοσύνην. καὶ γὰρ ταῦτα ἐν εἴδει ἐστὶ τῆς εὐκοινωνησίας, μᾶλλον δὲ πρεσβύτερα τῶν δικαιοπραγημάτων.
passages.english: Your bit of breath and all the fiery part that is mixed into you, though by nature they tend upwards, all the same obey the ordering of the whole and are held here in the compound. And all the earthy part in you, and the wet, though they tend downwards, have all the same been raised up and stand in a position that is not naturally theirs. So even the elements heed the whole: once they have been posted somewhere by force, they stay until, from there in turn, the signal for dissolution is given. Is it not terrible, then, that only the part of you that is of mind is disobedient and resents its own post? And yet nothing forced is ordered of it, only the things that are in accordance with its nature. Still it does not bear them, but is carried the opposite way. For the movement towards acts of injustice and acts of self-indulgence, towards angers and griefs and fears, is nothing other than the movement of one who is deserting nature. And whenever the ruling part is discontented with any of the things that happen, then too it leaves its own post. For it has been made for holiness and reverence for the gods no less than for justice. For these too come under good fellowship, or rather they come before acts of justice.

notes.note: A diminutive of the word for breath or air, one of the four elements in the body here. The diminutive is slightly belittling.
notes.other_reading: Your little portion of air

notes.note: The Greek has a plural, “the wholes”, Marcus’s usual phrase for the universe, rendered “the whole” throughout. The noun means an arrangement and is used of troops drawn up; “ordering” is meant to carry both arranging and commanding, since “posted” and “ordered” further on are from the same root.
notes.other_reading: the arrangement of the universe

notes.note: “The compound” is the body seen as a mixture of the elements.
notes.other_reading: here in the mixture that is you

notes.note: A different verb from “obey” in the first sentence: literally “listen to”, “answer a call”. “Heed” keeps it apart from “obey” and “disobedient”, the pair the argument runs on.
notes.other_reading: So even the elements obey the whole

notes.note: The verb is a military one, “to be posted”. “By force” can go with being posted, as the edition punctuates, or with staying.
notes.other_reading: once they have been posted somewhere, they stay there under force until

notes.greek: ἐκεῖθεν πάλιν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον τῆς διαλύσεως σημήνῃ
notes.note: The noun is the note given to start a song or a movement, a cue. “From there” is from the whole that posted them, and the adverb is taken as “in turn” (the order that posted them is answered by one that breaks them up), not as “a second time”. The verb has no stated subject.
notes.other_reading: until from there the cue is given for them to be dissolved back again

notes.note: The adjective is built on the Greek noun for mind. “Of mind” is the wording kept for it throughout the translation.
notes.other_reading: only the intelligent part of you

notes.note: The word means “place”, and also a soldier’s station. “Post” is taken because of the military verbs around it, and kept for the second occurrence.
notes.other_reading: resents its own place

notes.note: Literally “of one standing away from nature”. The verb is used of rebels and deserters, and that sense is taken.
notes.other_reading: of one who is withdrawing from nature

notes.note: A compound, “god-reverence”, that does not say whether one god or many is meant. The plural is taken, as in “the eldest of the gods” in 9.1.
notes.other_reading: reverence for god

notes.note: Literally “are in the form of good fellowship”, that is, are a kind of it. The noun is very rare; it is built on the root of the word rendered “social” elsewhere.
notes.other_reading: For these too are a kind of good fellowship

notes.note: Literally “older than”, which in Greek also means higher in rank or more to be honoured. “Come before” is meant to allow both.
notes.other_reading: or rather they are older than acts of justice

check.note: The Greek word names a tendency (“downward-tending”), parallel to “upward-tending” above. “Though they sink downwards” says they do sink, which the next words contradict.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “though they tend downwards”, and the first sentence reads “though by nature they tend upwards” so that the two match as they do in the Greek.

check.greek: μέχρις ἂν ἐκεῖθεν πάλιν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον τῆς διαλύσεως σημήνῃ
check.note: The adverb here is “back”, “in turn”, not “a second time”, so “sounds again” wrongly implies the signal has sounded before. “From that side” is vague for “from there”, the whole that posted them.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “they stay until, from there in turn, the signal for dissolution is given”. “Dissolution” is kept, and not the suggested “release”, because the Greek noun is the breaking up of the compound named in the first sentence.

check.greek: ἐπειδάν που καταταχθῇ σὺν βίᾳ, μένοντα
check.note: “By force” can go with being posted, as the comma in this text has it, or with staying; the second puts the force in the staying.
check.decided: Declined: “Once they have been posted somewhere by force, they stay” stands, since it follows the punctuation of the Greek as given, and a posting by force answers the “position that is not naturally theirs” of the sentence before. The note gives the other reading.

check.note: “Obey” and “disobedient” translate one Greek pair on which the argument runs; this is a different verb (“heed”, “answer the call”) and was also given as “obey”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “So even the elements heed the whole”, so that “obey” and “disobedient” are left to the one Greek pair. “Heed” is preferred to the suggested “answer to”, which in English suggests being held to account.

check.note: The Greek is a word of command (“is ordered”), part of a military run of words in the passage; “laid on” loses the order.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “nothing forced is ordered of it”. For the same reason “arrangement” in the first sentence is now “ordering”, a noun from the same Greek root.

check.note: “Senior to” is office English and unclear here; the Greek is “older than”, “ranking before”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “or rather they come before acts of justice”, which can be heard of time or of rank, as the Greek can.

check.note: The first half of the compound does not fix a number; “reverence for god” is equally possible.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Reverence for the gods” stays, since the plural is how Marcus speaks in the neighbouring passages (“the eldest of the gods” in 9.1), and “the divine” would be a third thing the word does not say. A note now records that the Greek leaves the number open.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “the intelligent part of you” for the adjective built on the Greek noun for mind.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the part of you that is of mind”, keeping “mind” for this root as in the passages settled earlier.

passages.greek: Καθ’ ἕτερον μὲν λόγον ἡμῖν ἐστιν οἰκειότατον ἄνθρωπος, καθ’ ὅσον εὖ ποιητέον αὐτοὺς καὶ ἀνεκτέον· καθ̓ ὅσον δὲ ἐνίστανταί τινες εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα ἔργα, ἕν τι τῶν ἀδιαφόρων μοι γίνεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὐχ ἧσσον ἢ ἥλιος ἢ ἄνεμος ἢ θηρίον. ὑπὸ τούτων δὲ ἐνέργεια μέν τις ἐμποδισθείη ἄν, ὁρμῆς δὲ καὶ διαθέσεως οὐ γίνεται ἐμπόδια διὰ τὴν ὑπεξαίρεσιν καὶ τὴν περιτροπήν. περιτρέπει γὰρ καὶ μεθίστησι πᾶν τὸ τῆς ἐνεργείας κώλυμα ἡ διάνοια εἰς τὸ προηγούμενον καὶ πρὸ ἔργου γίνεται τὸ τοῦ ἔργου τούτου ἐφεκτικὸν καὶ πρὸ ὁδοῦ τὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ ταύτης ἐνστατικόν.
passages.english: In one respect nothing is more our own than a human being, in so far as we must do good to them and bear with them. But in so far as some of them stand in the way of the works that are our own, a human being becomes for me one of the indifferent things, no less than sun or wind or wild animal. By these an activity may be hindered, but there are no hindrances to impulse and disposition, because of the proviso and the turning round. For the mind turns round every obstacle to its activity and shifts it into what comes first, and what holds back this work becomes a help to the work, and what stands in this road becomes a way forward on the road.

notes.note: The superlative of “one’s own, akin”: literally “a human being is the thing most our own”. The same adjective comes back in “the works that are our own”, so “own” is kept in both places.
notes.other_reading: a human being is the thing closest to us

notes.note: The Greek says only “the own works” without saying whose. They are taken as ours, following “us” before, though “me” follows.
notes.other_reading: stand in the way of my proper works

notes.note: The Stoic term for things that are neither good nor bad in themselves.
notes.other_reading: one of the things that make no difference

notes.greek: διὰ τὴν ὑπεξαίρεσιν καὶ τὴν περιτροπήν
notes.note: Two technical words. The first is literally “an exception made beforehand”: aiming at a thing with the proviso “if nothing prevents”, so that being prevented does not defeat the impulse. “Turning round” is explained by the next sentence, which uses the verb from the same root.
notes.other_reading: because it acts with reservation and can reverse things

notes.note: Literally “into what goes in front”: the obstacle itself becomes the mind’s first business. It can also be heard as “what leads forward”, something that furthers the activity, or as “something to be preferred”. “What comes first” is used for this word here and in 7.55 and 4.1.
notes.other_reading: and shifts it into something that furthers the activity

notes.greek: πρὸ ἔργου γίνεται τὸ τοῦ ἔργου τούτου ἐφεκτικὸν καὶ πρὸ ὁδοῦ τὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ ταύτης ἐνστατικόν
notes.note: Two idioms are played on: “for the work” means “useful” and “forward on the road” means “helpful”. The Greek sets each against “this work” and “this road”, and the English keeps “work” and “road” in both halves so the play shows.
notes.other_reading: what checks this work becomes useful, and what blocks this road helps one along

check.note: The link with “works that are our own” is kept, but “a human being is what is most our own” is not clear English; the sense is “closest to us”, “most akin”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “nothing is more our own than a human being”, which says the same as the Greek superlative in a clearer sentence. “Own” is kept, and not the suggested “closest to us”, because the same Greek adjective returns in “the works that are our own”; the note gives “closest to us”.

check.greek: διὰ τὴν ὑπεξαίρεσιν καὶ τὴν περιτροπήν
check.note: Two bare abstract nouns that a reader of today cannot unpack; “reservation” suggests hesitation or misgiving, where the Greek means acting on a proviso (“if nothing prevents”).
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “because of the proviso and the turning round”. “Proviso” replaces “reservation”, here and in 4.1; the two nouns are kept as nouns, without the suggested “the mind acts”, because the Greek names no subject here and the note and the next sentence explain them.

check.note: The Greek can be “what it is chiefly aiming at”, as the English had it with an added “its”, or “what leads forward”, something that advances the action, which fits the next clause.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “shifts it into what comes first”, without the added “its” and “aim”, and the same words are used for this Greek word in 7.55 and 4.1. The suggested “something that furthers it” is given in the note as the other reading, since the word’s plain sense is going first.

check.greek: πρὸ ἔργου γίνεται τὸ τοῦ ἔργου τούτου ἐφεκτικὸν καὶ πρὸ ὁδοῦ τὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ ταύτης ἐνστατικόν
check.note: The two Greek phrases are stronger than “something for”: “in aid of the work”, “forward along the road”. The English left the point, that the obstacle becomes a help, faint.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “what holds back this work becomes a help to the work, and what stands in this road becomes a way forward on the road”. The present tense is kept, since the Greek has adjectives here and no past.

passages.greek:
Εὐφροσύνη ἀνθρώπου ποιεῖν τὰ ἴδια ἀνθρώπου, ἴδιον δὲ ἀνθρώπου εὔνοια πρὸς τὸ ὁμόφυλον, ὑπερόρασις τῶν αἰσθητικῶν κινήσεων, διάκρισις τῶν πιθανῶν φαντασιῶν, ἐπιθεώρησις τῆς τῶν ὅλων φύσεως καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὴν γινομένων.

Τρεῖς σχέσεις· ἡ μὲν πρὸς τὸ ἀγγεῖον τὸ περικείμενον, ἡ δὲ πρὸς τὴν θείαν αἰτίαν, ἀφ’ ἧς συμβαίνει πᾶσι πάντα, ἡ δὲ πρὸς τοὺς συμβιοῦντας.
passages.english:
A human being’s joy is to do what is proper to a human being. And what is proper to a human being is goodwill towards their own kind, looking down on the movements of the senses, telling the persuasive impressions apart, and contemplating the nature of the whole and the things that come about in accordance with it.

Three relations: one to the surrounding vessel, one to the divine cause, from which all things happen to all, one to those with whom life is shared.

notes.note: The adjective means “peculiar to, belonging specially to”. It is repeated in the singular in the next clause, and “proper to” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: to do the things that are a human being’s own

notes.note: The noun is literally “looking over the top of”, and so disdain. “Movements of the senses” are the stirrings that sensation sets up.
notes.other_reading: disregard for the stirrings of the senses

notes.note: Literally “a telling apart of the persuasive impressions”. It is open whether this means judging among them or telling them from true ones.
notes.other_reading: sorting the merely plausible impressions from the true

notes.note: Chapter 27 begins here; it is a bare list with no verb. The noun means a standing relation to something.
notes.other_reading: Three ties

notes.note: “The vessel set around” is the body. From memory, unchecked: the manuscripts have a different word here, “cause”, and “vessel” is a correction that editors print.
notes.other_reading: one to the body that encloses us

notes.note: Literally “towards those living together with”. The Greek names no person, so the English is kept impersonal.
notes.other_reading: one to the people you live among

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “goodwill towards his own kind”, but the Greek has no “his” and speaks of a human being, not of a man.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “goodwill towards their own kind”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “sorting out the impressions that seem convincing”. “Sorting out” can be heard as settling a difficulty, and “seem” is not in the Greek, which has one adjective, “persuasive”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “telling the persuasive impressions apart”, in line with “tell false things from true” for the verb of the same root in 9.1.

passages.greek: Ὥσπερ τὰς ἄλλας δυνάμεις ἑκάστῳ τῶν λογικῶν σχεδὸν ὅσον ἡ τῶν λογικῶν φύσις, οὕτως καὶ ταύτην παῤ αὐτῆς εἰλήφαμεν. ὃν τρόπον γὰρ ἐκείνη πᾶν τὸ ἐνιστάμενον καὶ ἀντιβαῖνον ἐπιπεριτρέπει καὶ κατατάσσει εἰς τὴν εἱμαρμένην καὶ μέρος ἑαυτῆς ποιεῖ, οὕτως καὶ τὸ λογικὸν ζῷον δύναται πᾶν κώλυμα ὕλην ἑαυτοῦ ποιεῖν καὶ χρῆσθαι αὐτῷ, ἐφ’ οἷον ἂν καὶ ὥρμησεν.
passages.english: Just as the nature of rational beings [has given] each of the rational beings its other powers […], so we have received this one too from it. For in the way that that nature turns round everything that stands in its way and goes against it, gives it a place in what is fated, and makes it a part of itself, so too the rational animal can make every obstacle into material for itself and use it for whatever its impulse was set on.

notes.greek: Ὥσπερ τὰς ἄλλας δυνάμεις ἑκάστῳ τῶν λογικῶν σχεδὸν ὅσον ἡ τῶν λογικῶν φύσις
notes.note: The Greek is damaged here: the clause has no verb. “Has given” is supplied, in square brackets, on the strength of “we have received … from it” in the second half. From memory, unchecked: editors treat the sentence as corrupt or as having lost some words.
notes.other_reading: Just as each of the rational beings has had nearly all its other powers from the nature of rational beings, so we have received this one too from it

notes.note: These two words, literally “almost as much as”, do not join to anything in the sentence as it stands. They are left untranslated, and their place is marked by the bracketed dots.
notes.other_reading: its other powers, almost as many as the nature of rational beings itself has

notes.note: “This one” points forward to the power described in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: so we have received the following power too from it

notes.note: On the Greek as given, “that nature” is the nature of rational beings named in the first sentence. But what is said of it, that it gives every obstacle a place in what is fated and makes it a part of itself, is what Marcus says elsewhere of the nature of the whole. From memory, unchecked: editors have proposed “of the whole” in place of the second “of rational beings”.
notes.other_reading: For in the way that the nature of the whole turns round everything that stands in its way

notes.note: A compound of the verb “turns round” used in 5.20, and the same English is kept.
notes.other_reading: turns to its own purpose

notes.note: Literally “posts it into the fated”, into the order of what is destined.
notes.other_reading: fits it into destiny

notes.note: The verb is the one behind “impulse”. Literally “towards whatever sort of thing it had set out”.
notes.other_reading: for whatever purpose it had set out on

check.greek: Ὥσπερ τὰς ἄλλας δυνάμεις ἑκάστῳ τῶν λογικῶν σχεδὸν ὅσον ἡ τῶν λογικῶν φύσις
check.note: The Greek as given has no verb in this clause, and the words “almost as much as” do not construe. The English supplied “has had”, made “each” the subject and turned those words into “nearly all”, with no sign that the text is broken.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Just as the nature of rational beings [has given] each of the rational beings its other powers […], so we have received this one too from it”. The supplied verb stands in square brackets, the two words that cannot be construed are left out and their place marked, and two notes say plainly that the Greek is damaged and what was supplied.

check.note: On the text as given “that nature” is the nature of rational beings, but what is said of it is what Marcus says of the nature of the whole. The English follows the given text, which is right, but the reader gets no warning.
check.decided: Accepted: “That nature” is kept, since it is what the Greek as given says. A note now warns that the description fits the nature of the whole and that, from memory and unchecked, editors have proposed “of the whole” here.

passages.greek:
Οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ πόνος τῇ χειρὶ οὐδὲ τῷ ποδὶ παρὰ φύσιν, μέχρις ἂν ποιῇ ὁ ποῦς τὰ τοῦ ποδὸς καὶ ἡ χεὶρ τὰ τῆς χειρός. οὕτως οὗν οὐδὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ὡς ἀνθρώπῳ παρὰ φύσιν ἐστὶν ὁ πόνος, μέχρις ἂν ποιῇ τὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου. εἰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν αὐτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν, οὐδὲ κακόν ἐστιν αὐτῷ.

Ἡλίκας ἡδονὰς ἥσθησαν λῃσταί, κίναιδοι, πατραλοῖαι, τύραννοι.
passages.english:
Pain is not against nature for the hand or for the foot, so long as the foot is doing the foot’s work and the hand the hand’s. So too for a human being, as a human being, pain is not against nature, so long as they are doing a human being’s work. And if it is not against nature for them, it is not bad for them either.

What great pleasures robbers, catamites, father-beaters, tyrants have enjoyed!

notes.note: The word covers hard labour and pain. The hand and foot at their work suggest “toil”; but the conclusion, that it is not bad, and the pleasures of the next chapter answer the question whether pain is an evil, and the same word is set against pleasure in 9.1. “Pain” is used in both passages.
notes.other_reading: Toil is not against nature for the hand or for the foot

notes.note: Literally “the things of the foot”. “Work” is supplied; the Greek has no noun.
notes.other_reading: so long as the foot does what belongs to a foot

notes.note: The adjective is the ordinary word for “bad”, used by the Stoics for what is truly an evil.
notes.other_reading: it is not an evil for them either

notes.note: Chapter 34 begins here: a single exclamation with no stated conclusion, and none is added.
notes.other_reading: How great are the pleasures that have been felt by

notes.note: An abusive word for a man who takes the passive part in sex with men, and more loosely for any man held to be sexually shameless. “Catamites” is the nearest single English word.
notes.other_reading: debauched men

notes.note: Literally “father-strikers”. The word is used both of those who beat a father and of those who kill one; the English stays with the literal sense.
notes.other_reading: parricides

check.note: The Greek word is both “toil” and “pain”. The conclusion, that it is not bad for him either, answers the question whether pain is an evil, and the same word is “pain” in 9.1; “toil” fits the image of hand and foot at work, “pain” fits the argument.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Pain is not against nature for the hand or for the foot”, and “pain” again in the next sentence, so that the word is the same here and in 9.1, where it is set against pleasure as it is in the next chapter here. The note says that the word also means toil and that the image leans that way.

check.note: The Greek is a specific and harsh word for a man who takes the passive sexual role; “debauched men” is general and softer.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “catamites”, the nearest single English word for the specific sense, with a note on what it means. The suggested “perverts” is not used, because it is as general as the word it would replace.

check.note: The word covers both striking and killing a father; “parricides” is the other reading and suits the company of robbers and tyrants.
check.decided: Declined: The English reads “father-beaters”, since the Greek word is literally “father-striker” and does not of itself say that the father is killed. The note gives “parricides” as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “he” and “him” for a human being, where the Greek does not single out a man.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “so long as they are doing a human being’s work” and “it is not bad for them either”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft turned the sentence into a passive (“have been enjoyed by”) with “men who” twice; the Greek is active, with four bare nouns as its subject.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “What great pleasures robbers, catamites, father-beaters, tyrants have enjoyed!”, active and with the bare list of the Greek.

passages.greek: Τὸ ἔνδον κυριεῦον, ὅταν κατὰ φύσιν ἔχῃ, οὕτως ἕστηκε πρὸς τὰ συμβαίνοντα, ὥστε ἀεὶ πρὸς τὸ δυνατὸν καὶ διδόμενον μετατίθεσθαι ῥᾳδίως. ὕλην γὰρ ἀποτεταγμένην οὐδεμίαν φιλεῖ, ἀλλὰ ὁρμᾷ μὲν πρὸς τὰ προηγούμενα μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως, τὸ δὲ ἀντεισαγόμενον ὕλην ἑαυτῷ ποιεῖ, ὥσπερ τὸ πῦρ, ὅταν ἐπικρατῇ τῶν ἐπεμπιπτόντων, ὑφ’ ὧν ἂν μικρός τις λύχνος ἐσβέσθη· τὸ δὲ λαμπρὸν πῦρ τάχιστα ἐξῳκείωσεν ἑαυτῷ τὰ ἐπιφορούμενα καὶ κατηνάλωσε καὶ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐκείνων ἐπὶ μεῖζον ἤρθη.
passages.english: The thing that is master within, when it is in accordance with nature, stands towards what happens in such a way that it always shifts easily to what is possible and given. For it is not fond of any assigned material, but directs its impulse towards the things that come first, with a proviso, and what is brought in instead it makes into material for itself, like fire when it masters the things that fall on it, things by which a small lamp would have been put out. But a bright fire very quickly makes what is heaped on it its own, consumes it, and from those very things rises higher.

notes.note: Literally “that which is lord within”, another way of naming the ruling part. It is kept distinct from the usual term.
notes.other_reading: The ruling power within us

notes.note: Literally “when it is in the state that accords with nature”.
notes.other_reading: when it is in its natural state

notes.note: The participle means “marked off, assigned”. The verb is “loves”, and can also mean “is used to”.
notes.other_reading: For it does not love any appointed material

notes.note: Literally “towards the things that go in front”: the things it aims at first, as against what is brought in instead. It can also be heard as the Stoic “preferred things”, though the usual word for those is a different participle. “What comes first” is used for this word here and in 7.55 and 5.20.
notes.other_reading: towards the things that are to be preferred

notes.note: Literally “an exception made beforehand”: aiming at a thing with the proviso “if nothing prevents”. “Proviso” is used here and in 5.20.
notes.other_reading: with reservation

notes.note: Literally “what is brought in instead”, that is, in place of the thing first aimed at. The prefix can also be heard as “against”: what is brought in to oppose it.
notes.other_reading: and whatever is brought in against it it makes into material for itself

notes.note: The verb is from the root “one’s own”. The three verbs here are past tenses used for what always happens, so the English puts them in the present.
notes.other_reading: has quickly taken over what was heaped on it

check.note: “With reservation” reads today as “hesitantly, with misgivings”; the Greek means acting on a proviso (if nothing prevents).
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “with a proviso”, the same word as in 5.20, and the note explains the proviso.

check.note: “One” and “for it” are added; the Greek is “it is fond of no set (assigned, definite) material”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “it is not fond of any assigned material”, without the added words. “Assigned” is used, and not the suggested “fixed”, because the Greek participle means marked off or allotted.

check.note: “Its” and “aims” are interpretation: the Greek is “the things that come first”, which can be its primary objects or the things that are preferable.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “towards the things that come first”, without “its” and “aims”, and with the same words as in 5.20 and 7.55. The suggested “the things it puts first” is not used because “it puts” is again an addition; the note gives the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “whatever is brought in against it”. The first sense of the Greek verb is “to bring in instead”, and that answers “the things that come first” in the clause before.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “what is brought in instead”, and the note keeps “brought in against it” as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “what is possible and what is given”, and dropped the “but” that joins the next two clauses; the Greek has one article for “possible and given” and a plain “but”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “what is possible and given” and “it is not fond of any assigned material, but directs its impulse”.

passages.greek: ʽΟὐκ ἔστι χείρων οὐδεμία φύσις τέχνηςʼ καὶ γὰρ αἱ τέχναι τὰς φύσεις μιμοῦνται. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, ἡ πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων τελεωτάτη καὶ περιληπτικωτάτη φύσις οὐκ ἂν ἀπολείποιτο τῆς τεχνικῆς εὐμηχανίας. πᾶσαι δέ γε τέχναι τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν τὰ χείρω ποιοῦσιν· οὐκοῦν καὶ ἡ κοινὴ φύσις. καὶ δὴ ἔνθεν μὲν γένεσις δικαιοσύνης, ἀπὸ δὲ ταύτης αἱ λοιπαὶ ἀρεταὶ ὑφίστανται· οὐ γὰρ τηρηθήσεται τὸ δίκαιον, ἐὰν ἤτοι διαφερώμεθα πρὸς τὰ μέσα ἢ εὐεξαπάτητοι καὶ προπτωτικοὶ καὶ μεταπτωτικοὶ ὦμεν.
passages.english: “No nature is inferior to art”; for the arts imitate the natures. If that is so, the nature that is the most complete of all natures and embraces the most would not fall short of the ingenuity of art. Now all the arts make the inferior things for the sake of the superior; so the common nature does too. And it is from this that justice is born, and from justice that the rest of the virtues have their existence; for what is just will not be kept if we either care about the things in between, or are easily deceived, hasty and changeable.

notes.greek: Οὐκ ἔστι χείρων οὐδεμία φύσις τέχνης
notes.note: The edition prints this as a quotation and names no source. “Art” is any craft or skill, not fine art only.
notes.other_reading: No nature is worse than a craft

notes.greek: ἡ πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων τελεωτάτη καὶ περιληπτικωτάτη φύσις
notes.note: Greek says “the most complete of all the others”, an idiom for “of them all”. The second adjective means “most containing”: the nature that takes in all the rest.
notes.other_reading: the nature that is the most perfect and the most comprehensive of all

notes.note: Literally “the craftsmanly skill at contriving”.
notes.other_reading: the resourcefulness of the crafts

notes.note: “From here” points back to what has just been said, most naturally the making of the inferior for the sake of the superior. The Greek does not spell it out.
notes.other_reading: And from there justice has its origin

notes.note: The verb means “come to stand, have their basis”.
notes.other_reading: the other virtues are founded on it

notes.note: Literally “the middle things”: the things between good and bad, called “indifferent things” in 5.20. The verb can mean “care about, treat as making a difference” or “quarrel over”; the first is taken.
notes.other_reading: if we quarrel over the middle things

notes.note: A pair on one root: literally “apt to fall forward” (assenting too soon) and “apt to fall over to another side” (changing one’s judgment).
notes.other_reading: rash and unstable

check.note: The Greek is “from here”: justice has its origin from this, parallel to “and from justice” in the next clause. “This is where” gives a place, not a source.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “And it is from this that justice is born, and from justice that the rest of the virtues have their existence”, so that both halves name a source.

check.note: “The middle things” is literal, but a reader of today will not know that these are the things between good and bad, called “indifferent things” in 5.20.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “the things in between”, which is plainer. The suggested “between good and bad” is left to the note, because the Greek says only “the middle things” and does not name what they lie between.

passages.greek: Ὁ ἀδικῶν ἀσεβεῖ· τῆς γὰρ τῶν ὅλων φύσεως κατεσκευακυίας τὰ λογικὰ ζῷα ἕνεκεν ἀλλήλων, ὥστε ὠφελεῖν μὲν ἄλληλα κατ’ ἀξίαν βλάπτειν δὲ μηδαμῶς, ὁ τὸ βούλημα ταύτης παραβαίνων ἀσεβεῖ δηλονότι εἰς τὴν πρεσβυτάτην τῶν θεῶν. καὶ ὁ ψευδόμενος δὲ ἀσεβεῖ περὶ τὴν αὐτὴν θεόν· ἡ γὰρ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ὄντων ἐστὶ φύσις· τὰ δέ γε ὄντα πρὸς τὰ ὑπάρχοντα πάντα οἰκείως ἔχει. ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἀλήθεια αὕτη ὀνομάζεται καὶ τῶν ἀληθῶν ἁπάντων πρώτη αἰτία ἐστίν. ὁ μὲν οὖν ἑκὼν ψευδόμενος ἀσεβεῖ, καθόσον ἐξαπατῶν ἀδικεῖ· ὁ δὲ ἄκων, καθόσον διαφωνεῖ τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει καὶ καθόσον ἀκοσμεῖ μαχόμενος τῇ τοῦ κόσμου φύσει· μάχεται γὰρ ὁ ἐπὶ τἀναντία τοῖς ἀληθέσι φερόμενος παρ’ ἑαυτόν· ἀφορμὰς γὰρ προειλήφει παρὰ τῆς φύσεως, ὧν ἀμελήσας οὐχ οἷός τέ ἐστι νῦν διακρίνειν τὰ ψευδῆ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀληθῶν. καὶ μὴν ὁ τὰς ἡδονὰς ὡς ἀγαθὰ διώκων, τοὺς δὲ πόνους ὡς κακὰ φεύγων ἀσεβεῖ· ἀνάγκη γὰρ τὸν τοιοῦτον μέμφεσθαι πολλάκις τῇ κοινῇ φύσει ὡς παῤ ἀξίαν τι ἀπονεμούσῃ τοῖς φαύλοις καὶ τοῖς σπουδαίοις, διὰ τὸ πολλάκις τοὺς μὲν φαύλους ἐν ἡδοναῖς εἶναι καὶ τὰ ποιητικὰ τούτων κτᾶσθαι, τοὺς δὲ σπουδαίους πόνῳ καὶ τοῖς ποιητικοῖς τούτου περιπίπτειν. ἔτι δὲ ὁ φοβούμενος τοὺς πόνους φοβηθήσεταί ποτε καὶ τῶν ἐσομένων τι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, τοῦτο δὲ ἤδη ἀσεβές· ὅ τε διώκων τὰς ἡδονὰς οὐκ ἀφέξεται τοῦ ἀδικεῖν, τοῦτο δὲ ἐναργῶς ἀσεβές· χρὴ δὲ πρὸς ἃ ἡ κοινὴ φύσις ἐπίσης ἔχει (οὐ γὰρ ἀμφότερα ἂν ἐποίει, εἰ μὴ πρὸς ἀμφότερα ἐπίσης εἶχε), πρὸς ταῦτα καὶ τοὺς τῇ φύσει βουλομένους ἕπεσθαι, ὁμογνώμονας ὄντας, ἐπίσης διακεῖσθαι· ὅστις οὖν πρὸς πόνον καὶ ἡδονὴν ἢ θάνατον καὶ ζωὴν ἢ δόξαν καὶ ἀδοξίαν, οἷς ἐπίσης ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις χρῆται, αὐτὸς οὐκ ἐπίσης ἔχει, δῆλον ὡς ἀσεβεῖ. λέγω δὲ τὸ χρῆσθαι τούτοις ἐπίσης τὴν κοινὴν φύσιν ἀντὶ τοῦ συμβαίνειν ἐπίσης κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τοῖς γινομένοις καὶ ἐπιγινομένοις ὁρμῇ τινι ἀρχαίᾳ τῆς προνοίας, καθ’ ἣν ἀπό τινος ἀρχῆς ὥρμησεν ἐπὶ τήνδε τὴν διακόσμησιν, συλλαβοῦσά τινας λόγους τῶν ἐσομένων καὶ δυνάμεις γονίμους ἀφορίσασα ὑποστάσεών τε καὶ μεταβολῶν καὶ διαδοχῶν τοιούτων.
passages.english: Whoever does injustice is impious. For since the nature of the whole has made rational animals for the sake of one another, to help one another as each deserves and in no way to harm one another, whoever goes against its will is clearly impious towards the eldest of the gods. And whoever says what is false is also impious, towards the same goddess. For the nature of the whole is the nature of the things that are, and the things that are stand in close kinship to all that is the case. Further, this nature is also named Truth, and it is the first cause of all things that are true. So whoever says what is false willingly is impious in so far as they do injustice by deceiving; and whoever does so unwillingly, in so far as they are out of tune with the nature of the whole, and in so far as they are disorderly, fighting against the nature of the universe. For whoever is carried by their own doing towards what is opposite to the things that are true is fighting; for they had received starting points from nature beforehand, and by neglecting them they are now unable to tell false things from true. And again, whoever pursues pleasures as goods and runs from pains as evils is impious. For such a person must often find fault with the common nature, as allotting something to the worthless and the worthy against what they deserve, because often the worthless live among pleasures and get the things that produce them, while the worthy fall into pain and the things that produce it. Further, whoever fears pains will at some time also fear something that is going to be in the universe, and that is already impious. And whoever pursues pleasures will not hold back from doing injustice, and that is plainly impious. Now towards the things to which the common nature is equally disposed (for it would not make both if it were not equally disposed to both), those who want to follow nature, being of one mind with it, must also be equally disposed. So whoever is not, for their own part, equally disposed towards pain and pleasure, or death and life, or good repute and ill repute, which the nature of the whole uses equally, is clearly impious. When I say that the common nature uses these equally, I mean that they happen equally, in sequence, to the things that come to be and the things that come after them, by a certain original impulse of providence, by which from a certain origin it set its impulse towards this ordering of the universe, having conceived certain principles of the things that were to be and marked off powers to generate such existences, changes and successions.

notes.note: The first verb is “to do wrong”, from the root of “justice”; the second is “to fail in reverence towards the gods”. “Does injustice” and “is impious” are kept throughout so the chain of the argument shows.
notes.other_reading: The wrongdoer sins against the gods

notes.note: Literally “according to worth”. The opposite phrase, “against worth”, comes later in the passage, and the two are rendered to match.
notes.other_reading: to benefit one another according to worth

notes.note: “Eldest” also means most to be honoured. The word for nature is feminine in Greek, which is why the next sentence calls her a goddess.
notes.other_reading: towards the most venerable of the gods

notes.note: The verb covers both lying and saying what is false without meaning to. Since Marcus goes on to an unwilling case, “says what is false” is used.
notes.other_reading: And the liar is also impious

notes.greek: τὰ δέ γε ὄντα πρὸς τὰ ὑπάρχοντα πάντα οἰκείως ἔχει
notes.note: An obscure sentence. The second participle can mean “the things that exist”, which is hard to tell apart from “the things that are”, or “the things that are the case”, a sense the Stoics use of what is truly so. The second is taken, because the sentence is given as the ground for calling false speech impious; the point of the kinship is not stated.
notes.other_reading: and the things that are stand in close kinship to all the things that exist

notes.greek: ἀκοσμεῖ μαχόμενος τῇ τοῦ κόσμου φύσει
notes.note: A play on words: the verb “is disorderly” is built on the word kosmos, which means both “order” and “the universe”. English cannot keep the play without adding a word. The verb before it, “out of tune”, is a musical word for disagreeing.
notes.other_reading: in so far as they break order, fighting against the nature of the world-order

notes.note: The last two words can mean “through himself, by his own fault” or “contrary to himself”. The first is taken, which the next clause about neglect supports.
notes.other_reading: whoever is carried, against themselves, towards what is opposite to the things that are true

notes.note: Literally “starting points”, also “means, resources”: what nature gives one to begin from.
notes.other_reading: for they had received the means from nature beforehand

notes.note: The word covers pain and toil. Set against pleasure here, it is “pain”, as in 6.33.
notes.other_reading: and runs from hardships as evils

notes.note: The Stoic pair for people of no worth and people of real worth. They are not the words used for bad and good things elsewhere in the passage, so “the worthless” and “the worthy” keep the two pairs apart.
notes.other_reading: to the bad and the good

notes.note: Literally “holds itself equally”. The adverb “equally” comes seven times in the passage and carries the argument, so one word is kept for it.
notes.other_reading: the things towards which the common nature is indifferent

notes.greek: ἀντὶ τοῦ συμβαίνειν ἐπίσης κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τοῖς γινομένοις καὶ ἐπιγινομένοις
notes.note: Literally “I say X in place of Y”, that is, “by X I mean Y”. The datives may be things or people: those that come to be and those that follow them.
notes.other_reading: I mean that they befall equally, one after another, those who are born and those who are born after them

notes.note: The adjective means “ancient” and “belonging to the beginning”, and the noun “beginning” follows in the next clause; “original” and “origin” show that pair, as “impulse” twice shows the noun and its verb. The subject of the verb is not stated: providence or the common nature.
notes.other_reading: by a certain ancient impulse of providence, by which from some beginning it set out towards this ordering

notes.note: The noun is one word, “the setting in order”, built on kosmos. “Of the universe” spells out what the word contains.
notes.other_reading: towards this present arrangement of things

notes.note: The participle means “having gathered together” and also “having conceived” as a womb does; with “powers to generate” following, “conceived” is taken. The noun is elsewhere “reason”; in the plural here it is the Stoic term for the rational principles, like seeds, from which things unfold, so “principles” is used.
notes.other_reading: having gathered together certain reasons for the things that were to be

notes.greek: δυνάμεις γονίμους ἀφορίσασα ὑποστάσεών τε καὶ μεταβολῶν καὶ διαδοχῶν τοιούτων
notes.note: Literally “having marked off fertile powers of such comings-to-exist, changes and successions”. The first genitive can mean things that exist or their coming into existence.
notes.other_reading: and set apart fertile powers of such substances, changes and successions

check.note: “Ordered” is added to carry the play between “is disorderly” and kosmos; the same noun is plain “world” later. Defensible, but it is an addition.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The added “ordered” is removed, and the English now reads “in so far as they are disorderly, fighting against the nature of the universe”, with “universe” for this noun both times it occurs. The play on kosmos is explained in the note; the suggested “world-order” is not plain English.

check.note: The words are taken as “by his own fault”; they can also be read “contrary to himself”, against his own nature. The next clause supports the English, but the choice is silent.
check.decided: Accepted: “By their own doing” is kept, as suggested, since the next clause gives neglect as the reason. The choice is not silent: the note sets out “against themselves” as the other reading.

check.note: The prefix “beforehand” is dropped: he had been given them in advance.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “they had received starting points from nature beforehand”.

check.note: Marcus keeps two vocabularies apart: things wrongly taken as goods and evils, and people of no worth and of worth. “The bad and the good” after “goods … evils” runs the two pairs together.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the worthless and the worthy”, in both sentences where the pair occurs, so that the words for people stay apart from “goods” and “evils”.

check.note: “Are in pleasures” is not English.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “because often the worthless live among pleasures”.

check.note: “Evidently” today often means “apparently, it seems”; the Greek is “manifestly, in plain view”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “and that is plainly impious”. To keep this word apart from a different Greek word near the start, “plainly impious towards the eldest of the gods” there now reads “clearly impious”, the same English as for its cognate near the end.

check.greek: ὁρμῇ τινι ἀρχαίᾳ τῆς προνοίας, καθ’ ἣν ἀπό τινος ἀρχῆς ὥρμησεν
check.note: The Greek repeats two pairs, the noun “impulse” with its verb and “of the beginning” with “beginning”; “impulse … set out” and “original … beginning” showed neither. “A certain” was also dropped.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “by a certain original impulse of providence, by which from a certain origin it set its impulse towards this ordering of the universe”, so that both pairs can be heard and “a certain” is restored. The suggested “was impelled” is not used, because the Greek verb is active: the impulse is its own, not a push from outside.

check.note: The participle can be “having conceived”, which suits “generative”, or “having gathered together”; the English picks the first without sign.
check.decided: Accepted: “Having conceived” is kept, as suggested, and the note gives “having gathered together” as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft split the first long sentence and joined the halves with “so”, which the Greek does not have; it also had “he” and “himself” throughout where the Greek does not single out a man.
check.decided: Accepted: The sentence now runs “For since the nature of the whole has made … , whoever goes against its will is clearly impious”, as one sentence without an added “so”, and the passage uses “whoever … they” throughout.

check.greek: τὰ δέ γε ὄντα πρὸς τὰ ὑπάρχοντα πάντα οἰκείως ἔχει
check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “all the things that exist”, which in English cannot be told apart from “the things that are” and leaves the sentence saying nothing. The Greek participle also means “what is the case”, a sense the Stoics use of what is truly so.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the things that are stand in close kinship to all that is the case”, which lets the sentence do its work as a ground for calling false speech impious. The note says the sentence is obscure and gives “all the things that exist” as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “in due sequence” and, later, “this ordering of the world”; “due” is not in the Greek, and the settled word for kosmos is “universe”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “in sequence”, “in the universe” and “this ordering of the universe”.

passages.greek: Τῷ λογικῶ ζῴῳ ἡ αὐτὴ πρᾶξις κατὰ φύσιν ἐστὶ καὶ κατὰ λόγον.
passages.english: For the rational animal, the same action is in accordance with nature and in accordance with reason.

notes.note: “Reason” here and “rational” at the start are one root in Greek.
notes.other_reading: the same act is both natural and reasonable

passages.greek: Ὃ ἂν ἡ λογικὴ καὶ πολιτικὴ δύναμις εὑρίσκῃ μήτε νοερὸν μήτε κοινωνικόν, εὐλόγως καταδεέστερον ἑαυτῆς κρίνει.
passages.english: Whatever the rational and civic power finds to be neither of mind nor social, it judges, with good reason, to be inferior to itself.

notes.note: The second adjective means “belonging to a city, fitted for life as a citizen”. “Civic” is used, and kept apart from “social”, a different Greek word later in the sentence.
notes.other_reading: the faculty of reason and of citizenship

notes.note: The adjective is built on the Greek noun for mind: “having mind”. “Of mind” is the wording kept for it throughout the translation.
notes.other_reading: neither intelligent nor social

notes.note: Literally “with good reason”, on the same root as “rational”. It can go with “judges”, as taken here, or be heard as a comment by the writer.
notes.other_reading: it reasonably judges to be beneath itself

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “intelligent” for the adjective built on the Greek noun for mind.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “neither of mind nor social”, keeping “mind” for this root as in the passages settled earlier, and a note gives “intelligent” as the other wording.

passages.greek: Δικαιοσύνης κατεξαναστατικὴν ἀρετὴν οὐχ ὁρῶ ἐν τῇ τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου κατασκευῇ, ἡδονῆς δὲ ὁρῶ τὴν ἐγκράτειαν.
passages.english: In the make-up of the rational animal I see no virtue that rises up against justice, but I do see one that rises up against pleasure: self-control.

notes.note: A rare adjective from the verb “to rise up against” used in 5.15, and the same English is kept. The second clause does not repeat it; it is supplied there.
notes.other_reading: I see no virtue opposed to justice, but opposed to pleasure I see self-control

notes.note: Literally “having power over oneself”.
notes.other_reading: self-mastery

passages.greek: Οὐκ ἐν πείσει ἀλλ’ ἐνεργείᾳ τὸ τοῦ λογικοῦ καὶ πολιτικοῦ ζῴου κακὸν καὶ ἀγαθόν, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ ἡ ἀρετὴ καὶ κακία αὐτοῦ ἐν πείσει ἀλλὰ ἐνεργείᾳ.
passages.english: The bad and the good of the rational and civic animal lie not in what it undergoes but in what it does, just as its virtue and its vice lie not in what it undergoes but in what it does.

notes.note: The noun means being acted on, set against the noun for acting, which is “activity” in 5.20 and 8.7. The Greek has two abstract nouns; the English turns them into clauses.
notes.other_reading: not in passive experience but in activity

notes.note: “Belonging to a city, fitted for life as a citizen”; “civic”, as in 7.72.
notes.other_reading: the rational and political animal

notes.note: Neuter adjectives used as nouns: what is bad for it and what is good for it. The Greek has no verb; “lie” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: The evil and the good of the rational and civic animal

passages.greek: Ταὐτά ἐστι τὰ τοῦ κόσμου ἐγκύκλια, ἄνω κάτω, ἐξ αἰῶνος εἰς αἰῶνα. καὶ ἤτοι ἐφ’ ἕκαστον ὁρμᾷ ἡ τοῦ ὅλου διάνοια· ὅπερ εἰ ἔστιν, ἀποδέχου τὸ ἐκείνης ὁρμητόν· ἢ ἅπαξ ὥρμησε, τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν καὶ τί ἐντείνῃ; τρόπον γάρ τινα ἄτομοι ἢ ἀμερῆ. τὸ δ’ ὅλον, εἴτε θεός, εὖ ἔχει πάντα· εἴτε τὸ εἰκῇ, μὴ καὶ σὺ εἰκῇ.
passages.english: The cycles of the universe are the same, up and down, from age to age. And either the mind of the whole has an impulse towards each thing, and if that is so, accept what its impulse is towards; or it had an impulse once, and the rest follows as a consequence, and why do you strain? For in a way: atoms, or things without parts. In sum: if it is god, all is well; if it is randomness, do not act at random yourself as well.

notes.note: The breathing mark makes this a contraction of τὰ αὐτά, “the same things”. Without it the word would be ταῦτα, “these things”. The English follows the mark.
notes.other_reading: These are the cycles of the universe

notes.note: Literally “things that go in a circle”. The word can also mean what is ordinary and recurring. “Cycles” keeps the image of going round.
notes.other_reading: the ordinary run of the universe

notes.note: διάνοια is “thought” elsewhere in this translation. Here it is the faculty that has impulses, so the English reads “mind”.
notes.other_reading: the thought of the whole

notes.note: The verb and its relatives (ὁρμητόν, ὥρμησε) come three times and carry the argument, so “impulse” is used for all three. The Stoic term is ὁρμή; the verb more literally means “sets itself moving towards”.
notes.other_reading: either the mind of the whole sets itself moving towards each thing

notes.note: Literally “and why do you stretch yourself tight?”. The join with what goes before is abrupt, and the text here may have been doubted (from memory, unchecked). The words are translated as they stand.
notes.other_reading: and what are you straining at?

notes.greek: τρόπον γάρ τινα ἄτομοι ἢ ἀμερῆ
notes.note: The sentence has no verb and no stated subject, and how it follows from the question before it is not clear; the text may be damaged (from memory, unchecked). The English gives the words as they stand and supplies nothing. ἀμερῆ means things that have no parts and so cannot be divided.
notes.other_reading: for in a way it is atoms, or indivisible things

notes.note: This can be the set phrase “on the whole, in sum” or the noun “the whole”, which is named two sentences earlier. The English takes it as the set phrase.
notes.other_reading: As for the whole: if it is god, all is well

notes.note: The Greek is only “if god”, matched by “if the random”. It can mean “if what runs things is god” or “if there is a god”. The English keeps the two halves parallel.
notes.other_reading: if there is a god, all is well

notes.note: There is no verb: literally “not you too at random”. “Act” is supplied. εἰκῇ, “at random, without plan or purpose”, is the same word used just before of what runs things, where the English reads “randomness”.
notes.other_reading: do not be random yourself as well

check.greek: τρόπον γάρ τινα ἄτομοι ἢ ἀμερῆ
check.note: The Greek has no verb and no subject. “It is” is supplied and makes a definite statement out of words that hardly make sense as they stand; the text may be damaged, and “indivisibles” would be closer to ἀμερῆ.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “For in a way: atoms, or things without parts”, with nothing supplied, and the note says the sentence has no verb and may be damaged. “Things without parts” is kept because it is the literal sense of ἀμερῆ and plainer than “indivisibles”.

check.note: The Greek is only “if god”. “If there is a god” turns it into the question whether a god exists; in parallel with “if the random” it can equally be “if it is god”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if it is god, all is well; if it is randomness”, so the two halves match as they do in the Greek. A note records “if there is a god”.

check.note: Taken as the set phrase “in sum”. It can also be the noun, “as for the whole”, and the English chooses without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: “In sum” is kept, as suggested, and the note on these words records the other reading, “As for the whole”.

check.greek: εἴτε τὸ εἰκῇ, μὴ καὶ σὺ εἰκῇ
check.note: “All” is added. The supplied verb “be” gives “be at random”, which is not natural English for a person; “act” is the natural verb to supply.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “all” is dropped and “act” is supplied, so the English reads “if it is randomness, do not act at random yourself as well”. “Randomness” stands for the Greek “the at random” because “the random” is not English; the note says it is the same word in both halves.

check.note: “Rounds” is unclear to a reader of today. The word means the things that go in a circle, the recurring cycles.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The cycles of the universe are the same”.

check.note: “One by one” doubles the Greek word for “each” and adds emphasis the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: “one by one” is dropped and the English reads “has an impulse towards each thing”. The contrast with “once” in the next clause is still heard.

check.note: Found while settling: κόσμος was “the world”. This translation gives it as “the universe” wherever the whole ordered system is meant.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the cycles of the universe”.

part.left_out: Ἤδη πάντας ἡμᾶς γῆ καλύψει, ἔπειτα καὶ αὐτὴ μεταβαλεῖ κἀκεῖνα εἰς ἄπειρον μεταβαλεῖ καὶ πάλιν ἐκεῖνα εἰς ἄπειρον. τὰς γὰρ ἐπικυματώσεις τῶν μεταβολῶν καὶ ἀλλοιώσεων ἐνθυμούμενός τις καὶ τὸ τάχος παντὸς θνητοῦ καταφρονήσει.
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.26 here and begins its 9.27 with the rest of the chapter.

passages.greek:
Τὰ μέλλοντα μὴ ταρασσέτω· ἥξεις γὰρ ἐπ’ αὐτά, ἐὰν δεήσῃ, φέρων τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον ᾧ νῦν πρὸς τὰ παρόντα χρᾷ.

Πάντα ἀλλήλοις ἐπιπλέκεται καὶ ἡ σύνὸεσις ἱερά, καὶ σχεδόν τι οὐδὲν ἀλλότριον ἄλλο ἄλλῳ· συγκατατέτακται γὰρ καὶ συγκοσμεῖ τὸν αὐτὸν κόσμον. κόσμος τε γὰρ εἷς ἐξ ἁπάντων καὶ θεὸς εἷς δι’ ἁπάντων καὶ οὐσία μία καὶ νόμος εἷς, λόγος κοινὸς πάντων τῶν νοερῶν ζῴων καὶ ἀλήθεια μία, εἴγε καὶ τελειότης μία τῶν ὁμογενῶν καὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου μετεχόντων ζῴων.
passages.english:
Do not let what is to come trouble you. For you will come to it, if you have to, carrying the same reason that you now use on what is present.

All things are interwoven with one another, and the bond is sacred, and hardly anything is foreign to anything else. For they have been arranged together, and together they give order to the same universe. For there is one universe, made of all things, and one god, through all things, and one substance, and one law, the reason common to all living beings that have mind, and one truth, if indeed there is also one perfection for living beings that are of the same kind and share in the same reason.

notes.note: The Greek is a third-person command with no object: “let the things to come not trouble”. “You” is supplied, because the next verb is in the second person.
notes.other_reading: Let what is to come cause no trouble

notes.note: λόγος is “reason”, but can also be “account” or “argument”. “Reason” is used here and for the same word in the second chapter.
notes.other_reading: bringing the same reasoning

notes.note: As printed in the digitised text this is not a Greek word. It is read as σύνδεσις, “a binding together”, taking the fourth letter to be a slip for δ.
notes.other_reading: the binding-together is sacred

notes.note: “Have been arranged together”, as troops are drawn up in one formation. “Order” is kept for the next verb, which is made from κόσμος.
notes.other_reading: they have been ranked together

notes.note: A play on words. κόσμος means both “order” and “the universe”, and the verb, made from the same word, means “to join in putting in order” and also “to adorn”. The English gives the verb as “give order to” and the noun as “universe”, here and in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: together they adorn the same universe / together they order the same order

notes.note: After a run of items joined by “and”, this one has no “and”. “The reason common to all” can be a second name for the one law, or one more item in the list. The English sets it beside “one law” with a comma, as the Greek does.
notes.other_reading: and one law, and one reason common to all living beings that have mind, and one truth

notes.note: νοερός is “having mind”, from νοῦς, “mind”.
notes.other_reading: all intelligent living beings

notes.note: εἴγε can be a real condition (“if indeed”) or close to “seeing that”. The English keeps the condition.
notes.other_reading: seeing that there is also one perfection

check.note: κόσμον is translated twice, as “order” and as “world”. The Greek plays on one word, and the doubling is an expansion.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “together they give order to the same universe”, so the noun is translated once and the verb carries the sense of order. “Universe” stands where the suggestion has “world” because it is this translation’s word for κόσμος; the note explains the play.

check.greek: νόμος εἷς, λόγος κοινὸς πάντων τῶν νοερῶν ζῴων
check.note: The Greek sets “a reason common to all intelligent living beings” beside “one law” with no “which is the”, so it could also be a further item in the list. “Thinking living beings” is clumsy English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and one law, the reason common to all living beings that have mind, and one truth”, with a comma and no “which is”. The note gives the reading in which it is a separate item.

check.note: Found while settling: κόσμος was “world” in both sentences. This translation gives it as “the universe”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the same universe” and “one universe”.

check.note: Found while settling: “set in order together” used “order” for a verb that is not made from κόσμος, which blurred the play in the next verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “they have been arranged together”, and “order” is kept for the verb made from κόσμος.

check.note: Found while settling: the verb was “woven together”, while its noun is “interweaving” in 2.3 and 10.5.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “All things are interwoven with one another”.

passages.greek: Ὁποῖόν τί ἐστι τὸ λεγόμενον, ὅτι· συνέταξεν ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς τούτῳ ἱππασίαν ἢ ψυχρολουσίαν ἢ ἀνυποδησίαν, τοιοῦτόν ἐστι καὶ τό· συνέταξε τούτῳ ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις νόσον ἢ πήρωσιν ἢ ἀποβολὴν ἢ ἄλλο τι τῶν τοιούτων. καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖ τὸ συνέταξε τοιοῦτόν τι σημαίνει· ἔταξε τούτῳ τοῦτο ὡς κατάλληλον πρὸς ὑγίειαν, καὶ ἐνταῦθα τὸ συμβαῖνον ἑκάστῳ τέτακταί πως αὐτῷ ὡς κατάλληλον πρὸς τὴν εἱμαρμένην. οὕτως γὰρ καὶ συμβαίνειν αὐτὰ ἡμῖν λέγομεν ὡς καὶ τοὺς τετραγώνους λίθους ἐν τοῖς τείχεσιν ἤ ἐν ταῖς πυραμίσι συμβαίνειν οἱ τεχνῖται λέγουσι, συναρμόζοντας ἀλλήλοις τῇ ποιᾷ συνθέσει. ὅλως γὰρ ἁρμονία ἐστὶ μία καὶ ὥσπερ ἐκ πάντων τῶν σωμάτων ὁ κόσμος τοιοῦτον σῶμα συμπληροῦται, οὕτως ἐκ πάντων τῶν αἰτίων ἡ εἱμαρμένη τοιαύτη αἰτία συμπληροῦται. νοοῦσι δὲ ὃ λέγω καὶ οἱ τέλεον ἰδιῶται· φασὶ γάρ· τοῦτο ἔφερεν αὐτῷ. οὐκοῦν τοῦτο τούτῳ ἐφέρετο καὶ τοῦτο τούτῳ συνετάττετο· δεχώμεθα οὖν αὐτὰ ὡς ἐκεῖνα ἃ ὁ Ἀσκληπιὸς συντάττει. πολλὰ γοῦν καὶ ἐν ἐκείνοις ἐστὶ τραχέα, ἀλλὰ ἀσπαζόμεθα τῇ ἐλπίδι τῆς ὑγιείας. τοιοῦτόν τί σοι δοκείτω ἄνυσις καὶ συντέλεια τῶν τῇ κοινῇ φύσει δοκούντων, οἷον ἡ σὴ ὑγίεια, καὶ οὕτως ἀσπάζου πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον, κἂν ἀπηνέστερον δοκῇ, διὰ τὸ ἐκεῖ σε ἄγειν, ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ κόσμου ὑγίειαν καὶ τὴν τοῦ Διὸς εὐοδίαν καὶ εὐπραγίαν. οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτό τινι ἔφερεν, εἰ μὴ τῷ ὅλῳ συνέφερεν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἡ τυχοῦσα φύσις φέρει τι, ὃ μὴ τῷ διοικουμένῳ ὑπ’ αὐτῆς κατάλληλόν ἐστιν. οὐκοῦν κατὰ δύο λόγους στέργειν χρὴ τὸ συμβαῖνόν σοι· καθ’ ἕνα μέν, ὅτι σοὶ ἐγίνετο καὶ σοὶ συνετάττετο καὶ πρὸς σέ πως εἶχεν, ἄνωθεν ἐκ τῶν πρεσβυτάτων αἰτίων συγκλωθόμενον· καθ’ ἕτερον δέ, ὅτι τῷ τὸ ὅλον διοικοῦντι τῆς εὐοδίας καὶ τῆς συντελείας καὶ νὴ Δία τῆς συμμονῆς αὐτῆς καὶ τὸ ἰδίᾳ εἰς ἕκαστον ἧκον αἴτιόν ἐστι. πηροῦται γὰρ τὸ ὁλόκληρον, ἐὰν καὶ ὁτιοῦν διακόψῃς τῆς συναφείας καὶ συνεχείας ὥσπερ τῶν μορίων, οὕτω δὴ καὶ τῶν αἰτίων· διακόπτεις δέ, ὅσον ἐπὶ σοί, ὅταν δυσαρεστῇς, καὶ τρόπον τινὰ ἀναιρεῖς.
passages.english: When people say, “Asclepius ordered horse-riding for this person, or cold baths, or going barefoot”, it is the same kind of thing as saying, “The nature of the whole ordered an illness for this person, or a maiming, or a loss, or something else of that kind.” For in the first case “ordered” means something like this: he set this in order for this person as suited to health. And in the second, what falls to each person has in some way been set in order for them as suited to fate. For we say that these things “fall” to us in just the way that builders say the squared stones in walls or in pyramids “fall” into place, fitting with one another in a particular arrangement. For in general there is one fitting-together; and just as the universe is made complete, as the body it is, out of all bodies, so fate is made complete, as the cause it is, out of all causes. Even people with no training at all understand what I mean, for they say, “It brought him this.” So then, this was brought to this person, and this was ordered for this person. Let us accept these things, then, as we accept the things Asclepius orders. After all, many of those too are rough, but we welcome them in the hope of health. Let the carrying out and completion of what seems good to the common nature seem to you the same kind of thing as your own health, and so welcome everything that comes about, even if it seems rather harsh, because it leads you there: to the health of the universe, and to the good progress and success of Zeus. For it would not bring this to anyone if it did not bring good to the whole. For not even any ordinary nature brings anything that is not suited to what it governs. So you should hold dear what falls to you, for two reasons. One is that it came about for you, and was ordered for you, and stood in some relation to you, spun together from far back out of the oldest causes. The other is that what comes to each person individually is also a cause, for the one that governs the whole, of good progress and of completion and, by Zeus, of continuance itself. For the complete whole is maimed if you cut through the connection and continuity at any point at all, of its causes just as of its parts. And you do cut through it, as far as it lies with you, whenever you are discontented, and in a way you destroy it.

notes.note: The verb means “arranged together” and is also the ordinary word for a doctor’s order. Marcus then explains it by the same verb without its prefix (ἔταξε, τέτακται), “set in its place, set in order”. The English uses “ordered” for the first and “set in order” for the second, so that the link can be heard.
notes.other_reading: Asclepius prescribed riding for this person ... “prescribed” means: he assigned this to this person

notes.note: Asclepius is the god of healing. Sick people slept at his shrines and were given treatments to follow, often in dreams.
notes.other_reading: the god of healing ordered

notes.note: Literally “for this one”, the way Greek says “for so-and-so”. The form is masculine but is used of any person, so the English reads “this person”.
notes.other_reading: for this man

notes.note: Literally “a throwing away”, so a loss of any kind: of property, of a limb, of a person. The Greek does not say which, and the English leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: a bereavement / the loss of something

notes.note: εἱμαρμένη is the Stoic word for fate, literally “what has been allotted”. It is “fate” here and where it comes again below.
notes.other_reading: as suited to destiny

notes.note: A play on words that carries the argument. The verb means “to happen” and, literally, “to come together”, which is how builders use it of stones. “Fall” (“fall to us”, “fall into place”) is used for every use of the verb in this passage to keep the link visible; elsewhere in this translation the verb is “happen”.
notes.other_reading: we say these things “happen” to us in the same sense in which builders say the squared stones “come together”

notes.note: ἁρμονία is a joining or fitting of parts, and from that “harmony”. It picks up the verb “fitting” used of the stones just before, so “fitting” is kept.
notes.other_reading: there is one harmony

notes.note: Literally “is filled up into such a body”. “Such” can mean “the kind of body it is” or “so great a body”. The English takes the first, and does the same for “such a cause” in the matching clause.
notes.other_reading: is made up into so great a body ... so great a cause

notes.note: ἰδιῶται are people without special training, here in philosophy. The word does not mean “stupid”.
notes.other_reading: even complete laymen

notes.note: An everyday saying with no stated subject: literally “this it was bringing to him”. τοῦτο could be the subject or the object; it is taken as the object, with an unnamed “it” doing the bringing, because the verb comes back later with a nature as its subject. “Him” is the saying’s own word for whoever is being spoken of.
notes.other_reading: This brought it on him

notes.note: The same verb comes three times in this sentence: “let it seem to you”, “the things that seem good to the common nature”, which is the usual way of saying what someone has resolved, and “even if it seems rather harsh”. The English keeps “seem” for all three.
notes.other_reading: what the common nature has decided

notes.note: As printed in the digitised text these are two words, “there” and “you”: “it leads you there”. The same letters as one word (ἐκεῖσε, “to that place”) would give “it leads there” with no “you”, and the reason given would be about the universe alone. Both are possible Greek; the English follows the two words as printed, and the printed edition was not checked.
notes.other_reading: because it leads there: to the health of the universe

notes.note: Zeus here stands for the reason that runs the universe. εὐοδία is literally “a good road”, so a going well; εὐπραγία is “doing well”, success in what one does.
