notes.other_reading: the prosperity and welfare of Zeus

notes.note: A play on words: φέρειν is “to bring” and συμφέρειν is “to bring together” and so “to be good for”. The English reads “bring” and “bring good to” to keep the echo. The subject is not stated, as in the saying above; the next sentence shows that a nature is meant. The tense can refer to the present or the past.
notes.other_reading: it would not have brought this to anyone if it were not good for the whole

notes.note: Literally “the nature one happens to meet”, that is, any nature you like, such as that of a plant or an animal. The contrast is with the nature of the whole.
notes.other_reading: not even a chance nature

notes.note: The word covers both “to feel affection for” and “to be content with, to put up with”. The English takes the warmer sense, because it answers “welcome” above.
notes.other_reading: you should be content with what falls to you

notes.note: ἄνωθεν is “from above” and also “from the beginning, from far back”. Beside “the oldest causes” the English takes the sense of time.
notes.other_reading: spun together from above, out of the oldest causes

notes.note: Literally “being spun together”, the image of the thread the Fates spin. The Greek does not say with what it is spun together, and the English leaves that unsaid too.
notes.other_reading: woven in with your thread from the beginning

notes.note: The form can be masculine (“him who governs the whole”) or neuter (“that which governs the whole”). Zeus has just been named, and “good progress” was his two sentences before, which favours the masculine. The English reads “the one that governs” and so leaves it open; the Greek has no “his” or “its” with the three nouns that follow.
notes.other_reading: for him who governs the whole, a cause of his good progress

notes.note: The same word as the “maiming” in the first sentence (πήρωσιν), so “maimed” is kept.
notes.other_reading: the complete whole is mutilated

notes.note: The verb is “cut through, sever”, and it comes again in the next sentence. Literally “if you cut through anything whatever of the connection and continuity”.
notes.other_reading: if you break the connection and continuity at any point

notes.note: Literally “you take away, do away with”. It can also mean “kill”. The object is not stated; “it” is supplied, meaning the connection.
notes.other_reading: and in a way you do away with it

check.note: As printed the Greek is “there” plus “you”. The text may be the single word ἐκεῖσε, “to that place”, split by the digitised edition, in which case there is no “you”; ἐκεῖ with a verb of leading is also said to be less natural.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “because it leads you there”. The Greek as printed gives the verb its usual object, the same sentence addresses “you” three times, and ἐκεῖ with a verb of motion is ordinary Greek of this date, so nothing in the sentence requires the one word. The note gives “because it leads there” and says the printed edition was not checked.

check.note: εἱμαρμένη is “what is fated” here and “fate” three sentences later, though it is the same word and the later sentence explains this one.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as suited to fate”, so the word is “fate” both times.

check.greek: τὸ συνέταξε τοιοῦτόν τι σημαίνει· ἔταξε
check.note: Marcus explains the doctor’s verb by the simple verb inside it and then uses that verb of what happens to us. “Prescribed” and “assigned” share nothing, so the explanation cannot be seen in English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the doctor’s verb is now “ordered” throughout and the simple verb is “set in order”, so the English reads “‘ordered’ means something like this: he set this in order for this person”. “Ordered” alone for both, as suggested, would explain the word by itself.

check.note: εὐπραγία is doing well, success in action. “Well-being” suggests health or comfort and blurs into the “health” just before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the good progress and success of Zeus”.

check.note: The Greek is present and milder: “the things that seem good to the common nature”. “Has decided” adds a finished act of decision.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what seems good to the common nature”, which is present and no stronger than the Greek. It also keeps “seem” for a verb that comes three times in the sentence.

check.note: ἄνωθεν means “from above” or “from the beginning, from far back”. Next to “the oldest causes” the sense of time is at least as likely.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “spun together from far back out of the oldest causes”, and a note records “from above”.

check.note: The participle can be masculine or neuter. Zeus has just been named and is sworn by in this sentence, so the personal reading is open, and “that which” closes it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for the one that governs the whole”. “Its” is also removed from the three nouns that follow, since the Greek has no possessive there, and the note sets out both readings.

check.note: The same verb comes twice. “Cut away anything from” pictures removing a piece, while the verb means to cut through, to break the connection.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “if you cut through the connection and continuity at any point at all” and “you do cut through it”, so the picture is of severing and not of removing a piece. “Cut through” is used and not “break”, to keep the image of cutting.

check.note: γοῦν is “at any rate, at least”. It brings a supporting fact and does not add emphasis, as “certainly” does.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “After all, many of those too are rough, but we welcome them in the hope of health”.

check.note: Found while settling: κόσμος was “the world” in both places. This translation gives it as “the universe”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the universe is made complete” and “the health of the universe”.

check.note: Found while settling: “this man” and “assigned to him” were written where the Greek pronouns are used of any person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “this person” and “set in order for them”. “Him” is kept only in the quoted saying “It brought him this”, where English has no other natural word.

check.note: Found while settling: “suited to his health” added a possessive. The Greek is “suited to health”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “as suited to health”.

check.note: Found while settling: συνάφεια was “joining” here and “connection” in 4.45.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the connection and continuity”, so the word is the same in both passages.

passages.greek: Τὰ τῶν θεῶν προνοίας μεστά. τὰ τῆς τύχης οὐκ ἄνευ φύσεως ἢ συγκλώσεως καὶ ἐπιπλοκῆς τῶν προνοίᾳ διοικουμένων. πάντα ἐκεῖθεν ῥεῖ· πρόσεστι δὲ τὸ ἀναγκαῖον καὶ τὸ τῷ ὅλῳ κόσμῳ συμφέρον, οὗ μέρος εἶ. παντὶ δὲ φύσεως μέρει ἀγαθόν, ὃ φέρει ἡ τοῦ ὅλου φύσις καὶ ὃ ἐκείνης ἐστὶ σωστικόν. σῴζουσι δὲ κόσμον, ὥσπερ αἱ τῶν στοιχείων, οὕτως καὶ αἱ τῶν συγκριμάτων μεταβολαί. ταῦτά σοι ἀρκείτω καὶ δόγματα ἔστω. τὴν δὲ τῶν βιβλίων δίψαν ῥῖψον, ἵνα μὴ γογγύζων ἀποθάνῃς, ἀλλὰ ἵλεως ἀληθῶς καὶ ἀπὸ καρδίας εὐχάριστος τοῖς θεοῖς.
passages.english: What comes from the gods is full of providence. What comes from chance is not without nature, or without the spinning together and interweaving of the things that providence governs. Everything flows from there. And there is besides what is necessary, and what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part. And what the nature of the whole brings is good for every part of nature, and so is what preserves that nature. And the universe is preserved by changes: those of the elements and, in the same way, those of compound things. Let this be enough for you, and let these be your principles. As for your thirst for books, throw it away, so that you do not die grumbling, but truly gracious, and thankful to the gods from your heart.

notes.note: Literally “the things of the gods”, which can be their works or what comes from them. The next sentence has the same form, “the things of chance”, and the two are matched. “Everything flows from there”, two sentences on, takes up the sense “comes from”.
notes.other_reading: The works of the gods are full of providence. The works of chance

notes.greek: οὐκ ἄνευ φύσεως ἢ συγκλώσεως καὶ ἐπιπλοκῆς
notes.note: Literally “not without nature or spinning-together and interweaving”. The “or” may offer a second way of saying the same thing and not an alternative. Both nouns are images from thread and cloth.
notes.other_reading: not apart from nature, that is, from the spinning and weaving together

notes.note: “From there” has no stated place. It most naturally points back to providence, or to the gods.
notes.other_reading: Everything flows from that source

notes.note: Literally “there is added the necessary”. It is open whether necessity is a second thing beside providence or a feature of what flows from it.
notes.other_reading: and with it goes necessity

notes.note: Literally “what brings together”, and the next sentence uses the simple verb “brings” (φέρει); the echo is lost in the English. This translation usually gives the word as “is good for”. “Benefits” is used here so that it is not confused with ἀγαθόν, “good”, in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: what is good for the whole universe

notes.note: The adjective and the verb in the next sentence (σῴζουσι) are the same word, “keep safe, preserve”. “Preserve” is used for both, and the second sentence is turned into the passive.
notes.other_reading: what keeps that nature safe. And what keeps the universe safe is the changes

notes.note: δόγματα are settled beliefs one lives by, “principles” in this translation. The text is translated as given; some editions may print a word meaning “always” here in place of “and” (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: let them always be your principles

notes.note: A word for low muttering or complaining under the breath.
notes.other_reading: so that you do not die muttering

notes.note: Used of gods it means “kindly, well-disposed”; of people “gracious, good-humoured, at peace”. Here it is set against grumbling. “Gracious” is used here and for the same word in 3.16.
notes.other_reading: truly at peace / truly cheerful

check.note: A sentence beginning “For” reads at first as “because”, in a passage full of causal steps. The Greek has only “and” with a dative: good for every part.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And what the nature of the whole brings is good for every part of nature, and so is what preserves that nature.”

check.note: ἵλεως is “gracious, at peace, well-disposed”, the opposite of grumbling against the gods. It is not cheerfulness, which is another Greek word.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “cheerful” is given up and the English now reads “truly gracious, and thankful to the gods from your heart”. “Gracious” is used and not “at peace” so that the word is the same as in 3.16, where it describes the spirit within.

check.note: The Greek is only “the things of the gods” and then “the things of chance”. “What comes from” is one way to take it; “the works of the gods” is another.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “What comes from the gods” and “What comes from chance”. The Greek says only “the things of”, and “Everything flows from there”, two sentences later, takes up the sense “comes from”; “works” suits the gods but not chance. The note records “The works of the gods”.

check.note: Found while settling: κόσμος was “the world” in both places. This translation gives it as “the universe”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the whole universe” and “the universe is preserved”.

check.note: Found while settling: “the things compounded of them” added “of them”. The Greek has only “compounds”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “those of compound things”.

passages.greek:
Οἷς συγκεκλήρωσαι πράγμασι, τούτοις συνάρμοζε σεαυτὸν καὶ οἷς συνείληχας ἀνθρώποις, τούτους φίλει, ἀλλ’ ἀληθινῶς.

Ὄργανον, ἐργαλεῖον, σκεῦος πᾶν εἰ πρὸς ὃ κατεσκεύασται ποιεῖ, εὖ ἔχει· καίτοι ἐκεῖ ὁ κατασκευάσας ἐκποδών. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ὑπὸ φύσεως συνεχομένων ἔνδον ἐστὶ καὶ παραμένει ἡ κατασκευάσοσα δύναμις· καθὸ καὶ μᾶλλον αἰδεῖσθαι αὐτὴν δεῖ καὶ νομίζειν, ἐὰν κατὰ τὸ βούλημα ταύτης ἔχῃς καὶ διεξάγῃς, ἔχειν σοι πάντα κατὰ νοῦν. ἔχει δὲ οὕτως καὶ τῷ παντὶ κατὰ νοῦν τὰ ἑαυτοῦ.
passages.english:
Fit yourself to the things your lot has joined you to, and love the people your lot has put you among, but truly.

Every instrument, tool or utensil is as it should be if it does what it was made for; and yet in that case the one who made it is away. But in things held together by nature, the power that made them is inside and stays there. For that reason you should respect it all the more, and consider that if you keep to its will and live by it, everything is as your mind would have it. And in the same way, for the All too, what is its own is as its mind would have it.

notes.note: Literally “you have been allotted together with”. The next clause uses a different verb with the same image of drawing lots (συνείληχας). “Lot” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: the things with which you have been joined by lot

notes.note: The same “fit together” verb that is used of building stones in 5.8.
notes.other_reading: adapt yourself

notes.note: Three near-synonyms for a made thing that is used for something. The differences between them are slight and the three English words are approximate.
notes.other_reading: Every implement, tool, vessel

notes.note: Literally “is in a good state”, the phrase given as “all is well” in 9.28.
notes.other_reading: is in good order

notes.note: Literally “out from the feet”, that is, out of the way, gone off. It does not say the maker is dead, only that the maker is not there, as the next sentence shows.
notes.other_reading: the maker is out of the way

notes.note: As printed in the digitised text this form is irregular. It is read as κατασκευάσασα, “that made”, the same verb as “was made for” and “the one who made it” just before.
notes.other_reading: the power that constructed them

notes.note: The word joins respect, reverence and a sense of shame before someone.
notes.other_reading: you should revere it all the more

notes.note: Two verbs with no object: literally “if you are in a state and carry on through” in line with its will. They are given as “keep to” and “live by”.
notes.other_reading: if you are and continue in accord with its will

notes.note: An idiom, “to one’s liking”, whose literal sense is “according to mind”. Marcus uses it twice, the second time of the All, where the literal sense is felt. The English reads “as your mind would have it” to keep the word “mind”.
notes.other_reading: everything goes as you would wish. And so too for the All its own affairs go as it would wish

notes.note: Literally “for the all”, a name for the sum of things. It is a different word from “the whole” and from “the universe”, so the English keeps “the All”.
notes.other_reading: for the universe

check.note: “Out of the way” suggests “not obstructing”. The Greek means the maker is away, not present, as the next sentence shows.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and yet in that case the one who made it is away”.

check.note: “Is all right” sounds like “merely acceptable”. The Greek says it is in a good state, the phrase given as “all is well” in 9.28.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is as it should be if it does what it was made for”.

passages.greek:
ἐκεῖνος μέν φησιν ὅτι ʽπάντα νομιστί, ἐτεῇ δὲ μόνα τὰ στοιχεῖαʼ, ἀρκεῖ δὲ μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι τὰ πάντα νομιστὶ ἔχει· ἤδη λίαν ὀλίγα.

Περὶ θανάτου· ἢ σκεδασμός, εἰ ἄτομοι· εἰ δ᾽ ἕνωσις, ἤτοι σβέσις ἢ μετάστασις.

Περὶ πόνου· τὸ μὲν ἀφόρητον ἐξάγει, τὸ δὲ χρονίζον φορητόν· καὶ ἡ διάνοια τὴν ἑαυτῆς γαλήνην κατὰ ἀπόληψιν διατηρεῖ καὶ οὐ χεῖρον τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν γέγονε, τὰ δὲ κακούμενα μέρη ὑπὸ τοῦ πόνου, εἴ τι δύναται, περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀποφηνάσθω.

Περὶ δόξης· ἴδε τὰς διανοίας αὐτῶν, οἷαι καὶ οἷα μὲν φεύγουσαι. οἷα δὲ διώκουσαι. καὶ ὅτι, ὡς αἱ θῖνες ἄλλαι ἐπ’ ἄλλαις ἐπιφορούμεναι κρύπτουσι τὰς προτέρας, οὕτως ἐν τῷ βίῳ τὰ πρότερα ὑπὸ τῶν ἐπενεχθέντων τάχιστα ἐκαλύφθη.
passages.english:
He says, “All things are by convention, and in reality only the elements.” But it is enough to remember that all things are by convention. Already very few.

On death: either a scattering, if there are atoms; or, if there is a unity, either a snuffing out or a move elsewhere.

On pain: what cannot be borne carries one off, and what lasts can be borne. And the mind keeps its own calm by separation, and the ruling part has not become worse. As for the parts that are harmed by the pain, let them give their verdict on it, if they can.

On fame: look at their minds, what they are like, and what kind of things they run from and what kind of things they chase. And see that, as heaps of sand piled one on another hide the earlier ones, so in life the earlier things are very quickly covered by those piled on after.

notes.note: Literally “that man says”. The part given does not name him. The saying resembles one attributed to Democritus (from memory, unchecked), but no name is put into the English.
notes.other_reading: That well-known man says

notes.note: A rare adverb, “by custom, by convention, as people hold”. Because it is related to the word for law (νόμος), Marcus’s own restatement could be turning it to mean “by law”. “By convention” is kept in both places. The text of this sentence may be doubted (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: it is enough to remember that all things are governed by law

notes.note: “The elements”, the basic things everything is made of.
notes.other_reading: only the first components are real

notes.note: Three words with no verb, “already very few”, and nothing to say very few of what. The English gives the three words and supplies nothing. The likeliest sense is that the things to remember are by then very few; it could also be that very few things are left as real. The text may be doubted here (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: By then there is very little left to remember

notes.note: Literally “a making one”. It is the opposite case to atoms: a universe that is a single joined whole.
notes.other_reading: if all is one

notes.note: σβέσις is the putting out of a flame. μετάστασις is a change of place, and can also be a change of state.
notes.other_reading: either being put out or being changed into something else

notes.note: Literally “leads out”, with no object. “One” is supplied. The verb is a common way of speaking of leaving life.
notes.other_reading: what cannot be borne takes one out of life

notes.note: διάνοια is “thought” elsewhere in this translation. Here and under “On fame” it is the faculty, so the English reads “mind”.
notes.other_reading: thought keeps its own calm

notes.note: ἀπόληψις is a cutting off or shutting off, and the Greek does not say of what: the mind may cut itself off from the body’s pain, or shut the pain off. “Separation” leaves that open. The word is unusual in this sense.
notes.other_reading: by cutting itself off / by shutting the pain off

notes.note: τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, the Stoic term for the part of the soul that judges and decides, “the ruling part” in this translation.
notes.other_reading: the governing self has not become worse

notes.note: The verb means to declare an opinion or give a ruling. The point is that the judgment about the pain belongs to the damaged parts, if to anything.
notes.other_reading: let them say what they have to say about it

notes.note: δόξα is both “opinion” and “reputation”. The heading is about what others think of you, so “fame”.
notes.other_reading: On reputation

notes.note: “Their” has nothing before it to refer to. It means the people whose opinion makes up fame. The English keeps the bare “their”.
notes.other_reading: look at the minds of those people

notes.note: “That” depends on “look” at the start of the chapter. The English begins a new sentence and repeats the verb as “see”, which is the only word added.
notes.other_reading: look at their minds ... and at the fact that

notes.note: Heaps or banks of sand, on a shore or in a desert. The two “piled on” words in the sentence are closely related Greek verbs. The last verb is a past tense used for a general truth.
notes.other_reading: as dunes drifting one over another

check.note: The Greek is three words, “already very few”, with nothing to say very few of what. “That is” makes it sound as if the saying itself is the few things, and the result is unclear; the text may be doubted.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Already very few.”, the three Greek words with nothing supplied. The suggested “there is very little left to remember” says more than the Greek, so it is given in the note as the likeliest sense.

check.note: “A going out” will be read by many as leaving, the same as “a move elsewhere”. The word is the putting out of a flame.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “either a snuffing out or a move elsewhere”, which can only be heard of a flame. “Like a flame” is not added, because the Greek has the one word.

check.note: “Of life” is not in the Greek, which says only “leads out, carries off”. The sense is right but it is an explanation inside the text.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what cannot be borne carries one off”, and the note says that “one” is supplied.

check.note: The noun means a cutting off and does not say of what. The English decides that the mind cuts itself off; it could be the mind shutting the pain off.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “by separation”, which does not say what is cut off from what. The note gives both ways of taking it.

check.note: In the Greek this depends on “look”. After a full stop the English “And that, as dunes” is a sentence with no main verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And see that, as heaps of sand”, and a note says the verb is repeated from “look”.

check.note: θῖνες are heaps or banks of sand, typically on a shore, which drift over one another. “Dunes” is larger and more fixed than the picture needs.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “heaps of sand”, the plain meaning of the word. “Sandbanks” is not used because it suggests banks under water.

part.left_out: Φαίδρυνον σεαυτὸν ἁπλότητι καὶ αἰδοῖ καὶ τῇ πρὸς τὸ ἀνὰ μέσον ἀρετῆς καὶ κακίας ἀδιαφορίᾳ. φίλησον τὸ ἀνθρώπινον γένος. ἀκολούθησον θεῷ.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the opening of chapter 7.31 at the end of its section 7.21 and begins its 7.22 here, running on through 7.34.

passages.greek: τί ἐστὶ καὶ ἐκ τίνων συγκέκριται καὶ πόσον χρόνον πέφυκε παραμένειν τοῦτο τὸ τὴν φαντασίαν μοι νῦν ποιοῦν καὶ τίνος ἀρετῆς πρὸς αὐτὸ χρεία, οἷον ἡμερότητος, ἀνδρείας, πίστεως, ἀφελείας, αὐταρκείας, τῶν λοιπῶν. διὸ δεῖ ἐφ̓ ἑκάστου λέγειν· τοῦτο μὲν παρὰ θεοῦ ἥκει, τοῦτο δὲ κατὰ τὴν σύλληξιν καὶ τὴν συμμηρυομένην σύγκλωσιν καὶ τὴν τοιαύτην σύντευξίν τε καὶ τύχην, τοῦτο δὲ παρὰ τοῦ συμφύλου καὶ συγγενοῦς καὶ κοινωνοῦ, ἀγνοοῦντος μέντοι ὅ τι αὐτῷ κατὰ φύσιν ἐστίν. ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀγνοῶ· διὰ τοῦτο χρῶμαι αὐτῷ κατὰ τὸν τῆς κοινωνίας φυσικὸν νόμον εὔνως καὶ δικαίως, ἅμα μέντοι τοῦ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἐν τοῖς μέσοις συστοχάζομαι.
passages.english: What is it, and what is it compounded of, and how long is it in its nature to last, this thing that is now making the impression on me? And what virtue is needed for it: gentleness, for example, courage, good faith, simplicity, self-sufficiency, and the rest? So in each case one must say: this comes from god; this comes by the shared lot, and the spinning and winding together, and this kind of coincidence and chance; and this comes from one of my own tribe, a kinsman and partner, who does not know, however, what is in accordance with nature for them. But I do know. That is why I treat them according to the natural law of partnership, with good will and justly; and yet at the same time, in things that are neither good nor bad, I aim at what accords with worth.

notes.greek: τί ἐστὶ καὶ ἐκ τίνων συγκέκριται
notes.note: The part given begins in the middle of a sentence: these are indirect questions that depend on a verb in the part not given. No words are added. The indirect questions are turned into direct ones and made two sentences, and “this thing that is now making the impression on me” is moved to the end of the first.
notes.other_reading: [...] what it is, and what it is compounded of, and how long it is in its nature to last, this thing that now makes the impression on me, and what virtue is needed for it

notes.note: Literally “is by nature such as to stay”.
notes.other_reading: how long is it made to last

notes.note: φαντασία, the Stoic term for the way a thing presents itself to the mind, “impression” in this translation.
notes.other_reading: this thing that is now producing an appearance in me

notes.note: The word covers both trust and trustworthiness. In a list of virtues it is taken as keeping faith.
notes.other_reading: trustworthiness / trust

notes.note: Plainness, the absence of show or complication.
notes.other_reading: plainness

notes.note: The three “this” clauses are alternatives: of each thing one says whichever of the three applies. The same Greek can also mean “partly ... partly ... partly”.
notes.other_reading: one thing comes from god, another by the shared lot, another from one of my own tribe

notes.note: A rare word, “a drawing of lots together”, given as “the shared lot”.
notes.other_reading: by the joint allotment

notes.note: Two thread images together: σύγκλωσις is a spinning together, and the participle means “being wound up together”, as thread is wound. The Greek does not say with what. The English joins the two as “the spinning and winding together” and supplies no noun.
notes.other_reading: the spinning together that is wound up with the lot

notes.note: σύντευξις is a falling in with something, a coming together of events; it is from the same root as τύχη, “chance”. “This kind of” may go with both nouns or with the first only.
notes.other_reading: this sort of meeting, and chance

notes.note: “Partner, one who shares”. It is the same root as κοινωνία below, so the English reads “partner” and “partnership”; “fellow member” and “community” would also be possible. The Greek words for this person are masculine in form but single out no man, so the English refers back with “them”.
notes.other_reading: a fellow member ... the natural law of community

notes.note: τὰ μέσα, literally “the things in the middle”, is the Stoic name for things neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health or money. The English gives the meaning of the term.
notes.other_reading: in the things in the middle

notes.note: The verb is “I aim at”, with a prefix meaning “together” or “at the same time”. What is aimed at is “what accords with worth”, which may be the value of each thing or what the person deserves. The English leaves that open.
notes.other_reading: I aim, together with them, at what each thing is worth

check.note: A literal rendering of a school term for things that are neither good nor bad. A reader of today will not know what “the things in the middle” are.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in things that are neither good nor bad”, and the note gives the literal “the things in the middle”.

check.note: “Each” is added, and it fixes the reference to the middle things. The Greek is “what is according to worth”, which can also be what the person deserves.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “I aim at what accords with worth”, the same words as for this phrase in 4.10. The note gives both ways of taking it.

check.note: Beside “chance”, and after the images of lot and thread, the word means a falling together of events. “A meeting” suggests meeting a person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and this kind of coincidence and chance”.

check.note: “Thread” is supplied. The Greek has the action nouns, “the spinning-together that is wound up”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “thread” is removed and the English now reads “the spinning and winding together”. The suggested “wound up with it” is not used, because it supplies an “it” that the Greek also lacks.

check.note: “How long is it by nature to last” is not natural English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “how long is it in its nature to last”. “Made to last” is not used, because it brings in a maker, and the Greek speaks only of the thing’s nature.

check.note: Found while settling: “for him” and “I treat him” were written of a person the Greek does not single out as a man.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “for them” and “I treat them”.

part.left_out: Τοῖς δὲ εἰρημένοις παραστήμασιν ἓν ἔτι προσέστω, τὸ ὅρον ἢ ὑπογραφὴν ἀεὶ ποιεῖσθαι τοῦ ὑποπίπτοντος φανταστοῦ, ὥστε αὐτὸ ὁποῖόν ἐστι κατ’ οὐσίαν, γυμνόν, ὅλον δι’ ὅλων διῃρημένως βλέπειν καὶ τὸ ἴδιον ὄνομα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἐκείνων, ἐξ ὧν συνεκρίθη καὶ εἰς ἃ ἀναλυθήσεται, λέγειν παρ’ ἑαυτῷ. οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως μεγαλοφροσύνης ποιητικόν, ὡς τὸ ἐλέγχειν ὁδῷ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ ἕκαστον τῶν τῷ βίῳ ὑποπιπτόντων δύνασθαι καὶ τὸ ἀεὶ οὕτως εἰς αὐτὰ ὁρᾶν, ὥστε συνεπιβάλλειν ὁποίῳ τινὶ τῷ κόσμῳ ὁποίαν τινὰ τοῦτο χρείαν παρεχόμενον τίνα μὲν ἔχει ἀξίαν ὡς πρὸς τὸ ὅλον, τίνα δὲ ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, πολίτην ὄντα πόλεως τῆς ἀνωτάτης, ἧς αἱ λοιπαὶ πόλεις ὥσπερ οἰκίαι εἰσίν·
part.why: The 1634 translation begins its section 3.12 partway through the chapter, in the middle of a Greek sentence; the first part is its 3.11.

passages.greek:
Πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον οὕτως σύνηθες καὶ γνώριμον ὡς τὸ ῥόδον ἐν τῷ ἔαρι καὶ ὀπώρα ἐν τῷ θέρει· τοιοῦτον γὰρ καὶ νόσος καὶ θάνατος καὶ βλασφημία καὶ ἐπιβουλὴ καὶ ὅσα τοὺς μωροὺς εὐφραίνει ἣ λυπεῖ.

Τὰ ἑξῆς ἀεὶ τοῖς προηγησαμένοις οἰκείως ἐπιγίνεται· οὐ γὰρ οἷον καταρίθμησίς τίς ἐστιν ἀπηρτημένως καὶ μόνον τὸ κατηναγκασμένον ἔχουσα, ἀλλὰ συνάφεια εὔλογος καὶ ὥσπερ συντέτακται συνηρμοσμένως τὰ ὄντα, οὕτως τὰ γινόμενα οὐ διαδοχὴν ψιλήν, ἀλλὰ θαυμαστήν τινα οἰκειότητα ἐμφαίνει.
passages.english:
Everything that happens is as ordinary and familiar as the rose in spring and fruit in summer. For illness is like that too, and death, and slander, and plotting, and all the things that gladden or grieve fools.

What comes next always follows what went before as kin to it. For it is not like a counting-off of separate items that has only compulsion in it, but a connection that has reason in it. And just as the things that exist have been arranged to fit together, so the things that come to be show not bare succession but a wonderful kinship.

notes.note: ὀπώρα is the ripe fruit of late summer, and also the name of that season. θέρος is summer, and also the harvest.
notes.other_reading: the fruit at harvest time

notes.note: As printed in the digitised text the first word is the relative “which” (feminine), which does not fit the sentence. It is read as ἢ, “or”.
notes.other_reading: all the things that gladden fools or pain them

notes.note: Literally “in the manner of one who belongs to the household”. The noun from the same root (οἰκειότητα) ends the passage, so the English reads “kin” and “kinship”.
notes.other_reading: follows in a way that belongs to what went before ... a wonderful belonging-together

notes.note: Literally “a kind of counting-off, detachedly”, that is, a list of items with nothing joining them. The adverb is rare.
notes.other_reading: a mere enumeration of things hanging apart from each other

notes.note: Literally “what has been forced”. The point is a sequence in which each thing has to come next and nothing more can be said.
notes.other_reading: that has nothing but necessity in it

notes.note: εὔλογος is “reasonable, having good reason”. The English keeps the word “reason” visible.
notes.other_reading: a reasonable connection

notes.note: Two “together” words: “have been arranged together” and “in a fitted-together way”.
notes.other_reading: have been ordered together harmoniously

check.note: “As usual” is first read as the set phrase.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as ordinary and familiar as the rose in spring”.

passages.greek:
Ἤτοι ἀνάγκη εἱμαρμένης καὶ ἀπαράβατος τάξις ἢ πρόνοια ἱλάσιμος ἢ φυρμὸς εἰκαιότητος ἀπροστάτητος. εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀπαράβατος ἀνάγκη, τί ἀντιτείνεις; εἰ δὲ πρόνοια ἐπιδεχομένη τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι, ἄξιον σαυτὸν ποίησον τῆς ἐκ τοῦ θείου βοηθείας. εἰ δὲ φυρμὸς ἀνηγεμόνευτος, ἀσμένιζε ὅτι ἐν τοιούτῳ κλύδωνι αὐτὸς ἔχεις ἐν σαυτῷ τινα νοῦν ἡγεμονικόν, κἂν παραφέρῃ σε ὁ κλύδων, παραφερέτω τὸ σαρκίδιον, τὸ πνευμάτιον, τἄλλα· τὸν γὰρ νοῦν οὐ παροίσει.

ἢ τὸ μὲν τοῦ λύχνου φῶς, μέχρι σβεσθῇ, φαίνει καὶ τὴν αὐγὴν οὐκ ἀποβάλλει· ἡ δὲ ἐν σοὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ δικαιοσύνη καὶ σωφροσύνη προαποσβήσεται;
passages.english:
Either a necessity of fate and an order that cannot be overstepped, or a providence that can be appeased, or a jumble of randomness with no one in charge. If, then, it is a necessity that cannot be overstepped, why do you strain against it? If it is a providence that allows itself to be appeased, make yourself worthy of the help that comes from the divine. And if it is a jumble with nothing ruling it, be glad that in such a rough sea you yourself have in yourself a mind that rules. And if the sea carries you away, let it carry away the poor flesh, the bit of breath, the rest; for the mind it will not carry away.

Or does the light of a lamp shine until it goes out, and not lose its brightness, while the truth and justice and self-control in you will go out first?

notes.note: Literally “not to be stepped past”. It can mean that no one can break it, or that it does not itself step aside.
notes.other_reading: an order that never deviates

notes.note: A rare word from the verb for making a god well-disposed by prayer or offering, which comes again two sentences later. “Appeased” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: a providence that can be won over

notes.note: Literally “a mixing-up of randomness without anyone standing over it”. εἰκαιότης is from the adverb for “at random, without purpose”.
notes.other_reading: a purposeless confusion with no one presiding

notes.note: Literally “stretch against”, the image of pulling the other way.
notes.other_reading: why do you resist?

notes.note: “Without a ruler”. It is set against νοῦν ἡγεμονικόν, “a ruling mind”, in the same sentence, the word Marcus uses for the ruling part of the soul. “Rule” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: a leaderless jumble ... a mind to lead you

notes.note: Rough water, the swell and wash of waves. The word comes twice; the English reads “rough sea” and then “the sea”.
notes.other_reading: in such a surge

notes.note: Both are diminutives, “little flesh” and “little breath”, and they belittle. English has no single form for this, so “poor” and “bit of” are used.
notes.other_reading: the scrap of flesh, the puff of breath

notes.greek: ἢ τὸ μὲν τοῦ λύχνου φῶς
notes.note: The second chapter is taken to begin here, where the subject changes. The digitised text marks no break at this point; editions are believed to divide here (from memory, unchecked).
Soundness of mind shown as moderation and self-command.
notes.other_reading: moderation

notes.note: Literally “will go out beforehand”. Before what is not said: the sense is before you yourself do, as the lamp’s light lasts until the lamp goes out. The verb is the lamp’s verb with two prefixes, so “go out” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: will be put out before you are

check.note: “In such a surge” is not clear on first reading. The word is a rough sea, a swell of waves, and the image is carried on in “carries you away”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in such a rough sea” and “if the sea carries you away”.

check.note: Found while settling: the lamp’s verb was “is put out” and the same verb with prefixes was “go out”, so the echo between lamp and virtues was lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “until it goes out” and “will go out first”.

passages.greek: Εἰ μὲν οὖν ἐβουλεύσαντο περὶ ἐμοῦ καὶ τῶν ἐμοὶ συμβῆναι ὀφειλόντων οἱ θεοί, καλῶς ἐβουλεύσαντο· ἄβουλον γὰρ θεὸν οὐδὲ ἐπινοῆσαι ῥᾴδιον, κακοποιῆσαι δέ με διὰ τίνα αἰτίαν ἔμελλον ὁρμᾶν; τί γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἢ τῷ κοινῷ, οὗ μάλιστα προνοοῦνται, ἐκ τούτου περιεγένετο; εἰ δὲ μὴ ἐβουλεύσαντο κατ’ ἰδίαν περὶ ἐμοῦ, περί γε τῶν κοινῶν πάντως ἐβουλεύσαντο, οἷς κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν καὶ ταῦτα συμβαίνοντα ἀσπάζεσθαι καὶ στέργειν ὀφείλω. εἰ δʼ ἄρα περὶ μηδενὸς βουλεύονται (πιστεύειν μὲν οὐχ ὅσιον ἢ μηδὲ θύωμεν μηδὲ εὐχώμεθα μηδὲ ὀμνύωμεν μηδὲ τὰ ἄλλα πράσσωμεν ἃ παρ’ ἕκαστα ὡς πρὸς παρόντας καὶ συμβιοῦντας τοὺς θεοὺς πράσσομεν), εἰ δ’ ἄρα περὶ μηδενὸς τῶν καθ’ ἡμᾶς βουλεύονται, ἐμοὶ μὲν ἔξεστι περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ βουλεύεσθαι, ἐμοὶ δέ ἐστι σκέψις περὶ τοῦ συμφέροντος. συμφέρει δὲ ἑκάστῳ τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κατασκευὴν καὶ φύσιν, ἡ δὲ ἐμὴ φύσις λογικὴ καὶ πολιτική. Πόλις καὶ πατρὶς ὡς μὲν Ἀντωνίνῳ μοι ἡ Ῥώμη, ὡς δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ὁ κόσμος. τὰ ταῖς πόλεσιν οὖν ταύταις ὠφέλιμα μόνα ἐστί μοι ἀγαθά.
passages.english: If, then, the gods deliberated about me and about the things that had to happen to me, they deliberated well. For a god without deliberation is not easy even to imagine; and for what cause would they have had an impulse to do me harm? For what would they, or the community, which is what they take most thought for, have gained from it? But if they did not deliberate about me individually, they certainly did deliberate about the affairs of the community, at least, and these things too, which happen as a consequence of those, I ought to welcome and hold dear. But if in fact they deliberate about nothing (to believe that is not pious; or else let us not sacrifice, or pray, or swear oaths, or do the other things that we do at every turn towards the gods as present and living with us), if in fact they deliberate about nothing that concerns us, then I am free to deliberate about myself, and my inquiry is into what is of benefit. What benefits each is what accords with its own make-up and nature, and my nature is rational and civic. My city and fatherland, as Antoninus, is Rome; as a human being, the universe. So the things that are useful to these cities are the only things that are good for me.

notes.note: The verb is “to take counsel” and so both “to deliberate” and “to decide”. It comes seven times and “deliberate” is kept throughout.
notes.other_reading: If the gods made a decision about me

notes.note: From the same root: “without counsel”, which can mean one who does not deliberate or one who deliberates badly.
notes.other_reading: an ill-advised god

notes.note: Literally “were they going to set themselves moving”. “Impulse” is used for the verb, as for the Stoic term ὁρμή.
notes.other_reading: why would they have set out to do me harm?

notes.note: Literally “what was left over as a gain”. The Greek is a plain past tense, “what did they gain”; the English reads “would have gained”, since the harm is only supposed.
notes.other_reading: what did they, or the community, gain from that?

notes.note: “The common thing”, singular: the body to which all belong, an ordinary word for a community or commonwealth. In the next sentence the plural τῶν κοινῶν, “the common things”, is given as “the affairs of the community”, so that the one word is heard in both places.
notes.other_reading: the common good ... what is common to all

notes.note: The verb behind πρόνοια, “providence”: to think ahead on behalf of something.
notes.other_reading: for which above all they exercise providence

notes.note: Literally “these things too, happening by way of following on from those”. “These things” are what happens to me.
notes.other_reading: and what happens to me as a by-product of those decisions

notes.note: The ἢ after “not pious” is “or else”: if one did believe it, the acts of worship that follow would make no sense. The brackets are the editor’s.
notes.other_reading: it is impious to believe so; otherwise let us give up sacrificing

notes.note: Literally “for me there is inquiry about what benefits”. The Greek does not say “benefits me”; the next sentence says whom. This translation usually gives συμφέρει as “is good for”. “Benefit” is used here because the last sentence of the passage needs “good” for another word, ἀγαθά.
notes.other_reading: and my inquiry is into what is good for me

notes.note: “Belonging to a city (πόλις)”, that is, made for life with others as a citizen. The word for “city” follows at once, so the English reads “civic” to keep the link.
notes.other_reading: rational and social

notes.note: Antoninus is Marcus’s own name as emperor (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus).
notes.other_reading: as the emperor Antoninus

check.note: The verb means what advantage was left over, what was gained. “Come of it” is neutral and loses the point that the gods would gain nothing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For what would they, or the community, which is what they take most thought for, have gained from it?”

check.note: “Whole” is added, and the same word in the next sentence becomes “what is common to all”, although the argument turns on this one word.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “whole” is removed and one word is used for both, “the community” here and “the affairs of the community” in the next sentence. “The common good” is not used, because the Greek has no word for “good” here and the passage keeps “good” for its last sentence.

check.note: ἔξεστι is “it is open to me, I am free to”. It does not speak of ability.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “then I am free to deliberate about myself”.

check.greek: ἐμοὶ δέ ἐστι σκέψις περὶ τοῦ συμφέροντος
check.note: “Have to” suggests an obligation the Greek does not state, and “what benefits” with no object is not natural English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and my inquiry is into what is of benefit”.

check.greek: ὡς πρὸς παρόντας καὶ συμβιοῦντας τοὺς θεοὺς
check.note: Stiff, and “gods who are present” loses the article: it is the gods, treated as present and living with us.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “towards the gods as present and living with us”, which gives “the gods” their article. “As though the gods were” is not used, because in English it suggests that they are not, and it drops the Greek “towards”.

check.note: Found while settling: “since these things too happen” added a “since”. The Greek has only a participle, “happening”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “and these things too, which happen as a consequence of those, I ought to welcome and hold dear”.

check.note: Found while settling: κόσμος was “the world”. This translation gives it as “the universe”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “as a human being, the universe”.

passages.greek: Ὅτι “πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον δικαίως συμβαίνει” · ὃ ἐὰν ἀκριβῶς παραφυλάσσῃς, εὑρήσεις· οὐ λέγω μόνον κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς, ἀλλʼ ὅτι κατὰ τὸ δίκαιον καὶ ὡς ἂν ὑπό τινος ἀπονέμοντος τὸ κατʼ ἀξίαν. παραφύλασσε οὖν ὡς ἤρξω, καί, ὅ τι ἂν ποιῇς, σὺν τούτῳ ποίει, σὺν τῷ ἀγαθὸς εἶναι, καθὸ νενόηται ἰδίως ὁ ἀγαθός. τοῦτο ἐπὶ πάσης ἐνεργείας σῷζε.
passages.english: That “everything that happens, happens justly”. If you watch closely, you will find it so. I do not mean only according to the order in which one thing follows another, but that it is according to what is just, and as if by someone handing out what accords with worth. So keep watching, as you have begun, and whatever you do, do it with this: with being good, in the sense in which the good person is properly understood. Keep this in every action.

notes.note: The chapter opens with “that”, as a note of a point to hold on to, with no main verb. The quotation marks are the editor’s.
notes.other_reading: Remember that everything that happens, happens justly

notes.note: “Justly”, and also more loosely “rightly”. The explanation that follows (“according to what is just”) shows the strict sense is meant.
notes.other_reading: happens rightly

notes.note: “To keep watch beside”, to observe closely. It comes again as a command below and “watch” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: if you observe carefully

notes.note: Literally “according to the next-in-order”, that is, as one thing follows from another. The same “according to” then governs “what is just”.
notes.other_reading: not only in the order of cause and effect

notes.note: Literally “as it would be by someone distributing what accords with worth”. “Worth” can be what each deserves; the Greek has no “to each”.
notes.other_reading: as if by someone who gives each what they deserve

notes.note: Literally “in the way the good one has been conceived in the particular sense”. ἰδίως is taken as “in the strict, proper sense of the word”. ὁ ἀγαθός is masculine in form but means anyone who is good.
notes.other_reading: in the special sense in which a person is thought of as good

notes.note: “Keep safe, preserve”.
notes.other_reading: Hold on to this in everything you do

check.note: “To each” is added, and “done” before it is supplied. Neither is in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and as if by someone handing out what accords with worth”, with neither addition.

check.note: “According to sequence” is unclear English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “I do not mean only according to the order in which one thing follows another”. “According to” is kept so that it matches “according to what is just”, as the two phrases match in the Greek.

check.note: Found while settling: “the good man” was written where the Greek does not single out a man.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the good person”.

passages.greek: τὸ μὲν τυποῦσθαι φανταστικῶς καὶ τῶν βοσκημάτων· τὸ δὲ νευροσπαστεῖσθαι ὁρμητικῶς καὶ τῶν θηρίων καὶ τῶν ἀνδρογύνων καὶ Φαλάριδος καὶ Νέρωνος· τὸ δὲ τὸν νοῦν ἡγεμόνα ἔχειν ἐπὶ τὰ φαινόμενα καθήκοντα καὶ τῶν θεοὺς μὴ νομιζόντων καὶ τῶν τὴν πατρίδα ἐγκαταλειπόντων καὶ τῶν ποιούντων, ἐπειδὰν κλείσωσι τὰς θύρας. εἰ οὖν τὰ λοιπὰ κοινά ἐστι πρὸς τὰ εἰρημένα, λοιπὸν τὸ ἴδιόν ἐστι τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ φιλεῖν μὲν καὶ ἀσπάζεσθαι τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ συγκλωθόμενα αὐτῷ, τὸν δὲ ἔνδον ἐν τῷ στήθει ἱδρυμένον δαίμονα μὴ φύρειν μηδὲ θορυβεῖν ὄχλῳ φαντασιῶν, ἀλλὰ ἵλεων διατηρεῖν, κοσμίως ἑπόμενον θεῷ, μήτε φθεγγόμενόν τι παρὰ τὰ ἀληθῆ μήτε ἐνεργοῦντα παρὰ τὰ δίκαια. εἰ δὲ ἀπιστοῦσιν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄνθρωποι, ὅτι ἁπλῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως καὶ εὐθύμως βιοῖ, οὔτε χαλεπαίνει τινὶ τούτων οὔτε παρατρέπεται τῆς ὁδοῦ τῆς ἀγούσης ἐπὶ τὸ τέλος τοῦ βίου, ἐφ’ ὃ δεῖ ἐλθεῖν καθαρόν, ἡσύχιον, εὔλυτον, ἀβιάστως τῇ ἑαυτοῦ μοίρᾳ συνηρμοσμένον.
passages.english: To be stamped with impressions belongs to cattle as well. To be pulled by the strings of impulse belongs also to wild beasts, and to effeminate men, and to Phalaris and Nero. And to have the mind as leader towards what appear to be the fitting things to do belongs also to those who do not believe in gods, and those who desert their country, and those who do what they do once they have shut the doors. If, then, the rest is shared with those just mentioned, what is left as the good person’s own is to love and welcome the things that happen to them and are spun together for them; and not to muddy the spirit seated within the chest, nor disturb it with a crowd of impressions, but to keep it gracious, following god in good order, neither saying anything contrary to what is true nor doing anything contrary to what is just. And if all people disbelieve that the good person lives simply and modestly and cheerfully, the good person is not angry with any of them, and is not turned aside from the road that leads to the end of life, at which one must arrive pure, quiet, ready to be released, fitted to one’s own portion without being forced.

notes.note: Literally “to be stamped in the way of impressions”. The image is a seal pressed into wax; the adverb is from φαντασία, “impression”.
notes.other_reading: to receive the imprint of appearances

notes.note: The verb is used of puppets worked by strings. The adverb is from ὁρμή, “impulse”.
notes.other_reading: to be jerked about like a puppet by impulses

notes.note: Literally “man-women”. In ordinary use it is an insult for men thought unmanly. The English gives the sense and not the literal compound.
notes.other_reading: men who are half women

notes.note: Phalaris was a tyrant of Acragas in Sicily, a byword for cruelty; Nero is the Roman emperor.
notes.other_reading: a Phalaris or a Nero

notes.note: καθήκοντα is the Stoic term for acts that are fitting or appropriate, often translated “duties”. “Appear” can go with it two ways: things that seem to be fitting, or fitting things as they show themselves.
notes.other_reading: towards the duties that present themselves

notes.note: “Those who do”, with no object: the Greek does not say what they do behind shut doors, and a word may have dropped out. “What they do” is supplied by the English and stands for no Greek word; it is chosen because it gives the verb an object without saying what the object is. Editors are believed to supply a word meaning “anything at all” (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: those who do anything at all once they have shut the doors

notes.note: Masculine in form, but meaning anyone who is good, so the English reads “the good person” and “them”. In the last sentence the noun is repeated where the Greek has “him” and “he”, so that “them” can stand for the people who disbelieve.
notes.other_reading: the good man’s own ... he is not angry with any of them

notes.note: Literally “being spun together for him” or “with him”, the image of the thread of fate.
notes.other_reading: spun into the good person’s thread

notes.note: A δαίμων is a divine being below the gods; here it is the divine thing lodged inside a person, which Marcus elsewhere identifies with the mind. The English reads “spirit”.
notes.other_reading: the god seated within the chest / the guardian spirit

notes.note: To mix something so as to foul it, as water is muddied or dough kneaded.
notes.other_reading: not to defile / not to confuse

notes.note: The word used of a god who is kindly and well-disposed. “Gracious” is used here and for the same word in 2.3; of the spirit within it could also be “serene”.
notes.other_reading: to keep it serene

notes.note: This participle and the two after it (“saying”, “doing”) are masculine singular, and can describe either the spirit or the good person who keeps it. The English participles can be taken either way, as in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: while the good person follows god in good order, saying nothing contrary to what is true

notes.note: Literally “disbelieve him, that he lives ...”. It could also be “distrust him because he lives ...”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: if all people distrust the good person for living simply

notes.note: τέλος is both “end” and “goal”. Here it is where the road arrives and where one must be “ready to be released”, so the end; the other sense may also be heard.
notes.other_reading: the goal of life

notes.note: Literally “easily loosed”, like a knot that comes undone without trouble: ready to be let go from life.
notes.other_reading: easily set free

check.greek: τῶν ποιούντων, ἐπειδὰν κλείσωσι τὰς θύρας
check.note: The Greek as given has no object: “those who do, once they have shut the doors”. “What they do” is supplied and smooths over a gap where a word seems to have dropped out; editors are thought to supply something like “anything at all”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English still reads “those who do what they do once they have shut the doors”, because English needs an object and this one names nothing. The suggested “anything at all” rests on a conjecture remembered and not checked, so it goes into the note, which now says plainly that “what they do” is supplied and that a word may be missing.

check.note: “Guardian” is added. The Greek is “the spirit seated within his chest”.
check.decided: Accepted: “guardian” is removed and the English now reads “the spirit seated within the chest”. “His” is also dropped, since the Greek has no possessive there.

check.note: The participles (following, saying, doing) can go with the spirit or with the one who keeps it. After “keep it gracious” they read most naturally of the spirit, though saying and doing fit the person better.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “but to keep it gracious, following god in good order”. The Greek participles fit the spirit and the person equally in form, and the English participles can likewise be heard of either, while “himself following” would settle what the Greek leaves open. The note records the reading in which they describe the person.

check.note: Found while settling: “the good man”, “him” and “he” were written where the Greek does not single out a man.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “the good person” and “them”, and repeats “the good person” in the last sentence so that “them” there means the people who disbelieve.

check.note: Found while settling: “everything else” added an “every”, and hid the echo between “the rest” and “what is left”, which are one word in the Greek.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “If, then, the rest is shared with those just mentioned, what is left”.

part.left_out: Σῶμα, ψυχή, νοῦς· σώματος αἰσθήσεις, ψυχῆς ὁρμαί, νοῦ δόγματα.
part.why: The 1634 translation puts the chapter’s opening line at the end of its section 3.16 and begins its 3.17 here.

passages.greek: Ἤτοι ἀπὸ μιᾶς πηγῆς νοερᾶς πάντα ὡς ἑνὶ σώματι ἐπισυμβαίνει καὶ οὐ δεῖ τὸ μέρος τοῖς ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὅλου γινομένοις μέμφεσθαι· ἢ ἄτομοι καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ κυκεὼν καὶ σκεδασμός· τί οὖν ταράσσῃ;
passages.english: Either everything happens, one thing upon another, as to one body, from one source that has mind, and the part must not find fault with what comes about for the sake of the whole; or there are atoms, and nothing else but a stirred brew and a scattering. Why, then, are you troubled?

notes.note: Literally “a spring that has mind”. The image is of water from one source. νοερός is “having mind”, from νοῦς, “mind”.
notes.other_reading: from one intelligent spring

notes.note: The verb is “happens” with two prefixes, “upon” and “together”. The English gives the first as “one thing upon another”; it could also mean simply “happens to”. “As to one body” can mean that things happen to the universe as to a single body, or that they happen as things do within a single body.
notes.other_reading: all things befall it as they befall a single body

notes.note: “On behalf of the whole”, which can be “for its good” or “in its interest”.
notes.other_reading: what is done in the interest of the whole

notes.note: A drink made by stirring barley meal and other things into liquid; it separates unless kept stirred. It is used as an image of a mere mixture, and the English keeps it as a brew.
notes.other_reading: nothing but a hotchpotch and a dispersal

notes.note: “Troubled”, literally “stirred up”, which may answer the image of the stirred drink.
notes.other_reading: why then are you in turmoil?

check.note: The verb has a prefix: happens on top of, in addition, one thing following on another. “Happens” gives only the bare verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “everything happens, one thing upon another, as to one body”. “Happens” is kept for the simple verb, as elsewhere.

check.note: Found while settling: “one thinking source” did not show that the word is made from νοῦς, which this translation gives as “mind”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “from one source that has mind”.

part.left_out: τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ λέγεις· τέθνηκας, ἔφθαρσαι, τεθηρίωσαι, ὑποκρίνῃ, συναγελάζῃ, βόσκῃ;
part.why: The 1634 translation ends its section 9.38 at the question and begins its 9.39 with the chapter’s last sentence.

passages.greek: Ὅ τι ἄν σοι συμβαίνῃ, τοῦτό σοι ἐξ αἰῶνος προκατεσκευάζετο καὶ ἡ ἐπιπλοκὴ τῶν αἰτίων συνέκλωθε τήν τε σὴν ὑπόστασιν ἐξ ἀιδίου καὶ τὴν τούτου σύμβασιν.
passages.english: Whatever happens to you was being made ready for you beforehand, from all time, and the interweaving of causes was spinning together, from eternity, both your existence and the happening of this.

notes.note: Two different expressions are used: this one, “from the age”, and ἐξ ἀιδίου, “from the everlasting”. They are given as “from all time” and “from eternity”.
notes.other_reading: from the beginning of time ... from everlasting

notes.note: A past tense of continuing action, with a prefix meaning “beforehand”: “was being prepared in advance”. The verb is the ordinary one for building or fitting something out. The same tense is used for “was spinning”.
notes.other_reading: was prepared for you in advance

notes.note: Literally “what stands under”: a thing’s real existence, its coming to be something.
notes.other_reading: your very being / your substance

notes.note: The noun is from the same verb as “happens” at the start. “Of this” is the particular thing that happens to you.
notes.other_reading: and this event’s falling to you

check.note: The prefix meaning “beforehand” is not given, though “from all time” largely carries it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “was being made ready for you beforehand, from all time”.

passages.greek: Ὅσα ἑκάστῳ συμβαίνει, ταῦτα τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει· ἤρκει τοῦτο. ἀλλ’ ἔτι ἐκεῖνο ὡς ἐπίπαν ὄψει παραφυλάξας, ὅσα ἀνθρώπῳ, καὶ ἑτέροις ἀνθρώποις. κοινότερον δὲ νῦν τὸ συμφέρον ἐπὶ τῶν μέσων λαμβανέσθω.
passages.english: Whatever happens to each is good for the whole. That would be enough. But if you watch you will also see this, as a general rule: whatever happens to one person is good for other people too. Here, though, let “good for” be taken in the more ordinary sense, as applied to things that are neither good nor bad.

notes.note: “Is good for”, literally “brings together”. The sounds of “happens” (συμβαίνει) and “is good for” (συμφέρει) answer each other in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: is to the advantage of the whole

notes.note: A past tense, “this was enough”, used in Greek for what would be enough by itself.
notes.other_reading: That was enough

notes.note: “On the whole, in general, for the most part”. It limits the claim: this holds as a rule, not without exception.
notes.other_reading: in most cases

notes.note: The Greek has no verbs here: literally “whatever to a person, also to other persons”. The English supplies “happens” and “is good for” from the first sentence, in the same order, because the clause has the same shape as that sentence, with “a person” in place of “each” and “other people” in place of “the whole”. “Is good for” could be supplied twice, which is a different claim.
notes.other_reading: whatever is good for one person is good for other people too

notes.note: “More commonly”, that is, in the looser everyday sense of the word and not the strict Stoic sense in which only virtue is good for anyone.
notes.other_reading: in a broader sense

notes.note: Literally “the things in the middle”, the Stoic name for things neither good nor bad in themselves, such as health or money. The English gives the meaning of the term, as in 3.11.
notes.other_reading: as applied to the things in the middle

check.note: The Greek has no verbs. The English supplies “happens” in the first half and “benefits” in the second; it can as well be “whatever benefits one person benefits other people too”, a different claim, and the English reads as if Marcus wrote the verbs.
check.decided: Accepted: the choice is now stated in the note. The English keeps “happens” in the first half and “is good for” in the second, because the clause repeats the shape of the first sentence, and the note says that both verbs are supplied and gives “whatever is good for one person is good for other people too”.

check.note: “Closely” is not in the Greek here, as it is in 4.10.
check.decided: Accepted: “closely” is removed and the English now reads “if you watch you will also see this”.

check.note: A school term rendered literally. A reader of today will not know that “the things in the middle” are things neither good nor bad, such as health and wealth.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as applied to things that are neither good nor bad”, as in 3.11, and the note gives the literal words.

check.note: Found while settling: συμφέρει was “benefits”. This translation gives it as “is good for” where no other word in the passage needs “good”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English reads “is good for the whole”, “is good for other people too” and “let ‘good for’ be taken”.

passages.greek:
Κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν ἕκαστα περαίνεται· οὐ γὰρ κατ’ ἄλλην γέ τινα φύσιν ἤτοι ἔξωθεν περιέχουσαν ἢ ἐμπεριεχομένην ἔνδον ἢ ἔξω ἀπηρτημένην.

Ἤτοι κυκεὼν καὶ ἀντεμπλοκὴ καὶ σκεδασμὸς ἢ ἕνωσις καὶ τάξις καὶ πρόνοια. εἰ μὲν οὗν τὰ πρότερα, τί καὶ ἐπιθυμῶ εἰκαίῳ συγκρίματι καὶ φυρμῷ τοιούτῳ ἐνδιατρίβειν; τί δέ μοι καὶ μέλει ἄλλου τινὸς ἢ τοῦ ὅπως ποτὲ ʽαἶα γίνεσθαιʼ; τί δὲ καὶ ταράσσομαι; ἥξει γὰρ ἐπʼ ἐμὲ ὁ σκεδασμός, ὅ τι ἂν ποιῶ. εἰ δὲ θάτερά ἐστι, σέβω καὶ εὐσταθῶ καὶ θαρρῶ τῷ διοικοῦντι.
passages.english:
Each thing is carried through in accordance with the nature of the whole. For it is certainly not in accordance with any other nature, whether one that surrounds from outside, or one contained within, or one that stands apart outside.

Either a stirred brew and a mutual entanglement and a scattering, or unity and order and providence. Now if it is the first, why do I even want to spend my time in a random compound and a jumble of that kind? And why do I even care about anything other than how, one way or another, to “become earth”? And why am I even troubled? For the scattering will come upon me, whatever I do. But if it is the second, I feel reverence, I stand firm, and I take heart, relying on the one that governs.

notes.note: Literally plural, “of the wholes”, a set phrase for the universe. The English is “the whole”, the same as for the singular τοῦ ὅλου in the other passages.
notes.other_reading: the nature of all things

notes.note: The verb means to be carried through to its limit, accomplished, finished. “Carried through” is used here and for the same verb in 6.1. “Brought to its end” would be heard as “dies”, which the Greek does not say.
notes.other_reading: Each thing is accomplished

notes.note: The participle is from a verb meaning to hang off from something; it can mean “detached, separate” or “hanging from, attached to”. The English takes it as a nature standing apart outside. The Greek gives no object for “surrounds”, “contained” or “stands apart”, and none is supplied.
notes.other_reading: or one attached to it from outside

notes.note: A kykeon was a drink of barley meal and other things stirred into liquid, which has to be kept stirred to hold together. “A stirred brew” keeps both the stirring and the drink, and is also the English for the word in 4.27.
notes.other_reading: a porridge / a hotchpotch

notes.note: The first word means things tangling or interlocking with one another, the second their being scattered apart. Both seem to belong to the atomists’ account of the universe (from memory, unchecked). “Scattering” is used for σκεδασμός both times it occurs in the passage.
notes.other_reading: an interlocking and a dispersal

notes.note: The small word after “how” can make it indefinite (“how ever, in whatever way”) or can be temporal (“at some time”). The English takes it as indefinite, since the two words together commonly mean “in whatever way”.
notes.other_reading: except how, some day, to “become earth”

notes.note: The edition marks these words as a quotation, and the word for “earth” is a poetic form. It seems to echo a line of Homer about turning to water and earth (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: to “turn to earth”

notes.note: The first verb, “I revere” or “I worship”, has no object in the Greek. English “I revere” cannot stand alone, so the English is “I feel reverence”, which keeps the word used for the same verb in 6.36. The second verb means to be stable or steady, of footing or of mind.
notes.other_reading: I worship, I am steady

notes.note: The verb means to be of good courage and, with the dative that follows it, to be confident in someone. The English gives both sides: “I take heart, relying on”. It answers “why am I even troubled?” above.
notes.other_reading: I put my trust in the one that governs

notes.note: The form can be masculine (“him who governs”) or neuter (“that which governs”). “The one that governs” keeps it open. The same verb is used of managing a household or a city.
notes.other_reading: relying on him who administers it

check.note: The verb means that each thing is carried through, accomplished. “Brought to its end” will be heard as “is finished off, dies”, which the Greek does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Each thing is carried through”, the rendering settled for this verb across the translation. The verb speaks of a thing being accomplished, not of its dying, and the same English is used for it in 6.1.

check.note: The participle pictures a nature hanging apart, separate, outside the whole. “Detached outside” is hard to picture and leaves “outside what?” open.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “or one that stands apart outside”, which can be pictured. “It” is not added, because the Greek gives no object to any of the three descriptions, and the note says so.

check.note: The word names a particular drink made by stirring ingredients together. “Stirred mixture” keeps the stirring but loses the drink.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a stirred brew”, here and in 4.27, so the drink is kept along with the stirring.

check.note: The prefix makes the entangling mutual: things interlocking with one another. “An entangling” drops that.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “a mutual entanglement”. The prefix does make the tangling mutual, and one adjective shows it without lengthening the list of three.

check.note: The Greek has three nouns joined by “and” twice, exactly parallel to “unity and order and providence”. The comma made the second and third read as an explanation of the first.
check.decided: Accepted: The three nouns are now joined by “and” twice, as in the Greek, and the second set is given the same way: “unity and order and providence”.

check.note: The small word after “how” can be temporal (“at some time”) or can make “how” indefinite (“in whatever way”). The draft chose the temporal sense.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “how, one way or another, to ‘become earth’”. The two Greek words together usually mean “in whatever way”, and the temporal reading is kept in the note.

check.note: The preposition is “upon me”: the scattering will reach me, overtake me. “Come to me” is a little weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “will come upon me”, since the Greek preposition is “upon”.

check.note: The Greek verb stands without an object, but “I revere” with nothing after it is not something an English speaker says. “I worship” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “I revere” with nothing after it is not English, so the English now reads “I feel reverence”. “Worship” is not used because the same verb is “revere” in 6.36, where the argument needs that word.

check.note: The verb is “I take courage, I am confident”, relying on the one who governs, and it answers “why am I even troubled?” above. “Put my trust in” keeps the reliance and loses the courage.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “I take heart, relying on the one that governs”, which keeps the courage in the verb as well as the reliance.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek has the same small word, “even”, in all three questions, and the draft gave it in the first and the third only.
check.decided: Accepted: The second question now reads “And why do I even care”, so the three questions match as they do in the Greek.

passages.greek: Ἡ τοῦ ὅλου φύσις ἐπὶ τὴν κοσμοποιίαν ὥρμησε· νῦν δὲ ἤτοι πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν γίνεται ἢ ἀλόγιστα καὶ τὰ κυριώτατά ἐστιν ἐφ’ ἃ ποιεῖται ἰδίαν ὁρμὴν τὸ τοῦ κόσμου ἡγεμονικόν. εἰς πολλά σε γαληνότερον ποιήσει τοῦτο μνημονευόμενον.
passages.english: The nature of the whole set out by impulse to make the universe. But now either everything that comes about comes about as a consequence, or even the most important things, the ones at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse, are irrational. Remembering this will make you calmer about many things.

notes.note: This is the verb of the noun ὁρμή, “impulse”, which comes back later in the passage. On its own it means “set out for, started on”. The English gives both, “set out by impulse”, so that the act is clear and the repetition can be heard.
notes.other_reading: The nature of the whole had an impulse toward making the universe

notes.note: Literally “universe-making”. The word for the universe, κόσμος, also means order, so the making of an ordered arrangement is in the word.
notes.other_reading: toward the making of an ordered universe

notes.note: This can be temporal (“but now”, after that first impulse) or logical (“but as things are”). The plain “but now” allows both.
notes.other_reading: But as things are

notes.note: Literally “following after”. Things come about as a sequel to something earlier, here presumably the first impulse, though the Greek does not say to what, and the English does not supply it. The same phrase has the same English in 6.36.
notes.other_reading: comes about by following on from that

notes.greek: ἢ ἀλόγιστα καὶ τὰ κυριώτατά ἐστιν
notes.note: This is the hardest place in the passage. As printed, the second alternative says that even the chief things are “unreasoned”, a conclusion nobody could accept, which pushes toward the first alternative; the word could also be taken with the verb before it, leaving the rest as a separate statement. Editors have doubted or altered the text here (from memory, unchecked), and the English follows the printed words.
notes.other_reading: or it comes about without reasoning; and the most important things are those at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse

notes.note: The word means not reasoned out, not thought through. “Irrational” is used, since “without reason” in English would mean “for no cause”.
notes.other_reading: are unreasoned

notes.note: The adjective means “its own” or “particular, separate”. The English takes the second sense: after one general impulse at the start, a particular impulse aimed at particular things, as against things that merely follow.
notes.other_reading: directs an impulse of its own

notes.note: The Stoic term for the commanding part of a soul, here said of the universe. “The ruling part” is its English in every passage of this set.
notes.other_reading: the commanding faculty of the universe

notes.note: The word is from the calm of a still sea. The English is “calmer” and does not spell out the image.
notes.other_reading: more tranquil, like a sea without wind

check.note: The verb is a single past act: nature set out upon the making of the universe. “Had the impulse to make” can be read as only wanting to, and the next sentence depends on its having begun.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “set out by impulse to make the universe”, so the act is one that was begun and not only wanted. “Its own” is not added, because the Greek word for “own” or “particular” comes only later, with the second impulse.

check.note: This can be temporal (now, after that first impulse) or logical (“but as things are”). The English reads as temporal, which is probably right, but the other reading exists.
check.decided: Accepted: “But now” stays, as the point allows, and the note gives the other reading, “But as things are”.

check.note: The Greek word is “following-on”: things follow on from that first impulse. “By way of consequence” is abstract, and a reader may not see what it is a consequence of.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “comes about as a consequence”, which is plainer. “From that” is not supplied, because the Greek does not say what the things follow from; the note gives the literal “following after”.

check.note: The English takes “unreasoned” as what is said of “even the chief things”. That is the natural construction, but the word could also go with the verb before it, and the text of this sentence has been suspected (from memory, unchecked).
check.decided: Accepted: The construction is kept, as the point advises, and the note now records the second way of construing the words and that the text has been doubted.

check.note: In English “without reason” most easily means “for no reason, without a cause”. The Greek word means not reasoned, not thought out, irrational.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “are irrational”, since “without reason” would be taken as “for no cause”.

check.note: The adjective can mean “its own” or “particular, separate”. The second gives the contrast with things that merely follow on.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a particular impulse”, which gives the contrast with things that only follow. “An impulse of its own” is kept in the note.

check.note: The Greek is only “with regard to many things”. “In the face of” adds the picture of confronting troubles.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “calmer about many things”, since the Greek has no picture of facing anything.

passages.greek: Ὁ τοῦ ὅλου νοῦς κοινωνικός. πεποίηκε γοῦν τὰ χείρω τῶν κρειττόνων ἕνεκεν καὶ τὰ κρείττω ἀλλήλοις συνήρμοσεν. ὁρᾷς πῶς ὑπέταξε, συνέταξε, καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἀπένειμεν ἑκάστοις καὶ τὰ κρατιστεύοντα εἰς ὁμόνοιαν ἀλλήλων συνήγαγεν.
passages.english: The mind of the whole is social. At any rate it has made the worse things for the sake of the better, and has fitted the better to one another. You see how it has ranked things one below another, one beside another, and has given to each according to its worth, and has brought the best things to be of one mind with one another.

notes.note: The word means made for partnership or community, acting for a shared life. “Social” is the nearest plain word and is the English settled for it across this translation, though it is weaker than the Greek.
notes.other_reading: The mind of the whole is a mind for community

notes.note: The particle offers what follows as evidence for the claim, without the full force of “because”. The English is “at any rate”.
notes.other_reading: For instance / Certainly

notes.note: The words are “worse” and “better”, words of value that also cover weaker and stronger, inferior and superior. The plain pair is kept so that “the best things” at the end can be heard as the top of the same scale.
notes.other_reading: the inferior things for the sake of the superior

notes.note: Two verbs from one root of ranking, “ranked under” and “ranked together”, set side by side with no connective. Neither has an object in the Greek; “things” is supplied once.
notes.other_reading: how it has subordinated, how it has coordinated

notes.note: The form is the same for a statement and a question. The English takes it as a statement.
notes.other_reading: Do you see how it has ranked things

notes.note: The phrase is “what is according to worth”, a matter of rank or value.
notes.other_reading: has given to each what it deserves

notes.note: Literally “the things that are best” or “that hold first place”, a word built on the superlative of “better” above. Whether it means the same group as “the better” is not stated.
notes.other_reading: the things of the first rank

notes.note: Literally “sameness of mind”, the usual word for concord among citizens. “Of one mind” keeps the echo of “mind” in the opening sentence.
notes.other_reading: into agreement with one another

check.note: The Greek word means made for partnership, for community. “Social” in today’s English is vague when said of a mind.
check.decided: Declined: “Social” stays. It is the English settled for this word across the translation, so that a reader can follow the one Greek word from passage to passage, and the note gives the fuller sense, “a mind for community”.

check.note: The Greek words are “worse” and “better”, a judgement of worth. “Lower” and “higher” turn it into a picture of height that the Greek does not use.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the worse things for the sake of the better”. The Greek words judge worth and have no picture of height.

check.note: The Greek is two bare verbs built on the same root of ranking. “Some things” is added twice, “put together” reads as “assembled”, and “put under” leaves “under what?” unanswered.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “ranked things one below another, one beside another”. “Things” is supplied once only, and the two halves stand side by side without “and”, as the two verbs do in the Greek.

check.note: This can be a statement or a question (“Do you see how?”). The English has chosen the statement.
check.decided: Accepted: “You see” stays, as the point allows, and the note gives the question as the other reading.

check.note: This is the superlative step of the word translated “higher” two lines earlier: the better things, then the best things. “Higher” and “things that excel” hide that it is the same scale.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the best things”, after “the better” above, so the one scale shows.

check.note: The word is “being of one mind” and echoes “mind” in the first sentence. “Agreement” is correct but thinner and loses the echo.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “to be of one mind with one another”, which keeps the echo of “mind” in the first sentence.

check.note: Found while settling: “what it deserves” brings in a moral colour. The Greek phrase is “according to worth”, and worth is the scale of the whole passage (worse, better, best).
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “has given to each according to its worth”.

passages.greek: Ἡ τῶν ὅλων οὐσία εὐπειθὴς καὶ εὐτρεπής, ὁ δὲ ταύτην διοικῶν λόγος οὐδεμίαν ἐν ἑαυτῷ αἰτίαν ἔχει τοῦ κακοποιεῖν· κακίαν γὰρ οὐκ ἔχει οὐδέ τι κακῶς ποιεῖ οὐδὲ βλάπτεταί τι ὑπ’ ἐκείνου. πάντα δὲ κατ’ ἐκεῖνον γίνεται καὶ περαίνεται.
passages.english: The substance of the whole is obedient and ready, and the reason that governs it has in itself no cause for doing anything bad. For it has no badness, and it treats nothing badly, and nothing is harmed by it. And all things come about and are carried through in accordance with it.

notes.note: Here the stuff of which everything is made, the passive side of the universe as against the reason that works on it. The English is “substance”; “matter” would also serve.
notes.other_reading: The matter of the whole

notes.note: The dictionary sense is “ready, prepared”. A reader might expect “easily turned” or “pliable”, which belongs to a similar-looking word, εὔτρεπτος, used in 6.36. The English keeps to the word printed.
notes.other_reading: obedient and pliable

notes.note: The word covers reason, account and speech. Here it is the rational principle that runs the universe, and the English is “reason”.
notes.other_reading: the rational principle that governs it

notes.note: The word means cause, ground or motive. “Cause” is the English for it in the other passages too.
notes.other_reading: has in itself no reason to do anything bad
