notes.note: Three words from one root follow one another: “to do bad”, “badness” and “badly”. “Bad” is kept in all three so the chain shows. The first could also be “to do harm”, and the middle one is the usual word for vice.
notes.other_reading: no cause for doing harm; for it has no vice

notes.note: This can mean “treats nothing badly”, a common Greek idiom for doing harm to someone, or “does nothing in a bad way”. The English takes the first; the next clause then says the same from the side of the thing harmed.
notes.other_reading: and it does nothing in a bad way

notes.note: The pronoun is masculine because “reason” is a masculine noun in Greek. The English is “it”, not “him”.
notes.other_reading: in accordance with him

notes.note: The verb means to be carried through to the finish, accomplished. The English is the same as in 6.9; it does not mean that things perish.
notes.other_reading: come about and are accomplished

check.note: The word as given means “ready, prepared”. “Ready to hand” adds the picture of a tool lying within reach and is a slightly dated idiom.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “obedient and ready”. The word means ready or prepared, and “to hand” added a picture of a tool within reach.

check.note: In English “does nothing badly” means “does nothing incompetently”. The Greek, coming straight after “doing harm” and “badness”, means it does nothing in a bad, harmful way; “wrongly” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Does nothing badly” would be heard as “does nothing incompetently”, so the English now reads “it treats nothing badly”, taking the Greek as its common idiom for doing harm to something. “Wrongly” is not used because “bad” has to stay through the three words of one root; the other reading is in the note.

check.note: As in 6.9, the verb is “are accomplished, carried through to completion”. After “come about”, “are brought to their end” reads as “come into being and perish”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “come about and are carried through”, the same as in 6.9, so it cannot be heard as “come into being and perish”.

passages.greek: Ὡς ἓν ζῷον τὸν κόσμον, μίαν οὐσίαν καὶ ψυχὴν μίαν ἐπέχον, συνεχῶς ἐπινοεῖν καὶ πῶς εἰς αἴσθησιν μίαν τὴν τούτου πάντα ἀναδίδοται καὶ πῶς ὁρμῇ μιᾷ πάντα πράσσει καὶ πῶς πάντα πάντων τῶν γινομένων συναίτια καὶ οἵα τις ἡ σύννησις καὶ συμμήρυσις.
passages.english: To think constantly of the universe as one living thing, having one substance and one soul; and of how all things are handed up to its one perception; and how it does all things by one impulse; and how all things are joint causes of all the things that come about; and what the spinning together and winding together is like.

notes.note: The verb is an infinitive with no person, the form of a note to oneself or a rule. It is kept impersonal as “To think”.
notes.other_reading: Think constantly of the universe as one living thing

notes.note: The word means any living creature, an animal. The English is “living thing”.
notes.other_reading: as one animal

notes.note: The participle means holding, occupying or possessing. The English is the plain “having”.
notes.other_reading: holding one substance and one soul / made up of one substance and one soul

notes.note: The verb means to be given up or handed on, as a report is handed up to someone. The noun it leads to, αἴσθησιν, is sense-perception or awareness.
notes.other_reading: how all things are reported back to its single awareness

notes.note: In Greek a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb, so this is either “it (the universe) does all things” or “all things act”. The English takes the universe as subject: a living thing that has one perception and acts by one impulse.
notes.other_reading: and how all things act by one impulse

notes.note: Literally “causes together with”, each thing sharing in the causing of each event. The English is “joint causes”.
notes.other_reading: how all things help to cause all that comes about

notes.note: Two rare nouns from thread-work: the first is spinning threads together, the second winding or reeling them together. Both are kept as images. Whether the second is winding into a ball or weaving into a web is not settled.
notes.other_reading: what the spinning together and weaving together is like

check.note: The participle means “having, possessing, comprising”. “Holding one substance and one soul” is slightly odd English, as if the creature were gripping them.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “having one substance and one soul”, since “holding” suggested gripping.

check.note: The sense is “is delivered up, reported back” to the one perception. “Passed up” in today’s English also means “declined”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Passed up” can be misheard, so the English now reads “are handed up to its one perception”. “Delivered up” is not used because in English it suggests surrender.

check.greek: οἵα τις ἡ σύννησις καὶ συμμήρυσις
check.note: The Greek has the definite article: the spinning-together is taken as a fact, and the thought is what it is like. “What kind of … there is” makes its existence part of the question, and the two hyphenated coinages are heavy.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “what the spinning together and winding together is like”, so the spinning is taken as a fact, as the Greek article has it, and the hyphens are gone. “Of it all” is not added, because the Greek has no such words.

check.note: Found while settling: the Greek repeats one word, “all things”, four times in the passage, and the draft gave it as “everything” twice and “all things” twice.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “all things” each time, so the repetition can be heard.

passages.greek: Ἐνθυμήθητι πόσα κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν ἀκαριαῖον χρόνον ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν ἅμα γίνεται σωματικὰ ὁμοῦ καὶ ψυχικά. καὶ οὕτως οὐ θαυμάσεις εἰ πολὺ πλείω, μᾶλλον δὲ πάντα τὰ γινόμενα ἐν τῷ ἑνί τε καὶ σύμπαντι, ὃ δὴ κόσμον ὀνομάζομεν, ἅμα ἐνυφίσταται.
passages.english: Consider how many things come about at once in each of us in the same instant of time, things of the body and things of the soul together. And then you will not be surprised if many more things, or rather all the things that come about, exist at once within the one and entire thing, the very thing we call the universe.

notes.note: Literally “too short to be cut”, of a moment with no length. The English is “instant”.
notes.other_reading: in the same indivisible moment of time

notes.note: Two adjectives, “bodily” and “of the soul”, joined by “together”. The second covers everything the mind or life-principle does, not only what would now be called spiritual.
notes.other_reading: bodily and mental things alike

notes.note: The phrase corrects what has just been said: “or rather”. It is kept as a correction and not smoothed away.
notes.other_reading: many more, indeed all

notes.note: The participle means things that come to be or happen. “Come about” is used for this verb in both sentences, and in the neighbouring passages, because the argument runs from what comes about in us to what comes about in the universe.
notes.other_reading: all the things that happen

notes.note: Two adjectives used as a name: “the one” and “the all-together”. The English is “the one and entire thing”.
notes.other_reading: in the One and All

notes.note: A compound verb: to subsist or have being within something. The English is “exist … within”. The word before it, ἅμα, is “at once”, the same word as in the first sentence.
notes.other_reading: have their being at the same time within

check.note: The same verb returns in the second sentence as “all the things that come about”. The argument runs from what comes about in us to what comes about in the universe, so one English word is wanted.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “how many things come about at once in each of us”, the same words as “all the things that come about” in the second sentence.

check.note: The Greek has one word for “at once”, the same one as in the first sentence, and a verb meaning “exist within”. “Together” is extra.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “exist at once within”. “Together” is gone, since the Greek has only the one word for “at once”.

check.note: A small particle is dropped: “which is precisely what we call”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the very thing we call the universe”, which gives the small word of emphasis its weight.

passages.greek: Ἤτοι κόσμος διατεταγμένος ἢ κυκεὼν συμπεφυρμένος. ἀλλὰ μὴν κόσμος· ἢ ἐν σοὶ μέν τις κόσμος ὑφίστασθαι δύναται, ἐν δὲ τῷ παντὶ ἀκοσμία; καὶ ταῦτα οὕτως πάντων διακεκριμένων καὶ διακεχυμένων καὶ συμπαθῶν.
passages.english: Either an arranged order, or a stirred brew jumbled together. But in fact an order. Or can a kind of order exist in you, and disorder in the all? And this when all things are, as they are, separated out and spread out, and feel with one another.

notes.note: The word κόσμος is both “order” and the ordinary word for the universe, which is its English in the other passages. Here the argument turns on the same word being said of the all and of “you”, and on its opposite, ἀκοσμία, “disorder”, so the English is “order” every time.
notes.other_reading: Either a universe set in order

notes.note: A kykeon was a drink of barley meal stirred into liquid; “a stirred brew” is also its English in 6.10. The participle means kneaded or mixed up together. The manuscripts are said to be troubled at this point and the printed words to be partly an editor’s repair (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what is printed.
notes.other_reading: a hotchpotch all mixed up together

notes.note: A clipped statement with no verb. The two particles give the next step of an argument as a fact, “but in fact”, and nothing is supplied.
notes.other_reading: But there is an order

notes.note: Literally “a certain order”. The indefinite word may limit the claim (“some sort of order”) or simply mean “an order”.
notes.other_reading: can there be an order in you

notes.note: Literally “the all”. It is a different word from the ones given as “the whole” and “the universe” in the other passages, so the English keeps it literal.
notes.other_reading: and disorder in the universe

notes.note: The first two words mean “and that too”, adding a circumstance that makes the thing more striking. The third can mean “so much” or “in the way they are”, and the English takes the second.
notes.other_reading: And this when all things are so separated out

notes.note: Three descriptions of all things: sorted apart, poured out in different directions, and sharing in one another’s states (the Stoic term, literally “affected together”; “sympathy” is avoided because it now means pity). It is open whether all three are evidence of order, or whether the first two concede how separate things are and the third answers them. They are joined with plain “and”, as in the Greek.
notes.other_reading: when all things, though so distinct and so dispersed, still feel with one another

check.note: The Greek noun means both “universe” and “order”, and Marcus plays on it against “disorder” below. With “order” alone the reader does not see that the question is about the universe, and “an order that has been arranged” says the same thing twice.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The doubled wording is tightened to “an arranged order”, but “order” is kept in all three places. The argument needs one word that can be said of the all and of “you” and that has “disorder” as its opposite; the note says the Greek word is also “the universe”, as it is in the other passages.

check.note: The Greek particles state the next step of an argument as a fact: “but in fact it is”. “Surely” in English sounds like an appeal or a hope.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “But in fact an order.” The Greek particles state a step of the argument as fact, and there is still no verb, as in the Greek.

check.note: This is “the all”, a different Greek word from the one given as “the whole” in the other passages of this set, and the two should be kept apart.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “in the all”, which keeps this word apart from “the whole” of the other passages. “The universe” is not used because it is the English settled for κόσμος in the other passages.

check.note: The Greek idiom adds a circumstance that makes the thing just said more absurd. “And that, when” is an old-fashioned English idiom that a reader of today is likely to stumble on.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “And this when all things are, as they are, separated out and spread out, and feel with one another.” The three descriptions stay joined by plain “and”, without “still”, because the Greek does not say that the third answers the first two; the note gives that reading.

check.note: The participle is “poured out, diffused”. “Spread abroad” is archaic.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “spread out”, and the note gives the literal “poured out in different directions”.

check.note: The word means sharing in each other’s condition, responding to one another. “Affected together” could be read as merely “affected at the same time”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Affected together” could be heard as “affected at the same time”, so the English now reads “feel with one another”, which is what the two parts of the Greek word say. “Responsive” is not used because it leaves out the shared feeling.

passages.greek: Ἡ Ἀσία, ἡ Εὐρώπη γωνίαι τοῦ κόσμου· πᾶν πέλαγος σταγὼν τοῦ κόσμου· Ἄθως βωλάριον τοῦ κόσμου· πᾶν τὸ ἐνεστὼς τοῦ χρόνου στιγμὴ τοῦ αἰῶνος. πάντα μικρά, εὔτρεπτα, ἐναφανιζόμενα. Πάντα ἐκεῖθεν ἔρχεται, ἀπ’ ἐκείνου τοῦ κοινοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ ὁρμήσαντα ἣ κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν. καὶ τὸ χάσμα οὖν τοῦ λέοντος καὶ τὸ δηλητήριον καὶ πᾶσα κακουργία ὡς ἄκανθα, ὡς βόρβορος, ἐκείνων ἐπιγεννήματα τῶν σεμνῶν καὶ καλῶν. μὴ οὖν αὐτὰ ἀλλότρια τούτου οὗ σέβεις φαντάζου, ἀλλὰ τὴν πάντων πηγὴν ἐπιλογίζου.
passages.english:
Asia, Europe: corners of the universe. Every sea: a drop of the universe. Athos: a small clod of the universe. All of present time: a point of eternity. All things are small, easily changed, vanishing.

All things come from there: they have set out from that common ruling part, or they come as a consequence. So the gaping jaws of the lion too, and poison, and every kind of harm, like a thorn, like mud, are by-products of those revered and beautiful things. So do not picture them as foreign to what you revere, but consider the source of all things.

notes.note: Literally “angles”, then corners or nooks. The Greek has no verb in this run of phrases, and colons keep it as terse as it is.
notes.other_reading: Asia and Europe are nooks of the universe

notes.note: Without the article this is “every sea”, each open sea taken singly. It could also be read as “the whole sea”.
notes.other_reading: The whole sea: a drop of the universe

notes.note: Athos is a high mountain on a headland in northern Greece. The second word is a diminutive of “clod of earth”.
notes.other_reading: Athos: a little lump of soil

notes.note: The first word is a prick or dot, the mark a point makes. The second is the whole of time, here “eternity”. “Of” is kept, as in the three phrases before it.
notes.other_reading: a pinprick in the whole of time

notes.note: The compound means disappearing into something. The Greek does not say into what, and the list before it covers both the universe and time, so the English is “vanishing” and names nothing.
notes.other_reading: disappearing into it

notes.note: The participle means “having set out, started”, and is the verb of ὁρμή, “impulse”, as in 7.75, where the ruling part of the universe directs an impulse at things. The small word after it is printed with a breathing that would make it “which”, and that gives no sense; it is read as “or”.
notes.other_reading: set going by an impulse of that common ruling part, or as a consequence

notes.note: Literally “following after”: things that are not aimed at directly but come as a sequel. The Greek does not say to what, and the English does not either. The same phrase has the same English in 7.75.
notes.other_reading: or as a side-effect that follows

notes.note: The noun means doing harm, and most often wrongdoing or malice in a person. Beside jaws, poison, thorn and mud, the English takes it widely as “every kind of harm”. On the other reading it is human wickedness.
notes.other_reading: and all wickedness, like a thorn, like mud

notes.note: The small word means “like” or “as”. It can give thorn and mud as examples of harm, or it can compare: jaws, poison and harm are by-products in the way that a thorn and mud are. English “like” allows both.
notes.other_reading: such as a thorn, such as mud

notes.note: Literally “things born on top of” or “born after” something. It seems to be a Stoic term for what comes along with a thing without being its purpose (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: are after-growths of those revered and beautiful things

notes.note: The first adjective is said of what commands reverence and is from the same root as “revere” in the next sentence, so the English is “revered”. The second means beautiful or fine. The plural “those things” is not explained; it seems to point back to the ruling part and what it does.
notes.other_reading: of those holy and noble things

notes.note: The forms can be masculine or neuter: “him whom you revere” or “what you revere”. The English keeps the neuter.
notes.other_reading: as foreign to him whom you worship

check.note: The Greek is “of eternity”, the fourth in a row of “of” phrases. “In” breaks the series.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a point of eternity”, the fourth “of” in the row, as in the Greek.

check.note: The verb has a prefix “in”: vanishing into something, being lost in it. The English drops that; “vanishing into it” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: The prefix does mean vanishing into something, but the Greek names nothing for things to vanish into, and “it” in English would point at eternity alone when the list covers the universe as well as time. “Vanishing” stays, and the note gives the fuller sense.

check.note: The participle is simply “having set out, started from”. “By impulse” is added, and it suggests the impulse is the things’ own and not the ruling part’s.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “they have set out from that common ruling part”, without “by impulse”. The note says that the verb is the one behind “impulse” in 7.75.

check.greek: καὶ τὸ χάσμα οὖν τοῦ λέοντος
check.note: The first word is “also, even”: so the lion’s jaws too. The English keeps “so” and drops “too”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “So the gaping jaws of the lion too”.

check.note: The noun is abstract: doing harm, mischief, and most often wrongdoing by people. The English makes it a concrete “thing”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “every kind of harm”, which keeps the noun abstract. The note gives the reading “all wickedness”.

check.note: The Greek word is taken as introducing examples (“such as”). “Like a thorn” reads in English as a comparison.
check.decided: Declined: The Greek word is the ordinary one for “like” or “as”, and it can either give examples or compare these things to a thorn and to mud as plain cases of by-products. English “like” can be heard both ways too, so it stays, and a note now sets out the two readings.

check.note: The word means things produced in addition, by-products. “After-growths” is not a word a reader of today uses.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “by-products”, and the literal “things born after” is in the note.

check.note: The first adjective means “revered, august”, where “solemn” today means grave or serious. It is from the same root as “revere” in the next sentence, and the argument uses the link.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “those revered and beautiful things”, so the link with “what you revere” in the next sentence can be heard.

check.note: “That which” is stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “foreign to what you revere”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “either” before the first of the two ways, and the Greek has only “or” between them.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “they have set out from that common ruling part, or they come as a consequence”, with no “either”.

passages.greek: Τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τὸ κράτιστον τίμα· ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο τὸ πᾶσι χρώμενον καὶ πάντα διέπον. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τῶν ἐν σοὶ τὸ κράτιστον τίμα· ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ἐκείνῳ ὁμογενές. καὶ γὰρ ἐπὶ σοῦ τὸ τοῖς ἄλλοις χρώμενον τοῦτό ἐστι καὶ ὁ σὸς βίος ὑπὸ τούτου διοικεῖται.
passages.english: Of the things in the universe, honour what is supreme: this is what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, of the things in you too, honour what is supreme: this is what is akin to that other. For in your case too, this is what uses the others, and your life is governed by it.

notes.note: The word is the superlative both of “strong” and, in common use, of “good”: the mightiest and the best. “What is supreme” covers both, and is the same English both times.
notes.other_reading: honour the most powerful / honour what is best

notes.note: The verb means to honour or to value highly, and is used of honouring gods.
notes.other_reading: revere / hold in highest value

notes.note: Literally “making use of all”, as a workman uses tools. The same verb returns in the last sentence and “uses” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: that which employs all things

notes.note: The verb means to manage or conduct affairs. The English is “directs”, kept distinct from “governed” at the end, which is a different Greek verb.
notes.other_reading: and manages all things

notes.note: Literally “of the same family (or kind) as that one”, pointing back to what is supreme in the universe.
notes.other_reading: what is of the same kind as that

notes.note: The phrase means “in your case”, a different phrase from “in you” just before.
notes.other_reading: For in you too

check.note: The word is a superlative that means “strongest, mightiest” and equally “best, most excellent”. The English has chosen power both times.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “honour what is supreme” both times, which covers “mightiest” and “best” without choosing between them. The note gives both.

check.note: “As that” is unclear at first reading; “that” is the supreme thing in the universe just mentioned. The Greek word also carries kinship.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “what is akin to that other”, which keeps the kinship in the Greek word and makes clear that “that” is the supreme thing in the universe.

check.note: Two lines earlier “in you” stood for a different Greek phrase. This one is “in your case”, and the same English for both blurs a small step.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “For in your case too”, so the two different Greek phrases have different English.

passages.greek: Σπέρμα εἰς μήτραν ἀφεὶς ἀπεχώρησε καὶ λοιπὸν ἄλλη αἰτία παραλαβοῦσα ἐργάζεται καὶ ἀποτελεῖ βρέφος· ἐξ οἵου οἷον; πάλιν· τροφὴν διὰ φάρυγγος ἀφῆκε καὶ λοιπὸν ἄλλη αἰτία παραλαβοῦσα αἴσθησιν καὶ ὁρμὴν καὶ τὸ ὅλον ζωὴν καὶ ῥώμην καὶ ἄλλα (ὅσα καὶ οἷα;) ποιεῖ. ταῦτα οὖν ἐν τοιαύτῃ ἐγκαλύψει γινόμενα θεωρεῖν καὶ τὴν δύναμιν οὕτως ὁρᾶν, ὡς καὶ τὴν βρίθουσαν καὶ τὴν ἀνωφερῆ ὁρῶμεν, οὐχὶ τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ἧττον ἐναργῶς.
passages.english: A man lets seed go into a womb and goes away, and from then on another cause takes it over, works on it and brings a baby to completion. From what a thing, what a thing! Again: he lets food go down through the throat, and from then on another cause takes it over and makes perception and impulse and, in sum, life and strength and other things (how many, and what things!). So: to look at these things that come about under such a veil, and to see the power just as we see the power that presses downward and the power that rises upward, not with the eyes, but no less clearly.

notes.note: The Greek names no subject. The participle is masculine and the act is a man’s, and the tense is a past used for what generally happens. The English is “A man” and the present tense.
notes.other_reading: He let seed go into a womb and went away

notes.note: Literally “another cause, having received it”, as one takes over a thing handed on. The same phrase is repeated word for word in the second half, and the English repeats too.
notes.other_reading: a different cause takes charge of it

notes.note: Three words: “out of what sort of thing, what sort of thing”. The edition prints a question mark, but the words read as an exclamation of wonder and are punctuated so. The same word of wonder returns in the bracket below, “what things!”.
notes.other_reading: From what kind of beginning, what kind of result?

notes.note: The same verb as for the seed, “let go, released”, and “lets … go” is kept so the parallel shows. The subject is again unstated: “he” carries on from “a man”, since the Greek names no new subject, though anyone who eats is meant.
notes.other_reading: a person lets food go down through the throat

notes.note: Used as an adverb: “on the whole, in general”, summing up the list. The English is “in sum”.
notes.other_reading: and, altogether, life and strength

notes.note: A noun meaning a veiling or wrapping up. It is kept as an image: a veil under which the work goes on unseen.
notes.other_reading: that come about in such concealment

notes.note: This and the next verb are infinitives with no person, the form of a note to oneself. They are kept impersonal as “to look” and “to see”.
notes.other_reading: So look at these things, and see the power

notes.note: Two adjectives with “power” understood, each describing the power itself: the one that presses down with weight and the one that tends upward. Heavy things are seen to fall and light things to rise, but the power is not seen by the eyes.
notes.other_reading: the force that makes things heavy and the force that makes them rise

check.note: The verb is “went away, withdrew”. “Walks” adds a picture, and a casual tone, that the Greek does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “goes away”, since the Greek verb has no picture of walking.

check.note: The verb is “brings to completion”. “Finishes a baby” is odd English and can be misheard.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “works on it and brings a baby to completion”.

check.note: The Greek is a compact exclamation: from such a beginning, such a result. “From what, what a thing!” is hard to parse on first reading.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “From what a thing, what a thing!”, so that both halves are plainly exclamations. The Greek order is kept and “beginning” is not added, because the Greek has the same bare word twice; the same word in the bracket is now “what things!”.

check.note: The noun is “concealment, being veiled”. “Under such a covering” is literal and a little puzzling.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “under such a veil”. The Greek noun is a veiling, and a veil keeps the image where “so hidden from sight” would drop it.

check.note: In “to see the power in the way we see”, the eye first reads “the power in the way” as one phrase.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “to see the power just as we see”, so “the power in the way” can no longer be read as one phrase.

check.note: Both words describe the power itself: the one that presses downward and the one that tends upward. The English supplies objects (“things”, “them”) and makes both act on something else.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the power that presses downward and the power that rises upward”, with no objects supplied, since both words describe the power itself.

passages.greek: Ἴθι ἐπὶ τὴν ποιότητα τοῦ αἰτίου καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑλικοῦ αὐτὸ περιγράψας θέασαι· εἶτα καὶ τὸν χρόνον περιόρισον, ὅσον πλεῖστον ὑφίστασθαι πέφυκε τοῦτο τὸ ἰδίως ποιόν.
passages.english: Go to the quality of the cause; mark the cause off from the material and look at it. Then also set the limit of the time: the longest that this thing, with its own particular quality, can by nature last.

notes.note: The first word is “quality”, literally “what-sort-ness”. The second is “the causal”, the active element in a thing, set against “the material” in the next phrase. The English is “the cause”.
notes.other_reading: Go to what sort of thing the causal element is

notes.note: The verb means to draw a line around a thing, and so to mark it off. The pronoun is neuter and so points to the cause, not to the quality, and the English names it. It could also be the thing under examination as a whole.
notes.other_reading: isolate the thing itself from the material and study it

notes.note: The adjective from the word for timber or stuff: “the material”. Stoic analysis divides each thing into its material and its cause.
notes.other_reading: from the matter

notes.note: A different verb from the earlier one, but again one of drawing a boundary: to fix the limits of something. The English is “set the limit”.
notes.other_reading: Then determine the time as well

notes.note: Literally “how much at the most it is by nature such as to subsist”. The English is “the longest that this thing can by nature last”.
notes.other_reading: the utmost length of time it is of a nature to exist

notes.note: Literally “the thing qualified in a way of its own”. It seems to be the Stoic technical term for an individual as marked by its own particular quality (from memory, unchecked). The word repeats the root of “quality” in the first sentence, and the English repeats “quality”.
notes.other_reading: this individually qualified thing

check.note: In the Greek the pronoun is neuter and so points to “the cause” (“quality” is feminine). In the English “it” can be either the quality or the cause.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “mark the cause off from the material and look at it”. The Greek pronoun is neuter and so cannot be the quality, which is feminine.

check.note: This is a school term given as a school term, and a reader of today will take “qualified” as “having qualifications” or “limited”. The Greek is: this thing that is of its own particular quality.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “this thing, with its own particular quality”, which says what the school term means and repeats “quality” from the first sentence.

check.note: “Is of a nature to last” is correct but stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “can by nature last” in place of “is of a nature to last”.

passages.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικόν ἐστι τὸ ἑαυτὸ ἐγεῖρον καὶ τρέπον καὶ ποιοῦν μὲν ἑαυτὸ οἷον ἂν καὶ θέλῃ, ποιοῦν δὲ ἑαυτῷ φαίνεσθαι πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον οἷον αὐτὸ θέλει.
passages.english: The ruling part is what wakes itself and turns itself; it makes itself whatever it wants to be, and it makes everything that happens appear to itself the way it itself wants.

notes.note: The Stoic term for the commanding faculty of the soul, literally “the leading thing”. “The ruling part” is its English in every passage of this set.
notes.other_reading: The governing faculty

notes.note: The verb means to wake from sleep or to rouse into action. The image of waking is kept.
notes.other_reading: what rouses itself

notes.note: The verb means to turn, and so either to direct oneself somewhere or to change oneself. “Turns itself” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: and changes itself / and directs itself

notes.note: Literally “of whatever sort it may in fact wish”, an indefinite form. The second clause has a plain statement with an emphatic “itself”: “such as it itself wants”. The English is “whatever it wants to be” for the first and “the way it itself wants” for the second.
notes.other_reading: makes itself such as it may wish

notes.note: “To appear to itself”: the verb is the one behind the Stoic word for an impression. The claim is that the ruling part settles how each event looks to it.
notes.other_reading: makes everything that happens seem to it

check.note: The Greek sets the last two clauses against each other as a pair (makes itself, and makes what happens appear). The English runs all four verbs as one list with “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now sets the last two clauses apart as a pair after a semicolon: “it makes itself whatever it wants to be, and it makes everything that happens appear to itself the way it itself wants”.

check.note: The first clause is indefinite in the Greek (“whatever it may want”); this one is a plain statement (“such as it itself wants”). The English repeats “whatever”, and “as whatever it itself wants” is clumsy.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the way it itself wants”, a plain statement, where the first clause keeps the indefinite “whatever it wants to be”. “To itself” is kept, since the Greek has the reflexive.

passages.greek: Χρὴ καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα παραφυλάσσειν, ὅτι καὶ τὰ ἐπιγινόμενα τοῖς φύσει γινομένοις ἔχει τι εὔχαρι καὶ ἐπαγωγόν. οἷον ἄρτου ὀπτωμένου παραρρήγνυταί τινα μέρη· καὶ ταῦτα οὖν τὰ διέχοντα οὕτως καὶ τρόπον τινὰ παρὰ τὸ ἐπάγγελμα τῆς ἀρτοποιίας ἔχοντα ἐπιπρέπει πως καὶ προθυμίαν πρὸς τὴν τροφὴν ἰδίως ἀνακινεῖ. πάλιν τε τὰ σῦκα ὁπότε ὡραιότατά ἐστι, κέχηνε καὶ ἐν ταῖς δρυπεπέσιν ἐλαίαις αὐτὸ τὸ ἐγγὺς τῇ σήψει ἴδιόν τι κάλλος τῷ καρπῷ προστίθησι. καὶ οἱ στάχυες κάτω νεύοντες καὶ τὸ τοῦ λέοντος ἐπισκύνιον καὶ ὁ τῶν συῶν ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ῥέων ἀφρὸς καὶ πολλὰ ἕτερα, κατ’ ἰδίαν εἴ τις σκοποίη, πόρρω ὄντα τοῦ εὐειδοῦς, ὅμως διὰ τὸ τοῖς φύσει γινομένοις ἐπακολουθεῖν συνεπικοσμεῖ καὶ ψυχαγωγεῖ· ὥστε, εἴ τις ἔχει πάθος καὶ ἔννοιαν βαθυτέραν πρὸς τὰ ἐν τῷ ὅλῳ γινόμενα, σχεδὸν οὐδὲν οὐχὶ δόξει αὐτῷ καὶ τῶν κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν συμβαινόντων ἡδέως πως διασυνίστασθαι. οὗτος δὲ καὶ θηρίων ἀληθῆ χάσματα οὐχ ἧσσον ἡδέως ὄψεται ἢ ὅσα γραφεῖς καὶ πλάσται μιμούμενοι δεικνύουσιν, καὶ γραὸς καὶ γέροντος ἀκμήν τινα καὶ ὥραν καὶ τὸ ἐν παισὶν ἐπαφρόδιτον τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ σώφροσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς ὁρᾶν δυνήσεται· καὶ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα οὐ παντὶ πιθανά, μόνῳ δὲ τῷ πρὸς τὴν φύσιν καὶ τὰ ταύτης ἔργα γνησίως ᾠκειωμένῳ προσπεσεῖται.
passages.english: One should also take note of things like this: that even what comes about on top of the things that come about by nature has something graceful and attractive about it. For example, when bread is baking, some parts of it break open at the side; and so these parts too, which stand open like this and are in a way contrary to what the baker’s craft sets out to do, somehow look right and stir up an eagerness for the food in a way of their own. Again, figs gape open when they are at their ripest; and in olives ripened on the tree, the very nearness to rotting adds a certain beauty of its own to the fruit. And ears of grain bending down, and the frown on the lion’s brow, and the foam running from the mouths of wild boars, and many other things are far from good-looking if one looks at them by themselves; and yet, because they come as consequences of the things that come about by nature, they help to adorn them and they charm the mind. So if someone has a deeper feeling for, and understanding of, the things that come about in the whole, there is almost nothing, even among the things that happen as consequences, that will not seem to that person to be put together in a way that somehow gives pleasure. And that person will look even at the real gaping jaws of wild animals with no less pleasure than at all those that painters and sculptors show in imitation; and will be able to see a kind of prime and ripeness in an old woman and an old man, and to see with their own chaste eyes the seductive charm of the young. And many such things, which will not convince everyone, will strike only the one who has become truly at home with nature and its works.

notes.note: Literally “the things that come about on top of” the works of nature, what arises in addition to them: side effects, by-products. The English keeps “come about” for both halves of the phrase, as the Greek repeats one verb. “By-products” is avoided because it brings in a workshop the Greek does not have here.
notes.other_reading: even the by-products of the things that come about by nature

notes.note: ἐπάγγελμα is what a craft professes or promises to deliver. παρά here can be “contrary to” or, more mildly, “beside, outside”. The English reads “contrary to what the baker’s craft sets out to do”.
notes.other_reading: in a way outside what the art of baking professes

notes.note: The verb ranges from “are conspicuous” to “are becoming, suit”. The English takes the second, since the point is that they please.
notes.other_reading: somehow catch the eye

notes.note: “Gape” is kept here because the same root returns below in χάσματα, the “gaping jaws” of the wild animals.
notes.other_reading: figs split open when they are at their ripest

notes.note: A rare word for fruit ripened on the tree, fully ripe; a related form means “ready to drop from the tree”. The English keeps the literal “ripened on the tree”.
notes.other_reading: in olives ripe enough to drop

notes.note: The word names the skin above the eyes that is drawn down in a frown, and so the frown itself. The English gives the part and the look together, without a separate adjective.
notes.other_reading: the skin of the lion’s brow

notes.note: The word covers pigs and wild boars alike. Foam at the mouth points to the wild animal, so the English reads “wild boars”.
notes.other_reading: the foam running from the mouths of pigs

notes.note: ἐπακολουθεῖν is literally “follow upon”, and the school phrase κατ’ ἐπακολούθησιν in the next sentence is “by way of following upon”; “consequences” is used in both places so that the link can be heard. Neither of the next two verbs has an expressed object: the first is “join in adorning”, where the English supplies “them”, and the second is literally “lead the soul”, said of anything that attracts or entertains, where the English supplies “the mind”.
notes.other_reading: because they follow upon the things that come about by nature, they add to the adornment and draw the soul

notes.note: πάθος is usually a bad “passion” in Stoic writing; here it is neutral, a sensitivity or feeling. “Deeper” agrees in form with the nearer noun only, but an adjective placed after two nouns can cover both, and the English takes it so.
notes.other_reading: a feeling for the things that come about in the whole, and a deeper understanding of them

notes.note: The verb is very rare and its exact sense is uncertain: “to be constituted, to hold together”, possibly “to present itself”. ἡδέως (“with pleasure”) could describe how the thing is composed or how it strikes the viewer. “Pleasure” is kept because the same adverb returns in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: that will not seem to that person to present itself in a somehow pleasant way

notes.note: ὥρα is “season”, and so the bloom of a person at their best; it echoes ὡραιότατα (“ripest”) used of the figs above. “Ripeness” keeps that echo.
notes.other_reading: a kind of prime and bloom

notes.greek: τὸ ἐν παισὶν ἐπαφρόδιτον τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ σώφροσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς
notes.note: ἐπαφρόδιτον has Aphrodite in it: charm of the kind that draws desire, which is why the eyes are called σώφρονες, “self-controlled, chaste”. παισίν can be “boys”, “children” or the young in general, and the English keeps the wide word. The Greek has one verb for all three things seen, with the eyes placed next to this last one; the English repeats “see” so that the eyes stay beside it.
notes.other_reading: and will be able to see, with eyes that keep their self-control, a kind of prime and ripeness in an old woman and an old man, and the alluring charm of boys

notes.note: Literally “not persuasive to everyone”: things that not everyone would find believable or appealing. The verb that follows (προσπεσεῖται) is “will fall upon, will occur to”; the English reads “will strike”.
notes.other_reading: many such things, not credible to everyone, will occur only to the one who

notes.note: The verb is from the Stoic term for coming to treat something as one’s own or as kin (οἰκείωσις). “At home with” keeps the household image in the word.
notes.other_reading: who has genuinely made nature and its works their own

check.greek: τὸ ἐν παισὶν ἐπαφρόδιτον τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ σώφροσιν ὀφθαλμοῖς
check.note: ἐπαφρόδιτον is charm of the kind that belongs to Aphrodite, and παισίν can mean boys or the young as well as children; “the loveliness in children” takes the innocent reading, so the reader cannot see why chaste eyes are mentioned. The English had also moved the eyes forward, away from this item.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and to see with their own chaste eyes the seductive charm of the young”, with the eyes beside this last item as in the Greek. “Chaste” is kept for σώφροσιν because it is the plain English word for self-control in matters of desire; the note gives “self-controlled” and “boys”.

check.note: βαθυτέραν agrees with the nearer noun but can be meant for both: “a deeper feeling and understanding”. The English gave “deeper” to understanding only.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a deeper feeling for, and understanding of, the things that come about in the whole”. An adjective placed after two nouns most naturally covers both, and a bare πάθος would be odd in a Stoic writer; the note gives the narrower reading.

check.greek: καὶ ταῦτα οὖν τὰ διέχοντα οὕτως
check.note: οὖν is dropped and καί here is “too” or “even”: the Greek applies the opening claim to the bread, while the English only continued the description.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and so these parts too, which stand open like this”. “So” gives οὖν and “too” gives καί, so the bread is heard as a case of the opening claim.

check.greek: οὗτος δὲ καὶ θηρίων ἀληθῆ χάσματα
check.note: δὲ καί is dropped: “and such a person will also, or even, look at”. The καί marks the jaws of beasts as a further and harder case.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And that person will look even at the real gaping jaws of wild animals”.

check.note: ἐπισκύνιον names the part, the skin over the brows that is drawn down in a frown. “Scowling” spells out an expression that the Greek leaves in the noun.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the frown on the lion’s brow”. The added adjective is gone, and the noun’s own sense, the drawn-down skin of the brow, is given by “frown” and “brow” together.

check.greek: ὁ τῶν συῶν ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ῥέων ἀφρὸς
check.note: σῦς is pig or wild boar. “Boars” is the likelier reading with the foam, but it is a choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “wild boars”, which makes the choice plain, since “boar” alone can also mean a farm animal. The note keeps “pigs” as the other reading.

check.note: The verb is “help to adorn”, with the natural things they follow on as the understood object. “Add to the adornment” leaves the reader asking what is adorned.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they help to adorn them and they charm the mind”. “Them” is the things that come about by nature, the object the Greek leaves to be understood.

check.note: “The things that happen by way of following on” is accurate word for word but hard to understand as English; so, less badly, is “what comes along on top of” in the first sentence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the things that happen as consequences”, and the verb before it “because they come as consequences of the things that come about by nature”, so one English word still carries the repeated Greek word. “After-effects” and “mere” are not used, since the Greek speaks of following, not of time, and has no “mere”. The first sentence now reads “what comes about on top of”, keeping one verb for γίνομαι.

check.note: τι is dropped: “a certain beauty of its own”. Marcus qualifies each claim in this passage and the other qualifiers are kept.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a certain beauty of its own”.

check.greek: κατ’ ἰδίαν εἴ τις σκοποίη, πόρρω ὄντα τοῦ εὐειδοῦς
check.note: Found while settling: the draft’s “if one looked at them by themselves, they are far from good-looking” mixed its tenses and broke the list off with a colon.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and many other things are far from good-looking if one looks at them by themselves; and yet”. The sentence runs as one statement, as the Greek does, and nothing is added.

passages.greek: Τὰ πλεῖστα, ὦν ἡ πληθὺς θαυμάζει, εἰς γενικώτατα ἀνάγεται τὰ ὑπὸ ἕξεως ἣ φύσεως συνεχόμενα, λίθους, ξύλα, συκᾶς, ἀμπέλους, ἐλαίας· τὰ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν ὀλίγῳ μετριωτέρων εἰς τὰ ὑπὸ ψυχῆς, οἶον ποίμνας, ἀγέλας· τὰ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν ἔτι χαριεστέρων εἰς τὰ ὑπὸ λογικῆς ψυχῆς, οὐ μέντοι καθολικῆς, ἀλλὰ καθὸ τεχνικὴ ἢ ἄλλως πως ἐντρεχής, ἢ κατὰ ψιλὸν τὸ πλῆθος ἀνδραπόδων κεκτῆσθαι. ὁ δὲ ψυχὴν λογικὴν καθολικὴν καὶ πολιτικὴν τιμῶν οὐδὲν ἔτι τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιστρέφεται, πρὸ ἁπάντων δὲ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν λογικῶς καὶ κοινωνικῶς ἔχουσαν καὶ κινουμένην διασῴζει καὶ τῷ ὁμογενεῖ εἰς τοῦτο συνεργεῖ.
passages.english: Most of the things the crowd admires come down to the most general kind, the things held together by cohesion or by natural growth: stones, timber, fig trees, vines, olive trees. The things admired by people of a slightly better sort come down to the things held together by soul, such as flocks and herds. The things admired by people more refined still come down to the things held together by rational soul; not, however, rational soul as such, but in so far as it is skilled in a craft or adept in some other way, or merely in terms of owning a great number of slaves. But whoever honours rational soul as such, and as civic, no longer pays attention to any of the other things, but before everything else preserves their own soul rational and social in its condition and its movement, and works together with whoever is of the same kind toward this.

notes.note: Literally “are led back to the most generic”: are classed under the broadest, least specific kind of thing. The English reads “come down to” and keeps that phrase for the two later steps, where the Greek leaves the verb to be understood.
notes.other_reading: are referred to the most generic class

notes.note: Bare Stoic terms for the two lowest ways a thing is held together: ἕξις, the “holding” that makes a stone or a log one thing, and φύσις, “nature” in the narrow sense of the growing principle of plants. The English reads “cohesion” and “natural growth”, because plain “nature” would be taken as nature at large. The text as given prints ἣ where ἢ (“or”) must be meant, and likewise ὦν for ὧν and οἶον for οἷον; they are read so.
notes.other_reading: held together by a state or by nature

notes.note: μέτριος is “moderate, within measure”, and of people “decent, respectable”. The passage ranks people by what they admire (the crowd, those a little better, the more refined still), so the English gives the sense in use.
notes.other_reading: by people who are a little more moderate

notes.note: ψυχή here is the next step up: the life of an animal, not yet reason. “Soul” is kept because the passage climbs by repeating this one word (soul, rational soul, one’s own soul).
notes.other_reading: the things held together by animal life

notes.note: The word means “more graceful, more accomplished”, and was a usual way of saying “the more cultivated people”.
notes.other_reading: by people of still more taste

notes.note: καθολικός is “general, universal”. It is set against καθό, “in so far as”: rational soul valued in general, simply as rational soul, as against rational soul valued in one respect. “As such” is used both times the word occurs. It can also be taken as “universal”, the reason that all rational beings share.
notes.other_reading: though not rational soul as universal; and below, rational soul that is universal and civic

notes.greek: ἢ κατὰ ψιλὸν τὸ πλῆθος ἀνδραπόδων κεκτῆσθαι
notes.note: A compressed clause, taken as a third way of valuing rational souls: not for any skill but for the bare fact of owning many of them, as slaves. ψιλόν (“bare, mere”) is read with the owning; it could go with the number instead. πλῆθος is a great number, a mass.
notes.other_reading: or in terms of owning a bare quantity of slaves

notes.note: “Belonging to a city, fit for life as a citizen”. The English reads “civic” here and “social” for the different word κοινωνικῶς in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: rational soul as such, and as political

notes.note: The verb is literally “turns toward”; with this case it means “pays heed to, cares about”.
notes.other_reading: no longer turns to look at any of the other things

notes.note: τῷ ὁμογενεῖ is singular and can be masculine (“the one who is of the same kind”) or neuter (“what is of the same kind”). With a verb of working together the English takes it as a person. “Toward this” most likely means toward keeping the soul rational and social, so the sense is helping one’s fellow to do the same.
notes.other_reading: and works together with what is of the same kind toward this

check.note: The Greek has the bare school terms ἕξις and φύσις. “Natural growth” folds an explanation of φύσις into the text; it is the right explanation, but more than the word says.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “by cohesion or by natural growth”. φύσις here is the school name for the growing principle of plants, as the fig trees, vines and olive trees show, and plain “nature” would be read as nature at large, which holds stones and animals too. ἕξις is likewise given by its sense, “cohesion”, and the note records the bare terms.

check.note: καθολικῆς can be “rational soul in general, simply as rational” or “universal” in a cosmic sense. “As universal” is unclear and leans to the second; whatever is chosen must also work for καθολικὴν καὶ πολιτικήν below.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not, however, rational soul as such” and below “rational soul as such, and as civic”. The word is set against καθό (“in so far as”), so the contrast is between rational soul valued simply as rational soul and rational soul valued in one respect. The note gives “universal”.

check.greek: ἢ κατὰ ψιλὸν τὸ πλῆθος ἀνδραπόδων κεκτῆσθαι
check.note: ψιλόν goes with the owning: “or merely in respect of owning a quantity of slaves”. “In the bare sense” suggests the sense of a word, which is not the point, and “great” is added to πλῆθος.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “or merely in terms of owning a great number of slaves”, with “merely” on the owning and no talk of a sense. “Great” stays, because πλῆθος is not a neutral “number” but a multitude, and “a number of slaves” in English would mean only several.

check.note: ἐπιστρέφεται with the genitive is “pays attention to, cares about”. “Turns to look at” renders the root picture, not the meaning in use.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “no longer pays attention to any of the other things”. The note keeps the literal “turns toward”.

check.greek: λογικῶς καὶ κοινωνικῶς ἔχουσαν καὶ κινουμένην διασῴζει
check.note: “Keep their own soul being” is not clear English. ἔχουσαν with adverbs is “in a rational and social condition”, and διασῴζει is “keep safe, preserve”, which is stronger than “keep”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “preserves their own soul rational and social in its condition and its movement”.

check.note: The dative can be masculine or neuter. With συνεργεῖ (“works together with”) a person is the more natural reading; the English had chosen the neuter.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “works together with whoever is of the same kind”. The form allows either gender, and working together is most plainly said of a person; the note gives the neuter.

check.note: μέτριος of people is “moderate, decent, of a better sort”. “Measured” in today’s English describes a careful way of speaking or acting; the scale here is of people’s worth.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “people of a slightly better sort”. A new note gives the literal “a little more moderate”.

check.note: ἐντρεχής is “practised, adept, skilful”. “Sharp” suggests quick intelligence, a different quality; the pair is craft skill and other accomplishments.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “adept in some other way”. “Adept” is used instead of “accomplished” so that it is not confused with the “more refined” people, whose Greek word also means accomplished.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft began a new sentence here and dropped δέ, so the turn from what this person ignores to what they guard was lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now runs on as one sentence, “no longer pays attention to any of the other things, but before everything else preserves their own soul”.

passages.greek: Ἕκαστον πρός τι γέγονεν, ἵππος, ἄμπελος. τί θαυμάζεις; καὶ ὁ Ἥλιος ἐρεῖ· πρός τι ἔργου γέγονα, καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ θεοί. σὺ οὖν πρὸς τί; τὸ ἥδεσθαι; ἴδε εἰ ἀνέχεται ἡ ἔννοια.
passages.english: Each thing has come to be for something: a horse, a vine. Why are you surprised? Even the Sun will say, “I have come to be for some work,” and so will the other gods. So what are you for? For pleasure? See whether the idea holds up.

notes.note: Can be “why are you surprised?” or “what are you marvelling at?”. The English takes the first, as a reply to an imagined doubt about the opening claim.
notes.other_reading: What are you wondering at?

notes.note: The Greek word is both the ordinary word for the sun and the name of the sun as a god, Helios. “The Sun” with a capital keeps both, and “the other gods” shows that a god is meant.
notes.other_reading: Even Helios will say

notes.note: The Greek as given is unusual: literally “for something of work”, an indefinite with a genitive, read here as “for some piece of work, some task”. Other editions may print ἔργον, plain “for some work” (from memory, unchecked); the sense is the same either way.
notes.other_reading: for a certain task

notes.note: Literally “the being pleased”, the verb used as a noun. The preposition “for” is carried over from the question before.
notes.other_reading: To enjoy yourself?

notes.note: The verb is “bears up, holds out, puts up with”; ἔννοια is “thought, notion, understanding”. The English takes it as the idea just proposed, that you came to be for pleasure, and asks whether it stands. It can also be read with the understanding as the one that bears: whether your own notion of what you are will put up with that answer.
notes.other_reading: See whether your understanding will put up with that.

check.note: ἡ ἔννοια can be the thought just proposed (“see whether the idea holds up”) or your own understanding (“see whether your understanding puts up with it”). “See whether the thought can bear it” leaves the reader unable to tell which thought bears what, and “can” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “See whether the idea holds up.” The Greek has no object for the verb, so the reading that needs nothing supplied is taken, and “can” is gone. The note gives the other reading, in which the understanding is what does the bearing.

check.note: The text has ἔργου where ἔργον might be expected (from memory). Read either way the sense is “for some work”, so the English is unaffected.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, since “for some work” fits either form. The note now says that other editions may print ἔργον, from memory and unchecked.

passages.greek: Σίκυος πικρός; ἄφες. βάτοι ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ; ἔκκλινον. ἀρκεῖ, μὴ προσεπείπῃς· τί δὲ καὶ ἐγένετο ταῦτα ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ; ἐπεὶ καταγελασθήσῃ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπου φυσιολόγου, ὡς ἂν καὶ ὑπὸ τέκτονος καὶ σκυτέως γελασθείης καταγινώσκων ὅτι ἐν τῷ ἐργαστηρίῳ ξέσματα καὶ περιτμήματα τῶν κατασκευαζομένων ὁρᾷς. καίτοι ἐκεῖνοί γε ἔχουσι ποῦ αὐτὰ ῥίψωσιν, ἡ δὲ τῶν ὅλων φύσις ἔξω οὐδὲν ἔχει, ἀλλὰ τὸ θαυμαστὸν τῆς τέχνης ταύτης ἐστὶν ὅτι περιορίσασα ἑαυτὴν πᾶν τὸ ἔνδον διαφθείρεσθαι καὶ γηράσκειν καὶ ἄχρηστον εἶναι δοκοῦν εἰς ἑαυτὴν μεταβάλλει, καὶ ὅτι πάλιν ἄλλα νεαρὰ ἐκ τούτων αὐτῶν ποιεῖ, ἵνα μήτε οὐσίας ἔξωθεν χρῄζῃ μήτε ὅπου ἐκβάλῃ τὰ σαπρότερα προσδέηται. ἀρκεῖται οὖν καὶ χώρᾳ τῇ ἑαυτῆς καὶ ὕλῃ τῇ ἑαυτῆς καὶ τέχνῃ τῇ ἰδίᾳ.
passages.english: A bitter cucumber? Leave it. Brambles in the path? Turn aside. That is enough. Do not go on to say, “And why did these things come to be in the universe at all?” Because you will be laughed at by a person who studies nature, just as you would be laughed at by a carpenter and a shoemaker if you blamed them because you see, in the workshop, shavings and trimmings from the things being made. And yet they, at least, have somewhere to throw these, whereas the nature of the whole has nothing outside it. But the wonderful thing about this craft is that nature, having drawn a boundary around itself, changes into itself everything inside that seems to be decaying and growing old and to be useless, and that it makes other, fresh things again out of these very things, so that it neither needs substance from outside nor has any further need of a place to throw out what is too rotten. So its own space is enough for it, and its own material, and its own craft.

notes.note: “Let go of it, leave it”: a physical instruction, like “turn aside” in the next line. It can mean dropping the cucumber, throwing it away or simply leaving it alone.
notes.other_reading: Throw it away.

notes.note: ἀρκεῖ (“it is enough”) returns at the end as ἀρκεῖται (“is content with, finds enough in”), so “enough” is used in both places. The verb after it is “say in addition”.
notes.other_reading: That will do; do not add,

notes.note: A φυσιολόγος is one who gives an account of nature, a natural philosopher. The English reads “a person who studies nature” to stay plain.
notes.other_reading: by a natural philosopher

notes.note: “Condemning, finding fault”. The Greek gives no object; the English supplies “them”, the craftsmen, though it could be the workshop or the craft that is blamed.
notes.other_reading: if you found fault because you see

notes.note: The first word is what is scraped or planed off, the carpenter’s waste; the second is what is cut away round the edge, the shoemaker’s.
notes.other_reading: scrapings and offcuts

notes.note: Either “has nothing outside itself”, there being nothing beyond it, or “has no outside place” to throw things. The two come to much the same; the English leans to the first.
notes.other_reading: has no outside at all

notes.note: Literally “having marked a boundary round itself”, that is, having confined itself to itself. “Nature” and “craft” are both feminine in Greek, so the form alone does not say which does this; the run of the sentence and the last line, where nature is content with its own craft, show that nature is meant, and the English names it.
notes.other_reading: having limited itself to itself

notes.note: οὐσία here is the stuff things are made of. The English reads “substance” to keep it apart from ὕλῃ (“material”) in the last sentence, though the two seem to mean the same thing here.
notes.other_reading: needs no matter from outside

notes.note: A comparative: “the more rotten things”, or “the things that are too far gone”. The English takes the second.
notes.other_reading: the more rotten parts

check.note: ἄφες is a physical instruction parallel to “turn aside”. “Let it go” in today’s English means “stop minding it”, which moves the moral into the first line.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Leave it.” The verb is “let go of, leave”, an act like turning aside; “throw it away” is kept in the note because Marcus uses a different verb for throwing later in the passage.

check.greek: τὸ θαυμαστὸν τῆς τέχνης ταύτης ἐστὶν ὅτι περιορίσασα ἑαυτὴν
check.note: In the Greek, nature is the one that bounds itself and transforms things. In the English “it” reads as “this craft”, so the craft appears to draw a boundary around itself.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the wonderful thing about this craft is that nature, having drawn a boundary around itself, changes into itself”. Nature is named as the one acting, which the run of the sentence requires, while “this craft” is kept because the Greek says “this”, not “nature’s”. “Its own” before “boundary” is dropped, since the Greek has only “itself”.

check.note: The comparative is dropped: “what is more decayed”, “the rather rotten parts”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “what is too rotten”, which gives the comparative. “Rotten” is kept instead of “decayed” so that this word stays apart from “decaying”, which renders a different Greek verb earlier in the sentence.

passages.greek: Φέρει καρπὸν καὶ ἄνθρωπος καὶ θεὸς καὶ ὁ κόσμος· ἐν ταῖς οἰκείαις ὥραις ἕκαστα φέρει. εἰ δὲ ἡ συνήθεια κυρίως τέτριφεν ἐπὶ ἀμπέλου καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων, οὐδὲν τοῦτο. ὁ λόγος δὲ καὶ κοινὸν καὶ ἴδιον καρπὸν ἔχει καὶ γίνεται ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοιαῦθ’ ἕτερα, ὁποῖόν τι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος.
passages.english: A human being bears fruit, and so does god, and so does the universe; each bears it in its own seasons. But if usage has made the phrase well worn, in its strict sense, for the vine and things like it, that makes no difference. And reason has fruit, both shared and its own, and from it come other things of much the same kind as reason itself.

notes.note: No article: “god” or “a god”. The English reads “god” with a small letter and no article.
notes.other_reading: and so does a god

notes.note: The verb is the one for rubbing a thing smooth by use, and of words it means making them well worn, current. The Greek gives it no object; the English supplies “the phrase”, that is, “bear fruit”. κυρίως is taken as “in the proper, strict sense”; it can also mean “chiefly”.
notes.other_reading: But if usage has chiefly worn the phrase in on the vine and things like it

notes.note: Literally “this is nothing”.
notes.other_reading: that is nothing

notes.note: λόγος is “reason” but also “speech, word, account”. The English takes “reason”, as the thing that bears fruit in a human being; the sentence may also glance at “speech” after the remark on usage.
notes.other_reading: And speech has fruit

notes.note: “Fruit both common and private”: fruit shared with everyone and fruit that belongs to reason itself. The Greek does not say more.
notes.other_reading: fruit both for all in common and for itself

notes.greek: τοιαῦθ’ ἕτερα, ὁποῖόν τι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος
notes.note: “Other things of some such kind as reason itself is”: what reason produces is like reason, as fruit is like the plant. The small word τι loosens the likeness a little, which “much the same” gives.
notes.other_reading: and what grows from it is more of the same sort of thing as reason itself

check.greek: εἰ δὲ ἡ συνήθεια κυρίως τέτριφεν ἐπὶ ἀμπέλου καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων
check.note: τέτριφεν is “has made habitual by use”, applied to the vine, and κυρίως says this is where the word has its proper sense. “Worn the phrase down to its strict sense” turns this into erosion and makes the strict sense a result; δέ (“but”) is also dropped.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “But if usage has made the phrase well worn, in its strict sense, for the vine and things like it”. “But” is restored and the strict sense is no longer a result of the wearing. “Well worn” is used instead of “kept”, because the verb is about a word made familiar by rubbing, not about a word reserved.

check.greek: ὁ λόγος δὲ καὶ κοινὸν καὶ ἴδιον καρπὸν ἔχει
check.note: The first καί is the partner of the second (“both shared and its own”), which the English also translates as “both”. So καί is used twice and “too” has nothing to stand on.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And reason has fruit, both shared and its own”. “Too” is gone, and “And” gives δέ.

check.note: “Common” beside “fruit” reads today as “ordinary”. The pair is shared with all against private to itself.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “both shared and its own”.

check.note: One Greek word (οἰκείαις) is given twice, as “own” and “proper”, and “proper” in this sense is dated.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in its own seasons”.

check.greek: ὁποῖόν τι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ λόγος
check.note: τι softens the likeness: “of much the same kind”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “of much the same kind as reason itself”.

passages.greek: Δεῖ κατὰ λέξιν παρακολουθεῖν τοῖς λεγομένοις καὶ καθ’ ἑκάστην ὁρμὴν τοῖς γινομένοις, καὶ ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ ἑτέρου εὐθὺς ὁρᾶν ἐπὶ τίνα σκοπὸν ἡ ἀναφορά, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ ἑτέρου παραφυλάσσειν τί τὸ σημαινόμενον.
passages.english: One must follow what is said word by word, and what is done impulse by impulse; and in the latter case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the former watch closely for what is meant.

notes.note: “Word by word” or “phrase by phrase”: λέξις is a single expression. It is matched by “at each impulse” for actions; ὁρμή, “impulse”, is the Stoic term for the movement of the mind toward doing something.
notes.other_reading: follow what is said expression by expression

notes.note: Literally “the things that happen” or “come about”. Paired with “impulse” and set against “what is said”, it is taken as “what is done”.
notes.other_reading: and what happens, at each impulse

notes.note: The Greek says only “in the one case, in the other”, without saying which is which. The sense shows that the order is crossed: the aim belongs to what is done, and what is meant belongs to what is said. The English says “latter” and “former” so that a reader does not pair them the wrong way.
notes.other_reading: and in the one case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the other watch closely for what is meant

notes.note: “The reference”: what the action is referred to as its goal. There is no verb; the English supplies “is directed”.
notes.other_reading: to what target the reference is

check.greek: ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ ἑτέρου εὐθὺς ὁρᾶν ἐπὶ τίνα σκοπὸν ἡ ἀναφορά, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ ἑτέρου παραφυλάσσειν τί τὸ σημαινόμενον
check.note: The Greek says “in the one, in the other” without saying which is which, and the sense shows the order is crossed: the aim belongs to actions, what is signified to words. In English “the one, the other” is normally read as former and latter, which gives the reverse of the sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in the latter case see at once what aim it is directed at, and in the former watch closely for what is meant”. The order of the Greek is kept and nothing is named that the Greek does not name; the note records that the Greek has only “the one” and “the other”.

check.note: γινόμενα is “what happens, what is going on”; “what is done” narrows it to actions. With “at each impulse” the narrowing is probably right, but it is a choice.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “what is done”. The word is tied to “at each impulse”, and an impulse in the Stoic sense is a movement toward acting, so what comes about impulse by impulse is action. The note gives “what happens”.

passages.greek: Πρῶτον αἱ τραγῳδίαι παρήχθησαν ὑπομνηστικαὶ τῶν συμβαινόντων καὶ ὅτι ταῦτα οὕτως πέφυκε γίνεσθαι καὶ ὅτι, οἷς ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς ψυχαγωγεῖσθε, τούτοις μὴ ἄχθεσθε ἐπὶ τῆς μείζονος σκηνῆς· ὁρᾶτε γὰρ ὅτι οὕτως δεῖ ταῦτα περαίνεσθαι καὶ ὅτι φέρουσιν αὐτὰ καὶ οἱ κεκραγότες· ʽἰὼ Κιθαιρών.ʼ καὶ λέγεται δέ τινα ὑπὸ τῶν τὰ δράματα ποιούντων χρησίμως· οἷόν ἐστιν ἐκεῖνο μάλιστα· εἰ δ’ ἠμελήθην ἐκ θεῶν καὶ παῖδ’ ἐμώ, ἔχει λόγον καὶ τοῦτο· καὶ πάλιν· τοῖς πράγμασιν γὰρ οὐχὶ θυμοῦσθαι· καί· βίον θερίζειν ὥστε κάρπιμον στάχυν· καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα. μετὰ δὲ τὴν τραγῳδίαν ἡ ἀρχαία κωμῳδία παρήχθη, παιδαγωγικὴν παρρησίαν ἔχουσα καὶ τῆς ἀτυφίας οὐκ ἀχρήστως δι’ αὐτῆς τῆς εὐθυρρημοσύνης ὑπομιμνῄσκουσα· πρὸς οἷόν τι καὶ Διογένης ταυτὶ παρελάμβανε. μετὰ ταύτην ἡ μέση κωμῳδία καὶ λοιπὸν ἡ νέα πρὸς τί ποτε παρείληπται, ἣ κατ’ ὀλίγον ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκ μιμήσεως φιλοτεχνίαν ὑπερρύη, ἐπίστησον. ὅτι μὲν γὰρ λέγεται καὶ ὑπὸ τούτων τινὰ χρήσιμα οὐκ ἀγνοεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἡ ὅλη ἐπιβολὴ τῆς τοιαύτης ποιήσεως καὶ δραματουργίας πρὸς τίνα ποτὲ σκοπὸν ἀπέβλεψεν;
passages.english: First, tragedies were brought on as reminders of the things that happen, and that it is in the nature of these things to happen this way, and that what charms you on the stage should not weigh on you on the larger stage. For you see that these things have to be carried through this way, and that even those who cry out “O Cithaeron!” bear them. And some things are said usefully by those who write the plays. This above all, for example: “But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.” And again: “For one should not be angry with events.” And: “To reap life like a fruitful ear of grain.” And everything of that kind. After tragedy, the Old Comedy was brought on. It had a tutor’s frankness and, by its very plainness of speech, reminded people, not uselessly, of freedom from conceit. It was for some such purpose that Diogenes too took these things up. As for the Middle Comedy after it, and lastly the New, which little by little slipped down into cleverness at imitation, consider just what it has been taken up for. For it is not unknown that some useful things are said by these writers too; but the whole undertaking of this kind of poetry and play-making, just what aim did it look to?

notes.note: “Were brought forward, introduced”; the verb is also the ordinary one for bringing something on stage. “Brought on” is used here and for the Old Comedy, where the verb is repeated. “First” could also be read as “at first, originally”.
notes.other_reading: Tragedies were first introduced as reminders

notes.note: The Greek slips into a direct command to an audience in the plural: “do not be weighed down by these things”. The English turns it into “should not weigh on you” so that the sentence runs on. ψυχαγωγεῖσθε before it is literally “you have your souls led”, said of being entertained.
notes.other_reading: and that: “what entertains you on the stage, do not be vexed by on the larger stage”

notes.note: The form can be “you see” or the command “see”. With “for” it is taken as a statement.
notes.other_reading: For see that these things have to be carried through this way

notes.note: “To be carried through, completed”; the word suits both a plot and events in life. “To their end” is not added, since in English it would be heard as dying.
notes.other_reading: that this is how these things must be accomplished

notes.note: The cry of Oedipus in Sophocles’ Oedipus the King, addressed to Mount Cithaeron, where he was left to die as a baby (from memory, unchecked). ἰώ is a cry of grief.
notes.other_reading: “Alas, Cithaeron!”

notes.note: “This too has a reason”, or “this too makes sense”. The line and the two that follow are verse quotations, all three thought to be from lost plays of Euripides (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: this too is reasonable

notes.note: A dual: “my two children”. The form does not say whether they are sons.
notes.other_reading: I and my two sons

notes.note: As quoted, the line is a bare infinitive, “for not to be angry with things”, and stops before the word that governs it. The full verse is thought to end with a word for “one must” (from memory, unchecked), so “one should” in the English is supplied. πράγματα is “things, affairs, circumstances”.
notes.other_reading: “For to be angry with things is not ...”

notes.note: Again an infinitive cut loose from its sentence; in the original it probably said that life must be reaped. ὥστε is the poetic “like”. κάρπιμον is “bearing fruit”.
notes.other_reading: “that life is harvested like a ripe ear of grain”

notes.note: παρρησία is saying everything openly: frankness, outspokenness. The adjective is from παιδαγωγός, the attendant who minded a boy and corrected his behaviour, so the sense is frankness that disciplines and teaches.
notes.other_reading: an educating outspokenness

notes.note: “Absence of τῦφος”, the smoke of vanity and self-importance: so modesty, freedom from conceit. The comedy is said to remind people of this quality.
notes.other_reading: reminding people of modesty

notes.greek: πρὸς οἷόν τι καὶ Διογένης ταυτὶ παρελάμβανε
notes.note: Diogenes is the Cynic philosopher, known for blunt speech. “These things” is vague: probably this manner of plain speaking, possibly actual lines or devices of comedy. The verb is the same one used just after of comedy being “taken up”, so “took up” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: With some such end in view Diogenes too adopted this sort of thing

notes.greek: μετὰ ταύτην ἡ μέση κωμῳδία καὶ λοιπὸν ἡ νέα πρὸς τί ποτε παρείληπται
notes.note: “After it” belongs to the Middle Comedy, which came after the Old, as “after tragedy” does above. The verb is singular and treats the Middle and the New as one thing. ποτε sharpens the question, here and in the last sentence; “just what” gives it in both places.
notes.other_reading: After this, consider whatever the Middle Comedy, and lastly the New, has been taken up for

notes.greek: ἣ κατ’ ὀλίγον ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκ μιμήσεως φιλοτεχνίαν ὑπερρύη
notes.note: The verb is “slid, sank gradually”. φιλοτεχνία is love of craft, and so ingenuity or clever workmanship; “from imitation” says that the cleverness lies in lifelike representation. “Which” most naturally refers to the New Comedy, the nearest noun, but can be read of this later comedy as a whole.
notes.other_reading: comedy which by degrees sank into a love of craft in mimicry

notes.note: ἐπιβολή is a setting oneself to something: design, attempt, undertaking. σκοπός at the end is a mark aimed at; the English reads “aim”.
notes.other_reading: the whole design of this kind of poetry and play-making

check.note: As given, the quotation is a bare infinitive with no governing word, and “one should” supplies it. From memory the verse ends with a word for “one must”, but that word is not in the text supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “For one should not be angry with events”, since a bare “for not to be angry” cannot be read as English, and the note now says outright that “one should” is supplied and that the fuller verse is recalled from memory, unchecked.

check.note: μετὰ ταύτην is “after it”, after the Old Comedy, and belongs to the Middle Comedy’s coming, parallel to “after tragedy” above. Placed before “consider” it reads as an instruction about the order of thinking.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “As for the Middle Comedy after it, and lastly the New, ... consider just what it has been taken up for”, so that “after it” belongs to the Middle Comedy.

check.greek: καὶ λοιπὸν ἡ νέα πρὸς τί ποτε παρείληπται, ἣ
check.note: The relative ἥ has no noun repeated in the Greek. It is nearest to the New Comedy but can be read of this later comedy as a whole; the English repeated “the New” and so settled the question in the text.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “the New” is no longer repeated, and the English reads “and lastly the New, which little by little slipped down”. The clause stands next to “the New” because that is the nearest noun in the Greek too, and the note gives the wider reading.

check.note: “A love of craft in imitation” is hard to follow as English. φιλοτεχνία is ingenuity or showy workmanship, and ἐκ μιμήσεως says it comes from, or consists in, imitation.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “slipped down into cleverness at imitation”. “Mere” is not added, because the Greek has no word for it; the fall is already in the verb. The note gives the literal “love of craft”.

check.note: ποτε is dropped here, though the same particle is kept as “ever” in the last sentence. The perfect is “has been taken up”, against the past tenses used of tragedy and the Old Comedy.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “consider just what it has been taken up for”, with the perfect tense. The last sentence now reads “just what aim did it look to?”, so one English phrase answers the one Greek particle in both places.

check.note: The dual is “my two children”; sons or not is not said in the words given.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “my two children”. A note gives “my two sons”.

check.note: παρρησία here is outspokenness, saying things straight, as the next clause shows. “Freedom of speech” today means a civil right; “a tutor’s” is acceptable for the adjective.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a tutor’s frankness”. “Tutor” is kept instead of “schoolmaster”, because the Greek word names the attendant who minded and corrected one boy, not the teacher of a class.

check.note: Found while settling: the quoted verse begins with δέ (“but”), which the draft left out, though it kept the “for” at the head of the next quotation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.”

passages.greek: ʽἘρᾷ μὲν ὄμβρου γαῖα, ἐρᾷ δὲ ὁ σεμνὸς αἰθήρ,ʼ ἐρᾷ δὲ ὁ κόσμος ποιῆσαι ὃ ἂν μέλλῃ γίνεσθαι. λέγω οὖν τῷ κόσμῳ ὅτι σοὶ συνερῶ. μήτι δὲ οὕτω κἀκεῖνο λέγεται, ὅτι· φιλεῖ τοῦτο γίνεσθαι;
passages.english: “The earth loves the rain, and the holy sky loves,” and the universe loves to bring about whatever is to come. So I say to the universe: “I love along with you.” And is that, too, perhaps said in this sense: “this loves to happen”?

notes.note: The quoted line of verse stops here without saying what the sky loves. The English leaves it just as bare.
notes.other_reading: and the holy sky loves it too

notes.note: αἰθήρ is the bright upper air or heaven; σεμνός is “revered”, “holy”, “majestic”.
notes.other_reading: the majestic heaven

notes.note: The poet’s words end before this; from here Marcus speaks, reusing the poet’s verb. It is the verb of being in love and of strong desire. “Loves” is used for it throughout so that the last sentence can be heard.
notes.other_reading: and the universe longs to bring about

notes.note: The word means both the universe and its order. 'Universe' is used here and in 4.23.
notes.other_reading: the world

notes.note: The verb can mean simply “is about to” or “is destined to”. The plain future sense is translated.
notes.other_reading: whatever is destined to happen

notes.note: One compound verb, “I love together with you”; no object is given, so what is loved is left to the context.
notes.other_reading: I long along with you

notes.note: The particle μήτι usually opens a question expecting “no” (as in 6.43), but it can also float a tentative suggestion. It is taken as a suggestion here, since the sentence completes the thought.
notes.other_reading: Surely that, too, is not said in this sense: “this loves to happen”?

notes.note: An everyday Greek idiom: “loves to happen” means “tends to happen, usually happens”. The literal “loves” is kept because Marcus’s point depends on hearing the love in it. It is a different Greek verb from the “loves” of the lines above.
notes.other_reading: This tends to happen

check.note: φιλεῖ with an infinitive is the everyday Greek idiom for 'this tends to happen, this usually happens'. Marcus's point is that the ordinary idiom literally says 'loves'; the English gives only the literal half, and since 'this loves to happen' is not an English saying, the reader cannot see that a common phrase is being reread.
check.decided: Kept the literal “loves” and explained the idiom in a note; the English cannot carry both senses in the words alone.
